Regarding "Jewels, etc. (the lower section of the explanation of the Wheel of Dharma further explains): The *Sutra on Non-retrogression through Relying on Spiritual Friends* states that one makes offerings [to them] up until planting the roots of all virtues (*kuśalamūla*).
The *Śāstra* states that the root of wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) is the foundation of all virtues.

Some say that the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās* are called "all virtues" and constitute the root. The *Śāstra* states that one relies on the physical body (*rūpakāya*) through the activities of body and mind.
Because they have focused their ears, there is no practice for Bodhisattvas that surpasses [the cultivation of] body and mind.
Now, by offering the deeds of this sublime form-body (*rūpakāya*) to all Buddhas, they deeply plant the roots of virtue; they grasp their own body and mind, severing all doubts, and do not regress.

As it is said in the sutras, they are constantly praised as those who have reached the ultimate. This is because when Bodhisattvas enter the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), they sever the doubts regarding both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).

The two types of doubt—those regarding afflictions (*kleśa*) and those regarding the knowable (*jñeya*)—are exhausted. Doubt regarding the knowable is an obstacle to the two principles within the conventional truth;

doubt regarding afflictions is an obstacle to the principle of emptiness. Furthermore, doubt regarding the knowable refers to the delusions of *sāṃyojanīya-avidyā* (dust-like ignorance), while doubt regarding afflictions refers to the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*vitarka*).

When combined, these constitute the two obstacles (*dvaya-āvaraṇa*); when separated, they are the three delusions. Regarding the principles of phenomena and reality, this alone is what is constantly praised by all Buddhas.
"Thus it is attained; thus it is also attained. Regarding the matter of the non-retrogression of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the *Śāstra* asks:

"For what kinds of matters does one preach the Dharma so as to enter those respective dharmas and attain non-retrogression? As the Sūtra says, "One cultivates the body with loving-kindness (*maitrī*)," while the *Śāstra* says, "One cultivates the body and mind through great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-karuṇā*).

The Sūtra omits mention of the mind and speech, whereas the *Śāstra* omits mention of the speech; however, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (the *Zhengfahua jing*) possesses all three karmas (*trikarma*).
Although the phrasing may appear incomplete, the underlying meaning is fully contained; it is merely a matter of mutual concealment and revelation. This is the basis for this interpretation:
because Bodhisattvas engage in various activities—preaching the Dharma to others externally while internally entering into the realization of all phenomena—they cite the sutras as an explanation.

Because they cultivate their body and mind through great compassion, they permeate their bodies with loving-kindness and compassion, manifesting bodies within the five realms of existence to extract suffering and bestow happiness. This is "compassion."

With compassion perfuming the mouth, one speaks various dharmas to extract suffering and bestow happiness; with compassion perfuming the mind, one employs various skillful means to extract suffering and bestow happiness.
This reveals the practice of the two benefits: first, for self-benefit, one internally realizes all dharmas; second, for the benefit of others, one externally explains them.
Regarding "entering the realm of omniscience as it truly is" and "the non-retrogressive," these terms should be reversed [in order].
Entering the realm of reality as it is—the non-retrogression of omniscience—is distinct from the subsequent eighth stage, which is the wisdom of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
Here, "attaining omniscience" is termed "entering," referring to the person who attains it; thus, both the object and the wisdom are what is entered.
Regarding the non-retrogression based on the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena, as the sutra states: "Thoroughly penetrating the Great..."
The emptiness of both the innate and conceptualized dualities of self, which are known through wisdom, is called the "emptiness of self" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

The emptiness of both the innate and conceptualized dualities of phenomena, which are known through wisdom, is called the "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*). The seventh consciousness possesses both innate and conceptualized dualistic attachments to self and phenomena, yet it lacks conceptual attachments to phenomena or self.
The sixth consciousness possesses both conceptualized and innate dualistic attachments to phenomena and self. [The seventh] and the wondrous...
When the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (discriminative wisdom) is associated with it, one abandons the dualistic grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) that is conceptual;

when it induces the seventh consciousness to become associated with the *samatājñāna* (wisdom of equality), one abandons the innate dualistic grasping at a self and phenomena belonging to the seventh consciousness, and only then realizes the fruit of the wisdom of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā-jñāna*).

This truth revealed by the gateway [of these wisdoms] is as extensively explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Now, I maintain that both the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of self (*ātman-śūnyatā*) are seen within the Middle Way.
The Way is fundamentally different from the contemplation of the Separate Teaching; its nine entrances correspond to the realm of reality (*yathābhūta*).
Because one does not regress and reaches the other shore as described in the sutras, one exhausts the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which is termed "reaching the other shore."

[Commentary]: Regarding "one should perform what is to be performed" up to "a multitude of hundreds of thousands," the *Śāstra* states: "One should perform what is to be performed and abide in support without falling back.
The commentary omits the two characters "abiding in support" (*zhùchí*). The Sūtra contains two phrases: "His name is widely heard" up to "because of sentient beings.

Because he is able to support the Buddha-dharma and cause the Dharma not to perish, sentient beings hear his name, believe and incline toward it, practice and study it, and are thus able to deliver countless [beings].
Because [he benefits] hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, he is named "One Who Has Accomplished What Was to Be Done. That which a Bodhisattva ought to do is to benefit sentient beings.

[Commentary: The *Śāstra* states: "Second, regarding the gate of the undertaking of activities (*kṛtya-samādāna-mukha*)," it asks what pure stages (*viśuddha-bhūmi*) the various Bodhisattvas abide in, and so forth.
Regarding this, the *Śāstra* provides two interpretations. As for the gate of the undertaking of activities, it refers to the undertaking of all meritorious deeds (*guṇa-kṛtya*).
The first section of the commentary states: "It is shown in which purified grounds the various bodhisattvas abide, by what means, and within what spheres they should perform their duties.
This serves as the general heading. Regarding the explanation of the purity of the grounds (*bhūmi-viśuddhi*) in the following thirteen phrases, there should be a threefold division:
[1] non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; [2] ...; and [3] ... . (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly after the first point.)
Regarding the phrases: in which purified stage does one abide? Next, there are ten phrases concerning what causes; what are the subsequent two phrases?

They concern the sphere within which one should perform what is to be done. Therefore, in the summary and explanation, only the first two phrases of the heading are explained, while the third—concerning the sphere within which one should perform what is to be done—is not. As for "the purification of the stage," there are eight [points].
Regarding the phrase "Because from the fourth bhūmi upward, the practice of signlessness is tranquil and pure":

the commentary explains that in the eighth bhūmi, the practice of signlessness is effortless (*anābhoga*) and is not moved by the effortful practice of signs. Although one can achieve signlessness in the seventh bhūmi, it still involves effort;
in the eighth bhūmi, signlessness is both signless and effortless. Regarding the ninth bhūmi, "tranquil" (*śānta*): *śānti* means cessation.
"Quiescence" (*śānti*) is silence; it is the *dharmakāya*. The ninth stage is unmoved by effortful activity and is pure;

it is not defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*). This is the tenth stage. Because the principle of signlessness (*animitta*) is termed "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment," the final three stages are all spontaneously quiescent in signless practice, free from obstructions and pure; they are called "non-retrogression."

Because it does not regress due to the various defilements or signs, this understanding—carrying with it the path of teaching and the path of realization of the Distinct Teaching (*vyatibheda-śāsana*) according to the *Ratnakaranda-sūtra*—manifests the three contemplations of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), and the mind tends toward liberation.

If one were to refer to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), one should say "the first dwelling" (*prathama-vihāra*). The Master of the Treatise, relying on the Distinct Teaching, has provided this explanation; this should be reflected upon (etc.). Second.
Regarding the skillful means (*upāya*) by which [this is accomplished], there are four kinds: first, the skillful means of grasping the sublime Dharma (*saddharma*).

This consists of upholding the sublime Dharma and teaching it to others through the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Regarding this "grasping," the *Tri-svabhāva-śāstra* states: "As for upholding the sublime Dharma, the Sūtra says that all obtain *dhāraṇī*.
By obtaining *śruta-dhāraṇī* (retention of what is heard), one upholds the sublime Dharma so as not to abandon it. As for "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*), it means to sustain oneself.
Because one maintains it within the mind without forgetting, it is called "retention" (*dhāraṇī*). The *Śāstra* says: "By means of the eloquence of joyful speech.
The *Śāstra* says: "To speak for others. The *Sūtra* says: "To turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma," meaning to speak this irreversible wheel for the sake of others (the three preceding phrases).
Regarding the second [topic], the *Śāstra* states: "The skillful means of embracing a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), because one acts as one ought by relying upon a spiritual friend."
Regarding "one who acts": this subsumes three phrases from the Sūtra. "Relying upon a spiritual friend" corresponds to the Sūtra’s statement:
"making offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. "Doing what ought to be done" corresponds to the Sūtra’s statement: "planting the roots of merit in the presence of all Buddhas.
Here, "roots of merit" refers to the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), as these are precisely what ought to be done. For this reason, the Sūtra says: "He is constantly attended by all Buddhas."

[The above three phrases] are a praise. Regarding the third [topic], the skillful means of gathering sentient beings: because one does not abandon sentient beings, this is summarized in one phrase of the sūtra.

Because one cultivates the body with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and because one perfumes both body and mind with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one is able not to abandon any sentient being and can constantly rescue and deliver them.
Regarding the fourth, the skillful means of wisdom for gathering [beings]: it is through teaching and transforming sentient beings that one...
Because one enters that wisdom, this encompasses the three phrases of the sutra: "skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom, penetrating great wisdom, and reaching the other shore.

This is because by means of one's own three kinds of wisdom, one can cause sentient beings to grasp these three wisdoms. The first wisdom is the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), which is the wisdom for one's own benefit (*svārtha-jñāna*).
Now, it is said that this is common to all. The second wisdom is the wisdom of phenomena (*vastu-jñāna*), which is the wisdom for the benefit of others (*parārtha-jñāna*). Now...
That is to say, the knowledge of the ultimate shore (*pāramitājñāna*) which follows the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) is the true nature of the knowledge of reality.

Now, regarding the "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*) (the three preceding phrases), the treatise explains only the first two phrases of the initial heading and does not explain what kind of objective realm it constitutes or what should be done therein.
Therefore, what is the meaning of this inclusion of the three phrases in the sutra: "His name is widely renowned throughout immeasurable worlds"?
The phrase "equalizing the sphere" means that, as the sūtra states, one is able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings; this is what ought to be done.

Because the bodhisattva is endowed with the three types of knowledge (*jñāna*), etc., the fame of his renown spreads throughout the ten directions, and he delivers hundreds of thousands of sentient beings—this is precisely what the bodhisattva ought to do (the two preceding phrases).
In the second section of the treatise, following the phrase "furthermore," there is also the inclusion of [other qualities], etc.
Regarding the section on "Matters" (*vastu-mukha*), it is not mentioned in the present sutra; therefore, it is not employed in the commentary (and so forth).

Among the listing of the Bodhisattvas' names, they are briefly categorized into four pairs: first, the pair of those already perfected and those yet to be perfected, such as Mañjuśrī who is already perfected and Śrī-ghana (Avalokiteśvara) and others who are yet to be perfected;
second, the pair of householders and renunciants, such as Maitreya who is a renunciant and Bhadra who is a householder; third, this... [text fragment].
Regarding the other realms: Maitreya is the host here in this realm of Śrāvastī, while Avalokiteśvara is the guest in that other realm.
Regarding the four masters and guests: the Teacher Bhadrapāla is the host in the city of Rājagṛha, while Ratnakūṭa is the guest among the people of Vaiśālī.
Someone asks: "Why is Mañjuśrī listed first among these eighteen individuals? The answer is: because of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and [his disciple] Prabhāketu.
Regarding the statement that Śākyamuni preached this sutra because Mañjuśrī had already performed the work of opening the teaching, he is listed first.

Furthermore, because Mañjuśrī resolved Maitreya’s doubts and prompted the Buddha to arise and preach the sutra once he had attained meditative concentration, he is listed first. The Master of Hexi said:

"Mañjuśrī is a Great Being who travels through all directions; in the assemblies throughout the ten directions, he frequently serves as the starting point for the development of the teaching, and thus he is specifically mentioned here."

Furthermore, it is said that Mañjuśrī embodies the Buddhas of the three periods of time: the past Buddha Dragon-Seed Supreme Honored King (Nāgavarṇa-rāja), the present Buddha Mani-Jewel Accumulation (Maṇiratna-akṣaya), and the future Buddha who succeeds to the position [of Buddhahood]; thus, he is the Buddhas of the three periods. Question: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was also preached in a royal city;
why then is the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla mentioned first? Answer: Bhadrapāla is a native of the royal city, whereas the others are guests; therefore, the native is placed first.
"Constantly diligent" means that because sentient beings possess various sufferings, the Great Being must always rescue and deliver them; hence it is called "constant diligence.
To be without interval is "diligence," and to advance toward [the goal] is "progress. Since one constantly rescues and delivers others, one is endowed with the four *siddhāntas* (and so forth).
As for "without rest," this name is derived from a long period of time. The Sūtra says, "The courageous bestower" refers to one who realizes ultimate emptiness.

Because one does not give rise to cowardice or weakness when relinquishing body, life, and wealth, it is called "Jewel Moon" (*ratnacandra*); for with one's own wisdom, one illuminates the darkness of night. The commentary states: "Just as wisdom is clear and bright, the heat and affliction of the three poisons are thereby extinguished; like the moon—this interpretation is also shallow. Since that which is cleared is shallow, how could that which clears it be profound? Regarding "Moonlight" (*candraprabha*), it means using the light of one's own wisdom to dispel oppressive heat and humidity. The commentary states: "Just as moonlight can cool the burning heat of summer, so too does this Bodhisattva, through the light of his wisdom, dispel the heat and affliction of sentient beings' delusions. This interpretation is also shallow. Why? Because the moon is merely a physical phenomenon; how could its light truly extinguish the heat and affliction of sentient beings? Furthermore, the moon cannot illuminate the darkness of night within the pores of sentient beings, nor can it remove the darkness of ignorance from their minds. Therefore, these names are all provisional designations based on worldly analogies. As for "Dharma Cloud" (*dharmamegha*), it is because the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body is vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky, and because he rains down the great Dharma-rain to moisten and nourish all sentient beings. The commentary states: "The Dharma-body of this Bodhisattva is vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky; raining down the great Dharma-rain, he moistens and nourishes all sentient beings. Because he can cover all things, he is called 'Dharma Cloud. This interpretation is also shallow. Why? Because the Dharma-body is formless and invisible; how could it possibly cover anything? Furthermore, the Dharma-body is eternally quiescent and free from activity; how could it possibly rain down the Dharma-rain? Moreover, the Dharma-body is beyond words and speech; how could it possibly preach the Dharma? Therefore, these names are all provisional designations based on worldly analogies. As for "Cloud of Virtue" (*guṇamegha*), it is because the Bodhisattva’s virtues are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky, and because he rains down the great rain of virtue to moisten and nourish all sentient beings. The commentary states: "The virtues of this Bodhisattva are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky; raining down the great rain of virtue, he moistens and nourishes all sentient beings. Because he can cover all things, he is called 'Virtue Cloud. This interpretation is also shallow. Why? Because virtue is formless and invisible; how could it possibly cover anything? Furthermore, virtue is eternally quiescent and free from activity; how could it possibly rain down the rain of virtue? Moreover, virtue is beyond words and speech; how could it possibly preach the Dharma? Therefore, these names are all provisional designations based on worldly analogies. As for "Cloud of Wisdom" (*jñānamegha*), it is because the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky, and because he rains down the great rain of wisdom to moisten and nourish all sentient beings. The commentary states: "The wisdom of this Bodhisattva is vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky; raining down the great rain of wisdom, he moistens and nourishes all sentient beings. Because he can cover all things, he is called 'Wisdom Cloud. This interpretation is also shallow. Why? Because wisdom is formless and invisible; how could it possibly cover anything? Furthermore, wisdom is eternally quiescent and free from activity; how could it possibly rain down the rain of wisdom? Moreover, wisdom is beyond words and speech; how could it possibly preach the Dharma? Therefore, these names are all provisional designations based on worldly analogies. As for "Cloud of Samādhi" (*samādhimegha*), it is because the Bodhisattva’s samādhis are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky, and because he rains down the great rain of samādhi to moisten and nourish all sentient beings. The commentary states: "The samādhis of this Bodhisattva are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky; raining down the great rain of samādhi, he moistens and nourishes all sentient beings. Because he can cover all things, he is called 'Samādhi Cloud. This interpretation is also shallow. Why? Because samādhi is formless and invisible; how could it possibly cover anything? Furthermore, samādhi is eternally quiescent and free from activity; how could it possibly rain down the rain of samādhi? Moreover, samādhi is beyond words and speech; how could it possibly preach the Dharma? Therefore, these names are all provisional designations based on worldly analogies. As for "Cloud of Liberation" (*vimokṣamegha*), it is because the Bodhisattva’s liberations are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky, and because he rains down the great rain of liberation to moisten and nourish all sentient beings. The commentary states: "The liberations of this Bodhisattva are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky; raining down the great rain of liberation, he moistens and nourishes all sentient beings. Because he can cover all things, he is called 'Liberation Cloud. This interpretation is also shallow. Why? Because liberation is formless and invisible; how could it possibly cover anything? Furthermore, liberation is eternally quiescent and free from activity; how could it possibly rain down the rain of liberation? Moreover, liberation is beyond words and speech; how could it possibly preach the Dharma? Therefore, these names are all provisional designations based on worldly analogies. As for "Cloud of Power" (*balamegha*), it is because the Bodhisattva’s powers are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky, and because he rains down the great rain of power to moisten and nourish all sentient beings. The commentary states: "The powers of this Bodhisattva are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky; raining down the great rain of power, he moistens and nourishes all sentient beings. Because he can cover all things, he is called 'Power Cloud. This interpretation is also shallow. Why? Because power is formless and invisible; how could it possibly cover anything? Furthermore, power is eternally quiescent and free from activity; how could it possibly rain down the rain of power? Moreover, power is beyond words and speech; how could it possibly preach the Dharma? Therefore, these names are all provisional designations based on worldly analogies. As for "Cloud of Fearlessness" (*vaiśāradyamegha*), it is because the Bodhisattva’s fearlessnesses are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky, and because he rains down the great rain of fearlessness to moisten and nourish all sentient beings. The commentary states: "The fearlessnesses of this Bodhisattva are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky; raining down the great rain of fearlessness, he moistens and nourishes all sentient beings. Because he can cover all things, he is called 'Fearlessness Cloud. This interpretation is also shallow. Why? Because fearlessness is formless and invisible; how could it possibly cover anything? Furthermore, fearlessness is eternally quiescent and free from activity; how could it possibly rain down the rain of fearlessness? Moreover, fearlessness is beyond words and speech; how could it possibly preach the Dharma? Therefore, these names are all provisional designations based on worldly analogies. As for "Cloud of Unhindered Knowledge" (*pratisaṃvidmegha*), it is because the Bodhisattva’s unhindered knowledges are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky, and because he rains down the great rain of unhindered knowledge to moisten and nourish all sentient beings. The commentary states: "The unhindered knowledges of this Bodhisattva are vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky; raining down the great rain of unhindered knowledge, he moistens and nourishes all sentient beings. Because he can cover all things, he is called 'Unhindered Knowledge Cloud. This interpretation is also shallow. Why? Because unhindered knowledge is formless and invisible; how could it possibly cover anything? Furthermore, unhindered knowledge is eternally quiescent and free from activity; how could it possibly rain down the rain of unhindered knowledge? Moreover, unhindered knowledge is beyond words and speech; how could it possibly preach the Dharma? Therefore, these names are all provisional designations based on worldly analogies. As for "Cloud of Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇāmegha*), it is because the Bodhisattva’s great compassion is vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky, and because he rains down the great rain of great compassion to moisten and nourish all sentient beings. The commentary states: "The great compassion of this Bodhisattva is vast and pervasive, like a great cloud covering the sky; raining down the great rain of great compassion, he moistens and nourishes all sentient beings. Because he can cover all things, he is called 'Great Compassion
It is said that wisdom can destroy darkness like the light of the moon; this is also a profound understanding [and so forth].

"The full moon" means that there is nothing it does not perfectly illuminate and nothing it does not universally encompass. "Great power" means that the application of its wisdom is boundless. The commentary states:
"In the Way-gate, overcoming the Two Vehicles is 'great,' and extinguishing the ten evils is 'power. The commentary explains that overcoming the Two Vehicles is 'great,' but it merely achieves..."
The Bodhisattvas of the Hīnayāna teachings can eliminate the ten non-virtues as their power, yet this is merely the Mahāyāna [view].

Now, it is explained that overcoming the seven stages of expedient means constitutes the "Great," while eliminating the five abodes of ignorance constitutes "Power" and "Immeasurability. As for "the application of transformation being boundless," the commentary notes:

"The power of signlessness is not named after the measurement of signs; transcending the three realms means wisdom surpasses the path of arising and ceasing, and crossing beyond the three existences."

Now, as for "Bhadra," whose name means "Worthy Guardian" (Xiànshǒu): he is one whose wisdom in liberation surpasses that of the two [types of practitioners] regarding birth, death, cessation, and the path; who transforms both the internal and external within the triple world;
who is called "Worthy" because he borders on the ultimate and ranks as a near-sage; and who is called "Guardian" because his capacity for the Path is firm and steadfast.

[Commentary: In the section on Maitreya, it is cited that a king saw an elephant trainer taming an elephant. Seeing a female elephant running wild and beyond restraint, the trainer instructed the king to grasp a tree branch to avoid being gored by the elephant.
The king then rebuked the trainer. The trainer replied, "It is because his lustful mind is so intense;
it is not that his body is untamed. Three days later, once the lustful mind had subsided, he took the elephant and subjected it to the "burning of the seven irons" [a form of severe punishment].

The King ordered his elephant-keepers to force the elephant to swallow a ball of earth; only when the elephant died did he finally pardon its crime. The ministers asked, "Who could tame such a lustful mind?
At that time, a deva enlightened the elephant trainer, saying, "Only the Buddha’s teaching can tame it. Upon hearing this, the King resolved to become a Buddha.
To this day, he has indeed attained the fruit of being the successor to Śākyamuni Buddha. However, seeing the suffering of the elephant, one ought to say: [the elephant was tamed by the Buddha].
Alas, how tragic it is that even those who have been led and rescued by the eloquence of the One Who Bestows Joy have not yet escaped the conditions [of suffering].

I fear this refers to Śākyamuni’s stage on the path of cultivation, when his dwelling place for deer was set ablaze. To avoid the fire, he waded through water; there were many beasts that could not cross, so he used his own body as a bridge to carry them to the other shore.
Even after the lame hare arrived last and had just crossed, the deer king perished. As the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) says: "Su... [The text here appears to be truncated].
Bhadra—translated here as Shanxian (Good and Wise)—was the final disciple of the Tathāgata; he is none other than the one previously mentioned who was delivered last by means of the lame rabbit.
It is inappropriate to cite him as a parallel proof for Maitreya [and so forth]. As for Ratnakūṭa (Treasury of Jewels), it refers to the vast accumulation of manifold virtues;

the commentary notes that it signifies the accumulation of both the treasures of wealth and the Dharma. Regarding the mention of the "Guide" (Śāstṛ), it refers to the skillful opening of the path of wisdom; the commentary notes that this is accomplished through the Dharma.
Because he skillfully guides beings away from the heterodox, he is like a sea captain; he is a spiritual friend who shares the same realization of the perilous [path].
[Commentary]: "Unshakable by right wisdom" means that through the transformation of sentient beings by means of right wisdom, one is not moved by birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

[Commentary]: "The jewel-like mind" refers to the jewels of the three virtues. It is intermingled with the realm of sentient beings; there are no [realms] without form, and among the six paths, there are no hells.

As the commentary states (*et cetera*), among the fourfold assembly there are no *upāsikās*, among the eight classes of beings there are no *yakṣas* or *mahoragas*, and among the two kings there is no *cakravartin*. These are all present within the Prologue.
[Commentary] The *Antarābhava-sūtra* also states that those in the formless realm are transformed [by the Buddha]. The second fascicle of this sutra says:

"At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernatural power, went to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and gathered the sentient beings of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), bringing them to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for them; through such teachings as 'the consciousness of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,' all those of this class resolved upon the unsurpassed path of the True Dharma."

The true aspiration for the Path was realized in *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; furthermore, thirty-six billion *nayuta* of sentient beings, weary of their karmic lifespans, heard the pure Dharma and immediately attained the fruit of the Path. An immeasurable assembly of the fourfold community—*śrāvakas*, *bodhisattvas*, Avalokiteśvara, and others—were all present in the gathering, as described at length therein.
It is asked: Do sentient beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) possess the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)?

Question: It can be understood that those in the formless realm hear the Dharma; yet, since they lack auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), how can they hear the Dharma and give rise to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*)?
Answer: Previously, while in the desire or form realms, they heard the Mahāyāna teachings, which perfumed and established seeds.

Now, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, these serve as powerful conditions to strike and activate those previously perfumed Mahāyāna seeds and innate merits (*dharmatā-guṇa*), enabling them to manifest upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The appearance of these reflected images arises through the power of this world, enabling one to resolve upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), practice, and attain Buddhahood.

Since both principle and teaching are thus established, this interpretation is correct; therefore, even ordinary people of no discernment, with their four aggregates and limited bodies, can manifest transformed form-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and weep by the Buddha’s side with tears falling like rain.

[Commentary]: Since the noble Śakra belongs to the second stage (*bhūmi*) and the Brahmā kings belong to the seventh stage, among the ten kings, those corresponding to the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are bodhisattvas of the ten stages.

[Commentary: First Śakra is designated, followed by the listing of the four kings; fearing that this might be an error for the four Brahmās, one must then list the Brahmā King, the lord of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). [Commentary:

As for the mixing of karmic retribution with physical appearance and attire, it means that provisional beings and real beings alike receive the same karmic retribution, physical appearance, and attire.

"Various," it says. [The Commentary] explains "various" according to the teachings as follows: based on the eight sections, there should be four types. As for the causes and conditions: the eight different sections are for the sake of the world;
the assembly of devas and humans is for the sake of human beings; the assembly of ghosts and animals is for the sake of remedial treatment; and attaining the Way is the primary purpose.

Regarding the interpretation based on the single principle of origin and trace (*honjaku*): attaining the Buddha-way is the origin, while manifesting the eight stages as well as *anāsrava* (outflow-free) and *upāya* (expedient means) are all traces.

Regarding the interpretation through contemplating the mind: *anāsrava* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), *upāya* is the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the Buddha-way is the middle (*madhyamā*)—thus it possesses all four interpretations.
Therefore, the commentary states "and so forth" (*yún yún*).
[Commentary]: Regarding Śakra Devānām-indra, the new terminology renders it Śakradevānām-indra;
"Śakra" is his clan name, which translates as "Capable," while "Devānām-indra" translates as "Lord of Gods. The full name is "Capable Lord of Gods.
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* (*etc.*).
At the summit of Mount Sumeru, eighty thousand [yojanas] high, dwell the Trāyastriṃśa gods. At its four corners are four peaks where the Vajra-crested ones reside.
In the center is the palace named Sudarśana, ten thousand yojanas in circumference and five thousand in height, with golden walls.
Its ground is of various colors and soft to the touch; within it stands the Palace of Excellence.
It is one thousand yojanas in circumference, adorned outside by four gardens: Saṃtarpaka, Paruṣaka, Miśraka, and Nandana. The commentary states:
The Trāyastriṃśa gods dwell upon the summit of Mount Meru; each of the four peaks is eighty thousand [yojanas], and their dimensions are no different from those of the four lower sides.
Some say it is eight thousand [yojanas] in circumference, with each of the four sides being only twenty thousand. At each of the four corners of the mountain summit...
There is a peak, five hundred yojanas in both height and breadth, where a yakṣa deity named Vajrapāṇi dwells, protecting the devas.
At the summit of the mountain is a palace named Sudarśana, two thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference and ten thousand yojanas in total extent;
its golden walls are one and a half yojanas high, and it is the capital where Śakra, Lord of Devas, resides.

There is also a city; within that city is the Palace of Excellence (*Vaijayanta*), which, being fully adorned with various exquisite jewels, outshines the palaces of other devas, and is thus named "Excellence.

It measures two hundred and fifty *yojanas* on each side and one thousand *yojanas* in circumference. Outside [the city], it is adorned by four gardens, which are the places where these devas sport together:

first, the Garden of the Multitude of Chariots (*Caitraratha*); second, the Garden of Roughness (*Pāruṣyaka*); third, the Garden of the Mixed Forest (*Miśrakavana*); and fourth, [the Garden of Delight].
The Nandana Grove constitutes the outer adornment of the Great City.
[Commentary: Regarding the three luminaries and the four kings, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"Sumeru has four tiers; each is ten thousand [yojanas] apart from the next, and they extend outwards sixteen thousand [yojanas]."

The measurements are eight thousand, four thousand, two thousand, and one thousand [yojanas]. The Karoṭapāṇis, Mālādharas, Sadāmattas, and the Great Kings’ hosts dwell respectively on the four tiers. They also reside on the other seven mountains.
The treatise states: Mount Sumeru has four tiers; starting from the water’s edge to the first tier, the distance is...
The measurement is ten thousand *yojanas*, and so on, up to the fourth terrace from the third; each of these four terraces extends ten thousand [yojanas].
These four terraces project out from the side of Mount Sumeru, encircling it for its lower half.
The first terrace projects sixteen thousand [yojanas], while the second, third, and fourth project eight thousand, six thousand, and four thousand [yojanas] respectively.
On each of the four sides, there are two thousand yakṣa deities named Dṛḍhahasta who dwell on the first tier;
those named Mālādhara dwell on the second tier; and those named Sadāmatta dwell on the third tier—all three of these being celestial hosts belonging to the Four Great Kings.
On the fourth tier, the Four Great Kings themselves, together with their retinues, reside (and so forth).
Upon the seven golden mountains, such as Yugandhara and Īṣādhara, there are also celestial abodes belonging to the jurisdiction of the Four Great Kings;
these are villages situated upon the earth within the realm of the desire heavens. Among these deities, this heaven is the most extensive.
The *Dīrgha Āgama*, in the "Chapter on the Transformation of the Four Heavenly Kings," states: "One thousand yojanas due east of Mount Sumeru is the city of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
It is named Kṛtamālā; it is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and its sevenfold city walls are adorned with various jewels.
One thousand yojanas to the south of Mount Sumeru is the city of the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, named Sudarśana.
One thousand yojanas to the west of Mount Sumeru is the city of the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, named Cakravāḍasudarśana. One thousand [yojanas] to the north of Mount Sumeru...
Regarding the *yojana*: King Vaiśravaṇa has three cities—first named Bhīṣmā, second named Devasaṃmatā, and third named Bahudhvajā—which are sixty *yojanas* in length and breadth.
The current commentary states that "twenty-four thousand *li* in breadth" refers to the six thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth mentioned in the *Āgama*.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "named Moon," etc., there are two further interpretations—those concerning the Trace (迹) and the Origin (本), and those concerning the Contemplation of Mind (觀心)—which omit the Explanations of Causes and Conditions (因緣) and the Provisions of Teaching (約教).

Now, the three distinct lights are the World (世界); their respective names being "Pure" (淨) is the Mutual [Benefit] (各名淨); their respective production of goodness is the Counteractive (對治); and their respective manifestation of the Origin is the Ultimate Truth (第一義).

Thus, the Trace and Origin encompass the Explanations of Causes and Conditions, while the Contemplation of Mind encompasses the Provisions of Teaching. Consider this accordingly (*yathāyatham*). (Et cetera.)
Regarding the duration of light, the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states:
The sun and moon [are at] the midpoint of Mount Meru; Fifty-one and fifty [yojanas].
Midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise occur simultaneously In the four continents respectively. During the second month of the rainy season, The nights gradually increase by nine [muhūrtas].
The fourth [month] of winter is likewise; at night it decreases, and by day it is the reverse.
When the sun travels on its northern or southern paths, day and night increase by a lava. Because it approaches its own shadow, the lunar disc appears deficient. The treatise says:
Upon what do the sun, moon, and the various stars depend for their support? They depend upon the wind. This is said because the karma of sentient beings has increased.

The upper force, together with the wind, draws them upward so that they rise and revolve around Mount Sumeru, circulating in the air and supporting the sun and other luminaries so that they do not fall.

How many *yojana* is the distance from here to where they dwell? (The commentary states: the sun, moon, and others are forty thousand *yojana* away, which calculates to six hundred and forty thousand *li*).
They dwell level with the summit of Yugandhara and halfway up Mount Sumeru. What is the measurement of the sun and moon in *yojana*? The sun is fifty [yojana].
Among the fifty stars of a single month, the smallest is one *krośa* and the largest is sixteen *yojanas*.
The lower surface of the solar disc is composed of *sphaṭika* (crystal) fire-jewels, capable of heating and illuminating;

the lower surface of the lunar disc is composed of *sphaṭika* water-jewels, capable of cooling and illuminating (and so forth). As the treatise states: "When it is midnight in the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*), it is sunrise in the Eastern Continent (*Pūrvavideha*)."
When the sun sets in Jambudvīpa, it rises in Aparagoyānīdvīpa; because the path the sun travels over these continents differs, day and night undergo decrease and increase.
From the ninth day of the second half of the second month of the rainy season (*varṣā*), the nights gradually increase;

from the ninth day of the second half of the fourth month of the cold season (*hemanta*), the nights gradually decrease. (The commentary states: The first day of the second month of the rainy season is the sixteenth day of the fourth month; the first day of the first month is the sixteenth day of the third month.)

If the sixteenth day of the eighth month is the beginning of the second month of the rainy season, it corresponds to the fifteenth day of the tenth month in this region; if the sixteenth day of the eleventh month is the beginning of the fourth month of the cold season, it corresponds to the sixteenth day of the seventh month in this region;

if the sixteenth day of the second month is the beginning of the fourth month of the cold season, know that it corresponds to the sixteenth day of the tenth month in this region. The sequence of the increase and decrease of the days is the reverse of this [in the northern hemisphere].
(And so forth. If one adopts this principle, then from after the autumnal equinox is the period of increasing nights, and from after the vernal equinox is called...
"Day increases" (and so forth). This means that from the summer solstice onwards, it is called "night increase," and from the winter solstice onwards, it is called "day increase.
Question: Why do they increase and decrease? Answer: Because the sun moves southward and northward (and so forth). The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
"The maximum length of the increasing period is eighteen *muhūrtas*; the decreasing period is twelve; and the periods of equality for day and night are each [six]."
There are fifteen [units] (and so forth).
Regarding the increase of *lava*s during the day and night: thirty *lava*s constitute one *muhūrta*.

Over the course of one hundred and eighty days, the period increases to its maximum length of one hundred and eighty days, which amounts to six *muhūrta*s; the decrease is likewise. [The treatise asks: Why?
Therefore, at the beginning of the dark fortnight and the beginning of the bright fortnight, why is the lunar disc seen as incomplete? (The commentary states:

In the Western tradition, the dark moon comes first and the bright moon follows. In the *Lokaprajñapti*, it is explained thus: As the lunar palace moves near the solar disc, the moon is eclipsed by the light of the solar disc;
the remaining sides cast shadows that cover the lunar disc, causing it to appear incomplete at that time.

According to the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra), the fifth chapter states that at the beginning of the kalpa, before the three lights existed, the power of the merit of sentient beings caused a wind to blow upon two treasures—fire-essence and yellow gold—to form the sevenfold city-walls of the Sun Deity (*Sūryadeva*).
It is two thousand li from east to west and likewise in height and breadth from south to north; its circumference is eight thousand li. Furthermore, a turbulent wind blew upon white *vaiḍūrya*.
The city-walls of the Moon Deity (*Candradeva*) are made of the two precious substances, silver and [gold], and consist of seven tiers.
From east to west they measure one thousand nine hundred and sixty *li*, and their north-south height is likewise; their circumference is seven thousand eight hundred and forty *li*.

Furthermore, when turbulent winds blow, the crystal city-walls of the Star Deities (*Tārakadeva*) are held fast by great winds and revolve to the right; the largest of these have a circumference of seven [thousand *li*].
The distance ranges from one hundred and twenty *li* at its longest to forty-eight *li* at its shortest, with the minimum being twenty *li*.

This scripture differs from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. [Commentary: The scripture states that fifty *yojanas* equal forty *li*, which calculates to two thousand *li*; the treatise states that fifty-one *yojanas* and sixteen *li* calculate to eight hundred and sixteen *li*.

Because the sun travels along three paths, the days vary in length: during summer it travels the northern path, during winter the southern path, and during spring and autumn the middle path. The same applies to the moon.

There are three reasons for its waning: first, because it moves along the horn-path (*śṛṅgāṭaka-gati*); second, because its retinue of ministers and their attire are of lapis lazuli color and stand before it;
and third, because the sun’s sixty rays of light shine upon it. Furthermore, there are three reasons for its waxing: first, because the moon moves in a straight course;
second, because on the twenty-fifth day it stays in the main palace and its ministers do not stand before it; and third, because it emits light during those three days.

Because the moon does not receive [the light] at all, it is full. By practicing the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) of the lower grade and giving offerings such as lamps, one is born among the stars;
there are both males and females there, and the lunar palace also has both males and females. One day and night there corresponds to fifty years in the human realm.
Their height is ten *li*. By practicing the ten wholesome actions of the middle grade and concurrently giving lamps and other offerings, one is born in the solar palace.
There are men and women whose lifespan is equal to that of a day; knowing how to practice the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions and giving lamps and other offerings, they are born therein.

[Commentary] Regarding the causes and conditions within the realm of the Four Great Heavenly Kings, as for the "approximate teaching" (約教), it is explained according to the provisional and the real (本迹); herein, the causes and conditions are subsumed.
These four kings belong to different worlds, each presiding over two ghosts; they prevent people from being troubled by them. This represents the four virtues as a counteractive measure (pratipakṣa).

Regarding their inclusion within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the four "withered" aspects pertain to the *āgama* and *vaipulya* [Hīnayāna], while the four "flourishing" aspects pertain to the *vaipulya* [Mahāyāna] and the *pariniṣpanna*.
Thus, within the categories of origin and trace (*honji-matsu*), the remaining two are subsumed.

[Commentary: From the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven up to the two types of mastery (*dvividha-vaśitā*). Regarding the two types of mastery: "causing conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and "according to teaching" (*yathā-śāsana*) encompass the fundamental and the manifested (*mūla-nirmita*);
"causing conditions" encompasses the two heavens. "Differing from this world" refers to the transformation of the five desires for the sake of humans;

"the two types of mastery" refer to the remedial [teaching] that expresses the fundamental and the manifested, and because it is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), it encompasses causing conditions. As for "contemplating the mind" (*citta-vipaśyanā*) to encompass "according to teaching," one enters [the path].
The "Emptiness" (śūnyatā) encompasses the Shared and Distinct Teachings, while the "Middle" encompasses the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding the statement that above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven there are the Yāma Heaven and so forth, the *Abhidharmakośa* says:
"Having already explained the external receptacle world where the Trāyastriṃśa gods dwell, what is the receptacle world where the remaining gods with form reside? The verse says:"
Above this are the gods with form who dwell in celestial palaces suspended in space.
The treatise says: Regarding the aforementioned gods with form who dwell above the Heaven of the Thirty-three, what are they called?
They are the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.

The Heaven of Mastery over Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*), the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue (*Brahmapāriṣadya*), and the other sixteen abodes comprise twenty-two heavens in total, all of which rely upon the external vessel-world.

Regarding the exquisite sensory objects of the six desire-heavens: in the first two heavens, sexual union is the same as that of humans; in the remaining four, it consists of embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing.
(And so forth. Upon the knees of the male and female deities in those various heavens, boys and girls suddenly manifest through transformation (*upapāduka*).
The verse says: "Birth in the desire realm. The commentary says:
"Birth in the three [realms] of the desire realm refers to those sentient beings who delight in experiencing the various excellent objects of desire that are present before them."

Thus, there are those who exercise mastery over manifest objects of desire, namely sentient beings in the human realm and the four lower heavens who delight in enjoying various exquisite objects of desire created by themselves; they exercise mastery over these self-created exquisite objects of desire.
This refers to the fifth heaven, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), where sentient beings delight in enjoying various exquisite objects of desire created by others.

Regarding the objective realm: they exercise mastery over the sublime objects of desire created by others; this refers to the sixth [heaven], the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Creations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*). Question:
Why are humans and the beings of the first four heavens spoken of collectively, while the beings of the subsequent heavens are each established separately? Answer:
Because the afflictions (*kleśa*) of humans and those of the first four heavens are coarse, whereas the afflictions of the latter two heavens are subtle. Some say that humans and the four heavens...

Because they experience objects that arise spontaneously, these two are combined into one; because the fifth and sixth [heavens] enjoy objects emanated by themselves and others respectively, each is established as one [separate category], and so forth. Question: What is the measurement of their bodies? The verse says:
The height of the people of Jambudvīpa is three and a half cubits or four cubits; for the people of the eastern, western, and northern continents, it doubles respectively.
The commentary explains: For the most part, the bodies of the people of Jambudvīpa are three and a half cubits tall, though among them there are some who are taller.
The people of Pūrvavideha in the east are four *hasta* tall; those of Aparagoyānī in the west are sixteen *hasta* tall;

and those of Uttarakuru in the north are thirty-two *hasta* tall. (The commentary states: one *hasta* is eighteen inches according to the Zhou standard of King Ji. Thus, the southern continent is eight *zhang*, the eastern is sixteen *zhang*, the western is thirty-two *zhang*, and the northern is sixty-four *zhang*.

These are their bodily dimensions. As for their lifespans: in the south it is one hundred and twenty years, in the east two hundred and fifty years, in the west five hundred years, and in the north one thousand years. These are their lifespans. Therefore, it is said that they increase respectively because of the cause of observing the five precepts. [In] the south...

[The measurement for] the lower grade [of the heavens] is one-fourth of a *krośa* in the east, center, and west, and increases by one-fourth for each successive level up to the north. This is extracted from the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*. The verse says:
"In the heavens of desire, the *krośa* increases by one-fourth at each stage.
The commentary states: Among the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the body size of those in the lowest heaven is one-fourth of a *krośa*. Thus it is.

Thereafter, each successive level increases by one *krośa* up to the sixth heaven: the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*) are one and a half *krośas* tall; those of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven are two *krośas*;

those of the Yāma heaven are two and a half *krośas*; those of the Tuṣita heaven are three *krośas*; those of the Nirmāṇarati heaven are three and a half *krośas*; and those of the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven are four *krośas*. Regarding their lifespans: the gods of the Four Great Kings live five hundred years; those of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, one thousand years; those of the Yāma heaven, two thousand years; those of the Tuṣita heaven, four thousand years;

those of the Nirmāṇarati heaven, eight thousand years; and those of the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven, sixteen thousand years. One day and night for the gods of the Four Great Kings is equivalent to fifty human years; one day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa gods is equivalent to one hundred human years; one day and night for the Yāma gods is equivalent to two [hundred human years].

One hundred years in Tuṣita is one day and night in the human realm; four hundred years in Nirmāṇarati is one day and night in the human realm; eight hundred years in Paranirmita-vaśavartin is one day and night in the human realm; and one thousand six hundred years [in the latter] is one day and night in the human realm. Regarding those who have cultivated the causes for such long lifespans:

the Four Heavenly Kings cultivate the middle and lower grades of the ten wholesome paths (*daśakuśala*); Trāyastriṃśa, the middle-middle; Yāma, the middle-superior; Tuṣita, the upper-lower; Nirmāṇarati, the upper-middle; and Paranirmita-vaśavartin, the upper-upper. Each of these four divisions increases by one-quarter.

As for the increase in the size of the human body, it increases proportionally from five hundred years downward, as the lifespan doubles at each stage, and so forth. The *Śāstra* says: "Regarding the physical dimensions of the gods of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), the first, the Brahmakāyika heaven, is half a *yojana*."
The Brahmā-purohita gods are one full *yojana* in height; the Mahābrahmā gods are one and a half *yojanas*; and the Parīttābha gods are two *yojanas*.
Thus, it is said that for the first four [heavens], the increase is by half a *yojana* each. As for the gods above these, their heights all increase twofold:
the Apramāṇābha gods increase from two to four *yojanas*; the Ābhāsvara gods are eight *yojanas*; the Parīttaśubha gods are sixteen; and the Apramāṇaśubha gods are thirty.

The Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) has sixty-four [yojanas]; the Cloudless (Anabhraka) has one hundred twenty-five—though it should be stated as one hundred twenty-eight—minus three *śreṇī*;
the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava) has two hundred fifty; the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) has five hundred; the Unconscious (Asaṃjñisattva) also has five hundred;

the Without-Affliction (Abṛha) has one thousand; the Without-Heat (Atapa) has two thousand; the Good View (Sudarśana) has four thousand; the Good Appearance (Sudṛśa) has eight thousand; and the Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha) has sixteen thousand.
"Sixteen thousand" (The commentary states: From the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā upward, the physical stature and lifespan are equal;

if the height of the beings in the Retinue of Brahmā is half a *yojana* and their lifespan is half a *kalpa*, then up to the Ultimate Heaven, the height is sixteen thousand *yojanas* and the lifespan is likewise sixteen thousand *kalpas*, and so forth). Regarding the term *krośa*, this is translated as "shouting.

Regarding the statement that "the Cloudless [Heaven] is reduced by three," some say that from the "receiving of transformation" one first practices "non-transformation," which seems inverted; once it has been attained...
It is difficult to determine the lifespan; one should seek a different principle by adding [to the explanation].

One should say that because the lower transformative sensations resemble pleasure and desire, the mind is superior, and thus the karma created by this induces a superior lifespan and so forth. Because non-transformative sensations induce an inferior state of joy, the karma created by this induces a diminished lifespan and so forth.
Question: Since the state of joy is inferior, why is it said only that the three [lifespan, merit, and power] are diminished? (etc. Yugandhara.
Since there are neither suns nor moons above, how are day and night established, and how do luminous phenomena occur?
Day and night are established according to the opening and closing of flowers, such as the *kubjaka* and *padma*.

Furthermore, they are established based on the distinction between the singing and silence of birds, or based on the differences in the waking and sleeping states of the celestial hosts, or by means of the light from their own bodies serving as external illumination.
(As stated above) regarding the four formless heavens, the lifespans from the bottom upward are, in sequence, twenty thousand, forty thousand, sixty thousand, and eighty thousand kalpas.

A verse states: "In the Minor Light heaven and those above, the full and half [kalpas] constitute the kalpa. This refers to whether it is the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvarta*), formation (*vivarta*), or the intermediate (*antara*).

From the Minor Light heaven upward, the full [kalpa] constitutes the kalpa; for the various heavens below that, the half [kalpa] constitutes the kalpa. It is precisely for this reason that it is so explained.

The Great Brahmā King’s lifespan exceeds that of the Brahmakāyika devas by one and a half kalpas; this is because sixty intermediate kalpas—comprising twenty intermediate kalpas each for the periods of dissolution (*saṃvarta*) and formation (*vivarta*)—constitute one and a half kalpas. Thus, forty intermediate kalpas, which constitute three-quarters of that total, are established as the measure of the lifespan for the [lower] three heavens.

[Commentary: The intent of the question in the treatise is as follows: Does the period of dissolution encompass all forty intermediate kalpas collectively and designate them as one "kalpa of dissolution"? Or does it designate the twenty intermediate kalpas of the period of formation as one "kalpa"? This is considered in relation to the period of abiding (*sthiti-kalpa*).

One middle kalpa (antarakalpa) plus one lower and one upper middle kalpa constitute one kalpa; alternatively, eighty middle kalpas constitute one great kalpa (mahākalpa). Another interpretation holds that twenty middle kalpas of destruction, twenty middle kalpas of formation, and one upper and one lower middle kalpa constitute eighty great kalpas.

Some say this is based on the destruction by fire, water, and wind, where seven fires, one water, and one wind correspond to each destruction, following the one-kalpa lifespan of the First Dhyāna; thus, seven fires and one water destroy the Second Dhyāna.

Because the lifespan in the second dhyāna corresponds to eight kalpas, it is destroyed by seven cycles of fire and one cycle of water and wind; because the lifespan in the third dhyāna corresponds to sixty-four kalpas, [it is destroyed by six cycles of fire and one cycle of water and wind].
Question: Why is it not stated that the lifespan in the third heaven of the first dhyāna corresponds to one and a half kalpas?
And why is it not stated that the lifespan in the second heaven of the second and third dhyānas corresponds to two kalpas?
[Sūtra] Regarding "Sahā" and so forth: [The interlocutor] asks about Maheśvara-deva, who dwells at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

He is named Mahādeva and possesses great majestic power capable of overturning the world. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* both state that he is a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, Viṣṇu-deva—translated as "Pervasive Purity" (*Vaiśravaṇa*)—the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states, dwells at the summit of the third dhyāna.

At the beginning of the kalpa, water transformed and emerged level with the middle of the earth, where a thousand-petaled lotus flower appeared. From this flower, the Brahmā King descended and gave rise to the thought [of creating] the world.
It was empty, yet eight celestial sons suddenly manifested. Because of these sentient beings, the eight celestial sons became the parents of all beings.
The Brahmā King was the parent of these eight princes, and Viṣṇu was the parent of the Brahmā King.
Question: Since those two heavens are so vast, why do they not serve as the primary lords, but instead take the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna as their ruler?
Answer: Tracing back to the ultimate root, it is those two heavens; however, in the present context, it is based on the possession of speech and other such qualities (and so forth).
Regarding "Sahā," the new translation says *Sokha*, which means "Endurance. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Other masters say that the palaces of the first level of dhyāna [belong to them]."
Regarding the bases [of these worlds]: the first dhyāna corresponds to the four continents; the second dhyāna corresponds to a small chiliocosm;
the third dhyāna corresponds to a medium chiliocosm; and the fourth dhyāna corresponds to a great trichiliocosm.

Other masters say that the lower three dhyānas correspond respectively in measure to the small, medium, and great chiliocosms, whereas the measure of the fourth dhyāna is boundless. Thus, the verse says:
The four great continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma worlds—each one thousand of these is called a small chiliocosm.
A thousand times this small chiliocosm is termed a medium chiliocosm; a thousand times this medium chiliocosm is a great trichiliocosm.
All of these undergo formation and destruction simultaneously.

Ten thousand times ten thousand constitute a great trichiliocosm (*mahāsāhasralokadhātu*). If one says "ten billion," it means that one hundred million constitutes one billion, and ten million times ten million constitutes ten billion;

this is the Sahā world-system. Master En stated that the "Lord of the World" is the Lord of the Fourth Dhyāna, Śikhin is the Lord of the First Dhyāna, and Prabhāsa is the Lord of the Second Dhyāna—this also includes the Third Dhyāna. The present commentary follows the first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
It is said that the Lord of the Sahā World is raised up to manifest his lordship; Brahmā is distinguished from the common subjects by his transcendence of their station;
and Śikhin is designated by name to establish his title. *Śikhin* is translated as "Crest" because he has a fleshy protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) on his head that resembles a conch shell;

thus he is called Śikhin. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Correct Principles of Yoga), fascicle 30, states: "Because it is produced by extensive virtue, it is named Brahmā. This is Brahmā.

Because he is great, he is called Mahābrahmā; because others attain the intermediate dhyāna through his protection, because he was the first to be born and the last to pass away, and because his majesty and other qualities are superior, he is called Mahābrahmā. Because they receive what is emanated by Mahābrahmā, they are called the Brahmakāyikas;

because they stand in attendance and guard him in the presence of Mahābrahmā, they are called the Brahmapurohitas. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states that this refers to the first dhyāna.
The distinction between noble and base among the three heavens of the third dhyāna arises from the differences in their cultivation of the three grades of loving-kindness (*maitrī*):

the lower grade results in the Brahmakāyika, the middle grade in the Brahmapurohita, and the superior grade in the Mahābrahmā. This corresponds to what is stated in the present text regarding the further cultivation of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

As for the three heavens of the second dhyāna, they are called "Small Light" because the intrinsic radiance within those celestial realms is the least; as the light increases, [they are named accordingly].

Because its superior measure is difficult to fathom, it is called "Immeasurable Light" (*Apramāṇābha*). Because its pure light shines universally throughout its own level, it is called "Purity of Immeasurable Light" (*Ābhāsvara*).
Now, the present commentary states that the "Third Dhyāna Heaven of Light-Sound" refers to the blissful sensation of the mental faculty being designated as "purity.

Within its own level, this purity is the most inferior, hence it is called "Limited Purity" (*Parittaśubha*). As it increases further until it becomes difficult to fathom, it is called "Immeasurable Purity" (*Apramāṇaśubha*). This is that purity.
Because it is all-pervasive, it is named "Universal Purity" (Śubhakṛtsna). Within the fourth dhyāna, the abode of the gods in the space beneath the nine lower heavens is like clouds densely joined;
therefore, it is called "Cloud" (Abhra). Because their bodies are dense [there], they are called the "Dense-bodied" (Abhāsvara).

The gods above this have no further "cloud" stage; since they are at the head of those without clouds, it is called "Cloudless" (Anabhraka). Furthermore, there are other ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) there.

Because one must possess superior merit to be born there, it is called "Merit-Born" (*Puṇyaprasava*); the current commentary names it "Immeasurable Secret," which also implies receiving immeasurable merit.

Among the fruits of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), this is the most excellent, and is thus called "Vast Fruit" (*Bṛhatphala*). In the present text, because the waters of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) of the noble ones who have transcended desire wash away the stains of afflictions (*kleśamala*), it is called "Pure" (*Śuddha*);
and because it is the dwelling place of these pure bodies, it is called "Pure Abode" (*Śuddhāvāsa*).

Furthermore, it is said that because they abide here having eliminated the extremes of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they are called "Pure" (*śuddha*); because they are the dwelling place of the Pure Body (*śuddhakāya*), they are called "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Alternatively, because there is no mixture with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and they are the dwelling place of pure sages alone, they are called "Pure Abodes. "Fruitful" (*bṛhatphala*) means either "fruitful and mixed" or "fruitful and extensive.
Since this [Heaven] is the first among those without fruitfulness and mixture, and since it is the most inferior among those with fruitfulness and extensiveness, it is so named.

Therefore, it is called "Not Troubled" (*Atapa*). Because one has already skillfully subdued and eliminated the superior and middling grades of obstacles to the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, and because the mental disposition is tamed and free from all burning afflictions (*paridāha*), it is named "Not Troubled.
Alternatively, the afflictions that cause rebirth in lower realms are called "heat"; since this stage is the first to be free from them, it receives the name "Not Troubled.
Furthermore, because the fruit of the superior grade of mixed cultivation of dhyāna has now been clearly manifested and is about to be further revealed, it is so named.

Because the remaining grades of the obstacles to meditative concentration have been thoroughly cultivated, refined, and rendered extremely subtle and utterly pure, it is called "Excellent Vision" (Sudarśana).
Furthermore, there is no other place within the realm of form that can surpass this, hence it is called "Ultimate Form" (Akaniṣṭha);
or, because one has reached the final limit of the body which is the basis of all suffering, it is called "Ultimate."

[Commentary]: Regarding "one contemplates the mind for oneself," *brahman* (梵) is translated as "free from desire" (*vītarāga*), which is termed "pure" (*viśuddha*). In terms of the "original" (*hon*) and the "traced" (*seki*), the three [types of] attainment are originally pure;

it is only in terms of the traced that they are called "free from desire. As for "contemplating the mind," the three contemplations (*san-guan*) being free from the three delusions (*san-waku*) is what is meant by "contemplation free from desire.

To say "the assembly of *brahmans*" refers to the subjects of *brahmā*; originally, they are the pure assembly of the True Teaching (*jōkyō*), while in terms of the traced, they are the subjects of *brahmā*.
Regarding "contemplating the mind": that "one" contains the "immeasurable," which is the name for the "multitude" in the context of the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*).

Regarding "Brahmapurohita" (Brahma-Minister): this refers to the ministers of Brahma. As for "original and trace": the original is the Dharma-body Mahāsattva dwelling in the stages of *caryā*, *vihāra*, and *abhimukha*;

the trace is his acting as a minister. Regarding "contemplating the mind": the practice of the three contemplations assists the principle of the three truths. Regarding "Brahmā-rāja": he is originally [the one] who dwells...
The traces of the King Samādhi (Rājasamādhi) are so named because one who contemplates the mind employs the Middle Way to simultaneously negate and simultaneously illumine;

this is called the "Contemplation of Sovereignty. Regarding the three heavens of the Second Dhyāna: they are originally the traces of the three wisdoms, manifested as the three lights. Contemplating the mind is itself the three contemplations;
these three contemplations of the mind are simply the three lights. Regarding the three heavens of the Third Dhyāna: they are originally the principle of the Three Truths, which are without three.

The defilements of delusion are called the "traces of purity. For those who contemplate the mind through this divine ear, the threefold contemplation within a single mind purifies the five stages of dwelling;

this is called "pure contemplation. Regarding the nine heavens of the four dhyānas, they are called the "secret body" (*guhyakāya*): the original one body is itself the three bodies, and the three bodies are themselves the one body;

thus it is named the "secret body. To manifest these traces is merely a name for contemplating the mind through the divine ear. As for the contemplator of the mind, they contemplate the inconceivable provisional (*prajñapti*).
The one realm is the ten realms, and the ten realms are the one realm; being neither one nor ten is called the "Infinite Secret Contemplation. Regarding the term "Vipulaphala" (Broad Fruit):

its fundamental realization is the boundless body, hence it is named "Broad Fruit," while its provisional manifestation displays this name. Regarding the contemplation of the mind: its central contemplation is vast and extensive, hence it is named "Broad";
its principle reaches the ultimate limit, hence it is named "Fruit. Regarding the term "Non-conceptual" (asaṃjñin): it refers to fundamentally attaining the Middle Way.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is free from the two extremes; these names are merely provisional designations used to indicate it. For one who contemplates the mind: because it is emptiness, there is no thought of views;

because it is the provisional (*prajñapti*), there is no thought of the sands of phenomena (*dharmas*); because it is the Middle Way, there is no thought of ignorance. Because of the threefold contemplation within a single mind, there is no thought of sequential stages.
This is clarified through the six levels of realization (*ṣaḍ-yoga*). As for what is said to be "not cumbersome," it refers to the fundamental principle of true reality (*bhūta-tathatā*).
It is called "Non-affliction" (*avimala*) because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is pure; this is the name for its phenomenal manifestation (*vṛtti*). As for "contemplating the mind":

the three contemplations are themselves the Middle Way, whose essence can simultaneously illumine both [aspects], thereby forever departing from the three delusions. It is called "Not hot" because it fundamentally abides in the Dharma-realm, whose essential nature is cool;
this is the name for its phenomenal manifestation. As for "contemplating the mind": the three contemplations are cool and free from the heat of the three delusions. It is called "Good Vision."

One who has fundamentally attained the Buddha-eye perceives all objects as principle; this is why they are named "Trace of Good Vision" (*Sudarśana*). To perceive the three truths within a single thought-moment of the contemplating mind is called "Good Vision.
As for the term "Good Manifestation" (*Sudṛśa*), the clouds that obstruct the principle of the truths are what is manifested; the explanation follows the previous pattern (and so forth).
As for "Ultimate" (*Niṣṭhāgata*), having fundamentally realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is named the "Trace of the Ultimate"; this name refers to the contemplating mind.
To contemplate by means of the Middle Way is the ultimate contemplation; furthermore, because it is categorized according to the "six identities" (*liuji*), it is said:

"Contemplate this yourself. [Sūtra]: Regarding the eight dragons, they are first grouped into four pairs: (1) the pair capable of joy and capable of goodness; (2) the pair of the eight seas and nine heads;
(3) the pair of much suffering and little affliction; and (4) the pair relying on form and relying on mind. There are thus four meanings in total.

First, it is one of the five inconceivable powers (*acintya-bala*) of which the body of the dragon is the greatest. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Dharma-gates of the Hīnayāna comprise five inconceivable powers:
first, the power of karma; second, the power of the world; third, the power of dragons; fourth, the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
and fifth, the power of the Buddha. This [dragon] is one of these five. Second, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that evil dragons assist the asuras, while good [dragons] assist the devas.

"Dragon-Assisting Heaven" (Nāgānugrāhaka-deva) refers here to the next category of heavens in the list. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that when the devas and asuras were at war, the dragons fought on the side of the devas;
thus, we know they assist the devas. Therefore, the current commentary says: "The dragon coils its body to stem the ocean waters.
Third, it harmonizes yin and yang, bestowing grace upon humanity; the current commentary says: "It constantly protects [the land of] Makara."
This is so. Regarding the four external texts, the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the dragon is the sovereign among the scaly creatures (*linchong*);

it can become small or large, and can manifest in the hidden or the luminous. It ascends to heaven in spring and enters the abyss in winter. The *Guangya* states: "Those with scales are called *jiaolong*;
those with wings are called *yinglong*; those with horns are called *qiuliong*; and those without horns are called *chilong*. As for *Sāgara*, it is... [text continues]
Regarding the "Salt Sea Dragon" mentioned in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is also said that the dragon is named after the country. This country was situated near a rishi;
when the king encountered and awakened the rishi, the rishi cast a spell upon this country, causing it to become a sea.
The dragon resides therein, and thus it is named after its original country. As for Anavatapta, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that a dragon of the seventh stage arises from this pond.
The *Mahākaruṇāmegha-sarvasattvaparitrāṇaduḥkhadharmanirdeśa-vibhūtiprāpta* states that from within his scales, this dragon named Mānasī—

whose compassionate heart is described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as first sending clouds for seven days before rain falls to await all necessary conditions— causes waters to flow forth day and night without exhaustion, thereby rescuing all sentient beings of Jambudvīpa from the gates of suffering.
Only after this is it that it begins to rain; therefore, it is called the "mind of loving-kindness.

Furthermore, there are various nāgas who each recount how, in the past, they were laypeople in the presence of the seven Buddhas due to causes and conditions such as listening to the Dharma or practicing giving.
Later, when they returned to their abodes, people with faith provided them with various foods and drinks as offerings for the assembly, as well as [offerings] from the four directions.

After the monks had finished their meal, he diverted the food intended for them and gave it to me. Due to the karmic conditions of that act, he fell into the three evil realms and underwent various sufferings.
As his remaining karma was not yet exhausted, he has now been born among the nāgas, constantly enduring hot water, hot winds, hot sand, molten copper, and iron balls.
These enter his mouth and throat, scorching his throat and rotting his belly; they pierce through his entire body, passing straight through until they fall to the ground.
“May the World-Honored One please deliver me from this suffering. The Buddha said, “This transgression is difficult to escape. You should receive the Three Refuges;
only at the time of the final Buddha, Ruci, during the Bhadrakalpa, will your sin be extinguished.

The Buddha further said, “If a faithful donor gives food, water, or anything above that to the Sangha, and one privately consumes it or gives it to a layperson, this sin is heavier than [the aforementioned].”
