The Nāsīya Hell is as extensively described in the *Nāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* (*Yǒngwáng jīng*), etc.
[Commentary: As for the ten jewel mountains—first, Snow; second, Fragrance; third, Khadiraka; fourth, Ṛṣigiri;
fifth, Yugandhara; sixth, Aśvakarṇa; seventh, Nimindhara; eighth, Cakravāḍa; ninth, Īśādhara; and tenth, Sumeru—each of these is...
[This refers to] the King.
[Sūtra]: "The four gandharvas" refers to musical sounds (*gīta*). In Sanskrit, it is called *manu*, which is translated here as "pleasure," meaning that which causes people to find delight.
In this commentary, "musical sounds" is read with the tone *wu-jue* (five-four). If one says *śabdara*, it is translated as "agreeable sound."
It is also called *Yìrú* (如意), which in Sanskrit is *gandharva*; this is translated as "those who travel seeking fragrance," meaning they do not beg for food.

The present text says "smelling fragrance" (*xiùxiāng*), because they subsist purely on fragrance as their sustenance; hence they are said to "smell fragrance. Master Ēn states that there are two categories of music:
first, that which is not made of silk or bamboo, such as drums and stone chimes; second, that which is made of silk and bamboo, such as flutes and bamboo pipes.
Regarding the drums and chimes: those of the lower grade are called "music" (*yue*), while those of the higher grade are called "musical sound" (*yinyin*). Regarding the strings and flutes:

those of the lower grade are called "beauty" (*mei*), while those of the higher grade are called "beautiful sound" (*meiyin*). When it is asked whether these two categories are entirely "music with sound," why are the two lower grades not referred to as "sound"?

Therefore, the present commentary states that the *dhvaja* (banner) is "music without sound," and thus it is not called "sound"; it naturally has its own hierarchy, with the lower grade being as follows.
Regarding the names: "Superior Joy" (*yue-shang*) refers to beautiful music with sound; "Inferior Joy" (*yue-xia*) refers to musical tones. "Superior Sound" (*yin-shang*) refers to beautiful tones.

[Sūtra] Regarding the Asuras, there is a fivefold analysis: first, the translation of the name; second, clarifying their inclusion within the various realms of existence; third, defining their dwelling places; fourth, explaining the meaning of the name;
and fifth, the reasons for obtaining their retribution. First, regarding the translation of the name: they are called "Those Without Wine-Gods" (*wu-jiu-shen*) because... [text continues].
The retribution for observing the precept against drinking alcohol is that one obtains this body named "Non-Alcoholic" (*amada*).

Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Asura" means "not beautiful. They are not handsome; while the males are ugly, the females are beautiful. The current text also says they are "not upright. Mītiān (Kumārajīva) says:
"Asura" means "non-existent" (*amada*) and "surā" means "substance" (*śraddhā*); it is so called because they are full of deceit and crookedness.
To establish this name, others simply explain it as "gratitude" (*en*). However, the original term for that land is *asura*;
this is translated as "Non-God" (*fei-tian*). "A" means "not," and "sura" means "god. Because they are full of flattery and deceit and lack the conduct of gods, they are called "Non-Gods.
Second, regarding the classification of the various realms (*gati*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "They are included within the realm of gods (*deva-gati*)," though there are some variations.

The *Cittaviveka* states that they are subsumed under the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*). The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that they are subsumed under both the realms of hungry ghosts and animals (*tiryagyoni*).

This is the same as the present text. The *Gāthā-sūtra* states that they are subsumed under three realms: hungry ghosts, animals, and devas. Third, regarding the explanation of their dwelling places: the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* speaks of five classes of asuras;
the first, those who are extremely weak, dwell among the mountains and forests of the human world—this refers to those currently in the mountains of the Western Regions.
The "Great Hollow" (Dàyǒu Shēnkū), where much contention and strife prevail, is the palace of the Asuras;

those categorized here as belonging to the realm of ghosts in the current text dwell on the edge of the great ocean, similar to the other four classes. Those categorized here as belonging to the realm of animals in the current text dwell at the bottom of the great ocean.
Regarding the phrase "at the bottom of the ocean," the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that it is twenty thousand [yojanas] beneath the great ocean to the north of Mount Sumeru.
One thousand yojanas below is the palace of Rāhu; twenty-one thousand yojanas further down is the palace of Śūra;
now, at this point in the sūtra, is the palace of Bala; twenty-one thousand yojanas further down is the palace of Mālādhara;
now, at this point in the sūtra, is the palace of Khara-karṇa; twenty-one thousand yojanas further down is the palace of Vemacitra; now...

The *Sūtra* provides the same explanation of the name and meaning as in the fourth [section]. Now, following the sequence of the *Sūtra*: "Bāzhi" (婆稚) is newly transliterated as *Vajika*, which means "encircled.
What is now called "the bound one" (*pīfù*) refers to that person who was the vanguard of the Asuras; while fighting with Śakra, he was bound by Śakra.
Because he possessed courageous and powerful strength, he was able to escape from his bonds; therefore, the present text says he is "powerful" and acts as the sovereign (*di*).
"Releasing what was bound.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the two wisdoms of the original abiding—expedient and real—reach the shoulder blades," according to the following text, that which is on the back is called "carrying" (*hē*), while that which is on the shoulder is called "bearing" (*dān*).
That which is neither expedient nor real is named "carrying," whereas that which is both expedient and real is named "bearing"; therefore, it says "expedient and real."
Regarding *Vimā*, some say it means "jeweled ornament," used to adorn their garments. As for the question of why the *asuras* fight with Śakra, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The *asuras* possess beautiful women but lack the celestial nectar (*amṛta*); Śakra possesses the celestial nectar but lacks beautiful women.
Because they harbor mutual hatred and jealousy, they constantly fight. The fifth passage states: "In the past, there was a brahmin..."
This is as stated in the text.

[Commentary on the *Sūtra*]: Regarding the phrase "the original contemplation, etc.," the record’s interpretation may be erroneous. I now maintain that this clarifies the "original contemplation" within the section on Rāhu;

it should be said that the original realization of the two wisdoms—expedient and real—is manifested in its traces as the obstructing and sustaining of the sun and moon. As for the contemplative understanding, it is emptiness.
"Midst like the sun" means "just as the moon. Regarding the word *qì* (啟), the *Yùpiān* states it refers to "a multitude of mouths. [Commentary:

As for the question, "When the Garuḍas devour the four [kinds of beings], they consume those born by transformation all at once; since these are like extinguished lamp-flames and lack physical form, how can they be fit for consumption? The answer is:
before the bird has flown away, during that brief interval, they are indeed capable of being consumed as food. Furthermore, there is... [text continues].
[This] provides benefit and support.
[Commentary]: Regarding Vaidehī, the new translation is *Vaidhṛti-vistara*. *Vai* means "supreme and beautiful";
*dhṛti* means "body," which is the name for Pūrvavideha (Eastern Videha). That *Videha* is called *Vaidhṛti* when used in the masculine gender, whereas it refers to a woman.
In the language of the *śabda* (sounds), "Puṭṭalā" means "this son. This is the name of a mountain, and it is also the name of a deity on that mountain;
because she was obtained through a request from that [deity], he was named after her.

[Commentary] Regarding "contemplation" (*cintā*): it refers to being skillful at deliberation. It is also called "superior contemplation" (*cintā-viśeṣa*) because she excels all other women; therefore, [she is not so named] by [ordinary] thought.
Regarding the father who marked his son: because you previously harmed your own father, he is not mentioned [in this context].
The *Āgama* Sūtra states that after King Ajātaśatru had finished repenting, he still fell into the *Pakku* (柏毱) Hell, though he later emerged from it to become a Pratyekabuddha.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that King Ajātaśatru would have fallen into hell on the seventh day of the month had Jīvaka not arrived; however, having completed his repentance, he did not fall into it again.

The reason why the sūtras of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ is that the power of the Hīnayāna sūtras is inferior; thus, even heavy offenses become attenuated, yet one still falls into the minor hells.
The power of the Mahāyāna sūtras is superior; thus, heavy offenses are completely extinguished, and one does not fall.

Regarding the question of whether one who has committed an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya) may hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—if it is asked whether this applies to those who have already committed such an act or those who have not—it would contradict the *Āgama* and the *Samantapāsādikā*, for according to those texts, such a person has already entered the [stages of] the grounds (*bhūmi*).
If one has not yet finished serving his term in prison, he cannot become king; only after completing his sentence for killing his father can he become king.

If the commission of a parricide is subsumed under the category of karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*), then as long as the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) have not been eliminated, it is improper to hear the *Ekayāna* sūtra. This is identical to the case of the five thousand [monks] and the various devas who were removed from the assembly.
Since they are now present in this gathering, we know that at that time there was no actual parricide; the Lotus Sūtra reveals him to have been a person of expedient means (*upāya-puruṣa*).
Although he had already killed his father, because the sores on his body had not yet manifested, he came to listen to the sutra. In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, he was shown to be a real person;
when the sūtra proclaimed the extinction [of his sins], the King repented and attained rootless faith. If it were not a real sin, why would repentance be necessary?

Furthermore, this was a provisional practice intended to manifest the power of the true teaching, which can extinguish grave offenses and reveal the superior efficacy of the sūtra. To the ultimate point: [it serves to]... [the end].
Question: That ulcer was caused by false teachings and could not be extinguished; why then can this sutra, which is the teaching of the single reality, not extinguish it?
Answer: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* primarily clarifies the extinction of evil, while incidentally clarifying the production of goodness.

Know that from the five thousand [monks] who departed until they attained entry [into the path], this sutra primarily clarifies the production of goodness. By means of even a single hair’s breadth of goodness, King Ajātaśatru shall attain Buddhahood.

Although one who has committed the five heinous crimes does not sever their roots of goodness and shall likewise attain Buddhahood, this serves as a secondary clarification on the eradication of evil, as seen in the case of Devadatta receiving his prediction;
this is stated in its full detail, and it can be understood by reflecting upon how all four *siddhāntas* (purposes) are present. Question:

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of attaining "rootless faith," while the *Puyao* (Pu-chao) speaks of "pliant patience" (*anulomikī kṣānti*). How are these to be reconciled? Answer: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* refers to the outward manifestation (*li*), clarifying that [Devadatta] was indeed a sinner.
Because people thus attain faith, if one says they have attained "patience in conformity" (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*), sentient beings will think that actual sinners do not perish.
That sutra relies on the fundamental [nature], and therefore it speaks of "patience in conformity. Furthermore, he asked: "How many parricides does the King commit? One explanation says:

killing one's father, killing one's mother, and killing a noble person (*ārya*). The father is one who has attained the fruit of a *srotāpanna*; the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* says he is an *anāgāmin*. There are four types of such [parricide].

The mad elephant harmed the Buddha; there were two instances of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha; and it is said that only two [types of people] possess the two immediate transgressions (ānantarya): those who kill their father or an *arhat*.

Regarding the statement that one is not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas (*lokadharma*), this is also called the "eight impurities": first, fields; second, houses; third, male slaves; fourth, female slaves;
fifth, oxen; sixth, horses; seventh, gold; and eighth, silver.
[Sūtra] Regarding the passage "bowing at the Buddha’s feet" and so forth, the second section on the summary of the five merits states that the *Ekottarika Āgama* says:
first, it makes the body upright and handsome; second, one obtains a beautiful voice; third, one is born into a noble family; fourth, one is respected by others;
fifth, one will certainly be reborn in heaven. Because there are these five benefits, each [act of worship] is performed with prostration. (From *Yìzhuàn*, Scroll 2)
Tiantai Fahua Shuyi Zuan, Scroll Three (Original Text),
Composed by the Eastern Spring Śramaṇa Zhidu;
Commentary on the Separate Preface.
[Commentary] "To speak briefly in terms of mutual comparison within this specific teaching" means that it is based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, comparing its general and specific prefaces.

This differs from the previous explanation, which compared the general preface to the entirety of the Buddha’s lifetime teachings; as that [previous text] states: "The general preface applies to all teachings, etc."

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s introduction," this refers to the five elements within the specific introduction (*pratyutpanna-nidāna*), all of which proceed from the Buddha. For example, because of the Buddha, the assembly gathers; because of the Buddha, omens appear;

because of the Buddha, he points to one [teaching] while speaking of many; because of the Buddha, he enters meditative concentration, rains flowers, shakes the earth, and emits light. Such instances are all due to the Buddha.

The same principle applies to the arising of doubts, the posing of questions, and the answering of those questions. Therefore, it is called the "Buddha’s introduction. As for the "disciple’s sutra" (the *śrāvaka-sūtra*), its preceding and succeeding sections are explained as before.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "if one proceeds directly to the [common] etc.," this refers to the common and specific aspects in terms of the four flavors (*catur-rasa*). First, it is said that the text of the "Common Preface" is common in both form and meaning.
It is "common in form" because the five phrases beginning with "Thus have I heard" apply throughout the entire lifetime of the Buddha's teaching.

It is "common in meaning" because, within each respective division [of the canon], such as the *Avataṃsaka*, the two *Vaipulya* [Sūtras], and the three *Prajñāpāramitā* [Sūtras], they apply to the capacities of the audience within that specific division; they do not pertain to other divisions.
The *Ji* (Commentary) states that "the 'sections' (*bu*) encompass all teachings.

The *Ji* further explains that there are cases where "the meaning is common while the intent is distinct. Regarding the commonality of meaning, it is as previously described. Regarding the distinctness of intent:

although the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* shares its meaning with the two [lower] teachings, its intent lies in the Sudden; likewise, although the meaning of the "Milk" and "Square-Equivalence" (*Vaipulya*) teachings is common to the four [stages], their intent lies in the "Cream" and "Refutation" [stages].

The *Chixu* (Exposition) states that although the *Prajñāpāramitā* permeates all three intentions, it is specifically situated among the various flavors because it serves to refine and purify them like clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Next, the commentary on the separate introduction explains: "The text is distinct and the meaning is distinct" means that, for example, as with the *Vaipulya* sutras' joined canopy and the *Prajñāpāramitā*'s alms bowl, both the text and its meaning each reside within their own respective sections.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "the matter exists within the text of the sutra itself," there are distinctions in meaning while the underlying intent remains consistent. As for the distinctions in meaning, they are as previously explained.

As for the consistency of intent, it refers to the fact that throughout the entire dispensation (one generation), there is a distinct introductory section (*nidāna*). Thus, the Commentary states: "It applies to all teachings.

Next, the second layer of explanation further clarifies that while the text of the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*) is consistent, the meanings are distinct. The consistency of the text is the same as before; the distinctions in meaning are as follows:

For example, the *Avataṃsaka* corresponds only to the two [Hīnayāna] teachings; the Vaipulya corresponds to four; the Prajñāpāramitā corresponds to three; and the Deer Park [teachings] correspond to one. Thus, the Record states:

"Because the number of teachings corresponding to each section differs. Therefore, while the introductory texts are distinct, their meaning is universal. This distinction in text is as previously mentioned;

that the meaning is universal also refers to within each respective section, such as the *Avataṃsaka* having two, the Deer Park having one, the Vaipulya having four, and the Prajñāpāramitā having three.
The third reason is that the *Ji* (Record/Commentary) states: "This is a general enumeration of the extent of the teachings within the section.

This is because the former intention provides a general explanation corresponding to the entire dispensation (*ekayāna*), whereas the present meaning provides a specific explanation corresponding to the internal content of this particular section; thus, there is a distinction. Otherwise, it would result in the fault of redundancy (and so forth).

[Commentary] The phrase "Flower Land" specifically represents the meaning of this scripture. As for "the mystery of the intent not yet proclaimed," it refers solely to the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle following the attainment of meditative concentration;
because the multitude does not know this, it is called the "mystery of the intent."

[Commentary]: Regarding the doubt that [the Buddha] takes both the past and present as objects, it is said that immediately after finishing the preaching of the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, he entered that samādhi;
because [the audience] did not know what he would preach upon emerging from that samādhi, they were hesitant and in suspense. Thus it is said: "What indeed shall he preach? etc.

[Commentary]: Regarding the first interpretation based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is already unclear; the *Ji* (Record) states that while the "World" [interpretation] exists, the other three are all termed "unclear.
Now, observing this text, even Guangzhai lacks the "World" interpretation.

If the "arising in accordance with or contrary to [the truth]" were the "World," then how could it be said that the "person" (*pudgala*) is already unclear? Therefore, the four *siddhāntas* are entirely absent [in his system].
This is called "the lack of clarity.
[Commentary] It says: "The rain of flowers, the manifestation of the Middle Way, and the shaking of the earth collectively signify the 'one person.

Now, I fear that these various auspicious signs signify the 'one person,' while the single flower, the earth, and the light collectively signify the 'one principle. Otherwise, the element of 'joy of the multitude' would be missing" (consider this). Directly.
Regarding the statement "the bhikṣu and so forth," some say that the four groups—devas, nāgas, and so on—are taken as representative of humans, ghosts, and others;
thus, it is understood that the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs among humans are included within these four. Although nāgas, ghosts, and devas are added, the assembly of bodhisattvas is omitted.
Furthermore, it is said that Brahmā and Māra represent the assemblies of the gods of the realm of form and desire, while śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas represent the two assemblies among humans.
The term "humans and devas" encompasses the fourfold assembly; "śramaṇas" includes both non-Buddhist practitioners and renunciants; "brāhmaṇas" refers to the two lay assemblies;
and "Brahmā" encompasses all devas and māras—though as the lord of desire, he does not include spirits, animals, and so forth.

Furthermore, it is said that there are two types of noble ones (*ārya*), namely the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas; and two types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), namely the new and the old assemblies, as well as kings.

Regarding the "old" and "new" members of the assembly, these are termed the four groups of guests. Furthermore, it is said that among both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, there are two types: guests and residents.

For instance, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are Great Beings from other lands and thus serve as guests, whereas the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla is a native of this royal city and serves as a resident;
this illustrates the presence of both guests and residents among the Bodhisattvas. Among the Śrāvakas, Aniruddha is a native of Kapilavastu.
Humans are the guests within the King’s city, while the Śrāvakas are the long-standing residents; this refers to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), wherein there are both old residents and new guests.

[Commentary] It is said that although these categories are listed, there is no definitive judgment regarding ordinary beings versus sages, the inverse versus the compliant, the provisional versus the real, speech versus silence, the ancient versus the recent, the subtle versus the manifest, the shared versus the distinct, or the combined versus the solitary.
As for the "assembly of those who have formed karmic connections," these are ordinary beings who act as shadows and echoes [of the Buddha].

The three groups [of disciples] mentioned above are both noble and either regressive or progressive: Devadatta and King Bimbisāra are regressive, while the others are progressive. Regarding the provisional and the real: those who initiate [the teaching] as "echoes and shadows" (influences) are provisional;

those who respond to the capacity of the audience (the primary recipients) encompass both the provisional and the real. Regarding the formation of karmic conditions: it is exclusively real. Regarding speech and silence:

initiating [the teaching] is speech, while echoes and shadows are silence; responding to the capacity of the audience encompasses both speech and silence. Regarding the two types of comprehension—verbal and silent: verbal expression is the former, while silent reception is the latter. This concludes the section on the two modes of understanding.

Regarding the phrase "ancient and present," the four assemblies—beginning with the *pravrajita* (those who have gone forth)—in the past were common to all schools, both partial (*p'ien*) and perfect (*yüan*);

in the present, however, they refer exclusively to the opening of the provisional (*k'ai-ch'üan*) and the revelation of the real (*hsien-shih*). Regarding the phrase "subtle and manifest": that which can induce and give rise to [the response] moves from the subtle to the manifest;

those who are induced to become appropriate recipients (*dang-ch'i*) and establish a karmic connection (*chieh-yüan*) likewise proceed from the subtle to the manifest. Furthermore, while the first three assemblies serve as the manifest objects for establishing connections, [the fourth assembly] serves as the subtle object for establishing connections.
"Subtle" (*miao*) refers to the planting of seeds; "subtle ripening and liberation" (*shu tuo*) refers to attachment. Regarding the terms "common" (*gong*) and "distinct" (*bie*):

"common" refers to the four types of teachers—such as the *yǐngxiǎng* (influential) and others—who, in the past, shared their teachings with other doctrines. Because the *Zàng* and *Tōng* vehicles each possess the three vehicles, they are called "common.

Furthermore, "common" refers to the fact that the *Bié* and *Yuán* [teachings] transform many people together. As for the term "distinct," it refers to the fact that the capacities of those being transformed have not yet been transformed. This is what is meant by "distinct."

Regarding "both" (*kian*) and "exclusive" (*duk*): the four capacities for induction, such as the *Sūtra of the Initial Resolve*, were designated as "both" during the periods of the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā*, while they were called "exclusive" during the period of the Deer Park.
Now, in this present sutra, because it reveals and manifests [the truth] as solely the Perfect [Teaching], it is also called "exclusive. Regarding "bestowal" (*shi*) and "opening" (*kai*):

that which was previously identical to the provisional [teachings] is called "bestowal," whereas that which has now reached its ultimate revelation is called "opening. Regarding "origin" (*hon*) and "trace" (*seki*), it refers to the Initial Resolve.
The fundamental or ancient Buddha-dharma, the traces of the Dharmakāya Bodhisattva, pervade the five flavors.

[Commentary] Regarding "initiation": "expedient strategy" (*upāya*) refers to wisdom that discerns the capacity (*indriya*) and knows the timing (*kāla*). One who can initiate [the teaching] is a Bodhisattva who possesses the wisdom of expedient means to illuminate capacities;

because they reach [the truth] spontaneously and discern it without deliberation, it is called "expedient strategy. "Discernment" (*mian*) is also "illumination"; "timing" refers to the opportune moment.

This refers to the five periods of opportunity and the four occasions for exhortation. Regarding the four occasions for exhortation, there are preceding and succeeding opportunities, as well as those that are "ripe" and "unripe," which exist within the bodhisattva’s own mind;

therefore, it is said that he "knows. Because he leads [beings] to the presence of the Buddha, it is called "striking and raising. To strike, raise, and set in motion—that which strikes, raises, and sets in motion is what the bodhisattva strikes, raises, and sets in motion.
These constitute the five sequences. "Setting in motion" means causing the assembly to gather so that the Dharma may be preached. There is no other [purpose].

The measurement of meaning, entering meditative concentration, raining down flowers, the earth shaking, the joy of the assembly, the emission of light, the raising of doubts, and the questions and answers—all these are what is initiated [by this].
As for "accomplishing benefit," it refers to the different ways the four teachings’ capacities receive benefit across the five periods;

all are due to initiating the bodhisattvas now. When the Buddha arises from concentration and preaches the sutra, it corresponds to "forming karmic conditions according to the capacity" and "increasing the Path while diminishing birth. This is the name.

Regarding the phrase "accomplishing benefit is like an elephant felling a tree," the elephant is a metaphor for the arousal of the bodhicitta, the tree is a metaphor for the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*, and felling it is a metaphor for manifesting the *nirmāṇakāya* to teach the Dharma so that sentient beings may obtain benefit. This is called "the elephant calf obtaining its fill.

While there are four different ways of being "filled" corresponding to the differences in benefit across the four teachings, here the Buddha has definitively arisen to satisfy those of the Perfect (*vimala*) capacity—the "elephant calf."

[Commentary] The explanation further divides [the text] to clarify the meaning of the two characters "initiation" (*qǐ*) and "arousing" (*fā*), which encompass both the agent and the object; this corresponds to the meaning of the "Worldly" (*shìjiè*) [truth].

Furthermore, the four characters "strike," "elevate," "activate," and "move" correspond to the meaning of the "Human" (*wéirén*) [truth]. Furthermore, the four characters "strike," "activate," "elevate," and "move" correspond to the meaning of the "Remedy" (*duìzhì*) [truth].

Furthermore, the eight characters from "knocking upon the Buddha" onwards correspond to the meaning of the "Ultimate" (*dìyīyì*) [truth]. Now, it is said that the Buddha was precisely in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

This refers to the arousal of the bodhisattvas' resolve, not to the opening of the Buddha’s [teaching]. It is after the meditative concentration that the sutra is preached and the four benefits are then revealed.

As for the attainment of benefit within the introduction, whether it be seeds ripening in the past or attaining liberation within the present introduction, these are all the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) and should not be considered different from the four *siddhāntas* (reflect on this).
[Sūtra]: To surround is to encircle; to sit all around is called "encircling. To present wealth is an act of offering; to provide the means of sustenance is called "nourishing.

To be careful and reverent is called "respectful" (*gōng*). In this commentary, it is said that being humble and careful is "respectful"; to look up to and admire is "reverent" (*jìng*). In this commentary, it is said that solemn ritual is "reverent";

when reverence is extreme, it is "venerable" (*zūn*); when veneration is profound, it is "weighty" (*zhòng*). In this commentary, it is said that utmost mindfulness and focused concentration [constitute weightiness].

To keep [the Buddha] in mind is "veneration" (*satkāra*); to focus one's attention upon him is "reverence" (*gurukāra*). To speak of his excellence in principle is called "praise" (*praśaṃsā*); to discuss his virtues in relation to specific matters is called "eulogy" (*stuti*).
Among these four phrases, the first two refer to physical action (*kāyakarman*), the next one to mental action (*manaskarman*), and praise and eulogy to verbal action (*vākkarman*).

Furthermore, regarding "surrounded by a great assembly," the *Śāstra* explains that when the Buddha is surrounded by a great multitude, his virtue becomes even more exalted; once he is thus honored, the people [also] honor him.

Because he will certainly receive that Way, it is said that he is surrounded by radiance; this is like the Brahmā gods surrounding the Brahmā King, or the Trāyastriṃśa gods surrounding Śakra, or as one contemplates the lion throne within the sandalwood forest.
[Commentary] Regarding that which has already been explained within the "Marvelousness of Responsive Resonance," these recorded textual passages present the sequence of the Ten Marvels in prose:

the Marvel of Wisdom corresponds to the sixth auspicious sign (the light from between the eyebrows); the Marvel of Conduct corresponds to the second auspicious sign (entering meditative concentration);

the Marvel of the State corresponds to the third auspicious sign (the rain of flowers); the Marvel of Supernatural Powers corresponds to the fourth auspicious sign (the shaking of the earth); and the Marvel of the Retinue corresponds to... [the fifth auspicious sign].
The fifth auspicious sign, "Joy of the Multitude," refers to the following: within the verse, "sublime fragrance" (*miāo xiāng fēng*) corresponds to the "sublime object" (*jìng miào*);

"mounted upon" (*chéng miào*) refers to the "sublime position" (*wèi miào*). Here, the "sublime object" and the "sublime position" constitute the beginning of the position, while "mounted upon" constitutes the end of the position;

thus, the four auspicious signs of the flowers encompass the three excellences (*miào*). Regarding the "sublime resonance and response" (*gǎnyìng miào*), it takes the sequence of the fourfold assembly’s doubts expressed in the prose introduction as the catalyst (*jī*).

Seeing the eight thousand [beings] is the manifestation of the excellence of response, as it signifies that wisdom is capable of responding; thus, it manifests the subtlety of the resonance between stimulus and response.

The celestial drum is the introductory text for the answer to the question below, manifesting the subtlety of the preaching of the Dharma. The practice of others in various lands refers to the bodhisattvas of other realms diligently practicing various deeds;
this text manifests the subtlety of benefit. Therefore, these six auspicious omens encompass both sides and correspond to the ten subtleties (*daśa-sūkṣma*). Now, furthermore...
The commentary states: "These six auspicious omens in this land correspond to the ten subtleties (daśa-prakāra-sūkṣma), as explained in the *Śū* [the *Fahua xuanyi shiqian*].
The *Jì* [the *Fahua wenju*] explains: 'In our school’s interpretation, auspicious omens must signify something.

Thus, when the Great Matter is enacted by the Great Person, causing great spiritual resonance, the omen of emitting light signifies the two subtleties of Resonance and Spiritual Power; these are the one great capacity and the one great benefit for human beings.'"

The manifestation of great principle refers to the auspicious signs of rain falling from the heavens and the earth shaking, which represent the three excellences of stage, object, and vehicle; this is the first excellence of principle.

The necessity of a great retinue to assist the great assembly refers to the auspicious sign of the joy of the multitude, representing the excellence of the benefit of the retinue, the excellence of the teaching through the preaching of the Dharma, and the excellence of wisdom;
this is the first excellence of teaching. The simultaneous fulfillment of the great time and great destiny refers to the auspicious sign of entering meditative concentration.
The manifestation of wondrous conduct is precisely the singular practice, which differs from that of others (reflect on this).

[Commentary: Regarding those who expound the Mahāyāna sūtras, the *Bai fa shu* states: "The myriad practices are termed 'vehicle' (*yāna*); alternatively, True Suchness (*tathatā*) may also be called a vehicle.
If the myriad practices constitute the vehicle, it is a *dharmadhāraya* (appositional) compound; being both a vehicle and great, it is called 'Great' (*mahā-*) [Vehicle]."

Regarding the "Vehicle that is both the Substance and the Function" (*tǐ-chéng*), it is also called "Great. This name combines these two meanings: it is both a "Vehicle" and "Great.

Furthermore, concerning the phrase "penetrating True Suchness" (*zhēnrú*) and so forth: "Great" refers to True Suchness, which is the primary meaning (*zhǔ-yì*); "Vehicle" belongs to the myriad practices, which is the secondary meaning (*kè-yì*).

This is an *upapada* compound (*yī-zhǔ shì*), like "myriad practices depending on the substance of True Suchness. This interpretation holds that substance and function are not fused, thereby constituting the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*).
The commentary (*yì*) states [as follows]: The present sub-commentary (*shū*) says that the "Great Cause" and "Great Fruit" combined constitute the Mahāyāna;

this means it is both a vehicle (*yán*) and great (*dà*). Because the myriad practices are vast and numerous, they are called "great"; because one proceeds from cause to fruit, it is called a "vehicle. Thus, it is said to be "both vehicle and great," which is identical to the *dharmadhāraya* (possessive) compound.
If, as stated below, the ten wonders (*shí miào*) explain the seven greatnesses (*qī dà*), then the wonder of the object (*jìng miào*) is the principle (*lǐ*).
The name "Great" (Mahā) is the very essence of the Vehicle; it is synonymous with the remaining six Greats in their meaning of being the "Vehicle" (yāna) and the "basis" (āśraya).
Furthermore, in this particular school’s Perfect Teaching (Eka-yāna), the Mahāyāna is not analyzed through the six types of compound (ṣaḍ-vigraha). Why?

If one were to say it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound), then since in this Perfect Teaching birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is identical to nirvāṇa, birth-and-death cannot be taken as the primary member [of the compound]. If one were to say it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), then "one" would be identical to "the immeasurable," which is not the case.

If it were taken as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), the term "one" would not be established; if it were taken as a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound), then since it is one yet three, and three yet one, what numerical designation could there be?
If it is argued that it is a *bahuvrīhi*, it is like saying a wealthy man is called "wealthy" because he possesses money and jewels;

the five aggregates, being merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*), are not themselves called "wealthy. It is only by taking possession of the money and jewels that the conventional designation is called a "wealthy man. Therefore—
Regarding the term "possessing wealth" (*sādhana-vigraha*): since the present perfect jewel-dharma is itself the self, there is no possession of wealth.
If one speaks of it as an "approximation" (*upapada-vigraha*), it is like saying that among the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), mindfulness first observes;

mindfulness has clear recollection as its nature, while wisdom (*prajñā*) has discernment as its nature. These two are distinct. Now, when it says that mindfulness is the "observer," [it refers to this].

Because it is proximate to wisdom (*prajñā*), if one explains it according to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), there is no proximity because thought and wisdom are non-dual and mutually identical.

"Among the mental factors (*caitta*) within the eight consciousnesses, wisdom (*prajñā*) becomes the four wisdoms," and so forth. [The *Śū* (Commentary) states:

Regarding the meaning of the "four wheels" as distinct stages, the third fascicle of the *Zhíguān* (Contemplation and Practice) says: "In the three places where the two streams flow together, a question is posed:

'In the *Yíngluò jīng* (Sutra of the Necklaces), the sequence of stages from beginning to end is listed; it is only at the first stage (*bhūmi*) that the three contemplations manifest before one, and the path-contemplation (*mārga-vipaśyanā*) and cessation-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) flow together.'"

Now, for what reason are the eighth stage of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the first stage of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), and the first dwelling of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) all judged to be "dual-flow" (shuangliu)?
That answer states that one borrows the eighth stage of the Distinct Teaching to establish the lower level of the Shared Teaching;

this "borrowing the high to establish the low" and so forth includes borrowing the first dwelling of the Distinct Teaching to establish the first dwelling of the Perfect Teaching. When the high borrows from the low to become high, one must not dogmatically cling to the *yǐngluó* (necklace).
The *Yingluo* (Necklace) distinct stage is definitively situated in the first bhūmi; because its exposition of the stages is exhaustive and clear, nothing surpasses it, and thus we borrow from it.
[Commentary: Regarding "the name is common but the meaning is perfect," the text says, "We today are truly arhats," and also, "We today are truly śrāvakas.
While these names are the same as those in the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings, their meanings differ. Why is this?

He has merely slain the thieves of the four abidings (*catur-vihāra*), yet ignorance still remains; by slaying both the general and specific delusions, he attains the *nirvāṇa* of a Tathāgata, and thus the meaning of "slaying the thieves" is perfected.

Furthermore, while they [the two vehicles] belong to the realm of birth-and-death (*pariccheda*) and do not arise beyond it, they still give rise to the three kinds of mental aggregates within the stainless realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), as stated in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*. Now, however, both the birth-and-death and the transformation (*pariṇāma*) realms are absent.

The meaning of "arising" and "non-arising" is perfected therein; such a person is an *arhat* (one worthy of offerings) within the realm [of conditioned existence], but not an *arhat* outside the realm.

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "He who makes offerings to you is not called a field of merit. Thus, while the meaning of being "worthy of offerings" is partial [in the case of the former], here it is universal.

Since one is universally worthy of receiving offerings therein, the meaning of "offering" is perfected. Therefore, the three meanings [of arising, non-arising, and being worthy of offerings] are perfected in an Arhat. As for those called "true Śrāvakas," they—

However, while those of the Hīnayāna hear the sounds of the Four Truths from others in a partial manner, [the Bodhisattva] is now able to cause the entire dharma-realm to hear the sound of the Buddha-way—
the single reality of the Four Truths— so that all who hear may fully realize the meaning of "hearer" (śrāvaka). Thus,
one knows that one should rely on the meaning and not on the words (and so forth).
[Commentary]: Regarding the distinct meaning of "worthy sages" (*xiánshèng*) up to the *Xuányì* (Profound Meaning), the ninth fascicle of the *Xuányì* states:

"Although the thirty minds (*sānshí xīn*) equally possess the significance of being worthy sages, they are designated as 'worthies' (*xián*) because their subduing [of afflictions] is extensive while their severance [of them] is slight; whereas from the ten stages (*shídì*) onward, they are designated as 'sages' (*shèng*) because their subduing is slight while their severance is extensive.

Furthermore, regarding the designation of the ten abidings (*shízhù*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuán*) as "worthy sages": compared to the Distinct Teaching (*bié*), they are called "worthies," but compared to the Perfect Teaching, they are called "sages"—this is in relation to the Distinct Teaching.
Because the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are distant, those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) at the thirty minds [of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten transferences] are sages and worthies.

"Perfect" refers to sages; within the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), they are worthies. Looking toward the Distinct ten stages, [the ten abodes, etc. are near; thus, the ten stages up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) are sages, and Subtle Enlightenment (*miaojue*) is the sage.

Regarding the Distinct Teaching, the ten abodes are themselves worthies. Looking toward the Distinct practices and directions, they are called worthies and worthies. As it is recorded (and so forth), some say that in the Distinct [teaching], the ten...

Abiding in this stage is superior to the "Perfect" (yuan) because it is called "Noble" (sheng); thus, they are termed "Worthy and Noble" (xian-sheng). When the distinct stages (bie-di) are compared to the Perfect stages, they are called "Noble";

when the distinct faith (xin) is compared to the Perfect faith, it is called "Worthy. Now, what is meant by "practice and direction" (xing-xiang) refers to the distinct teaching (bie-jiao) in relation to itself, not in comparison to the Perfect [teaching]. (And so forth.)

[Commentary: "The great assembly’s hearts rejoiced" up to "the Supreme Respondent" constitutes the meaning of causes and conditions (*nidāna*). "Internal and external differences" refers to the world;

"question and answer" refers to the removal of doubts (*pratipakṣa*); "extraordinary joy" refers to the arising of wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma*); and "single-mindedly contemplating the Buddha" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

[Sūtra]: “Illuminating eighteen thousand [worlds] in the eastern direction, etc. [Commentary]: It is said that the eastern direction is now clarified as the beginning because, according to the two gates of the fundamental and the trace, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the One Vehicle’s cause and fruit are like the eastern direction, while the remaining thirty positions are like the other three directions.
The mention of “ten thousand” (*wan*) signifies the perfection of the stages; because one stage is all stages, it is represented by “ten thousand. Eight.
"Thousand" signifies the numerical position; although a single position contains all positions, all are identical to the one.

This refers to the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), which distinguishes between cause and fruit. "Eight thousand" signifies the remainder; the other three directions—square, circular, and incomplete—are to be understood by analogy.
[Sūtra]: Regarding "nothing is not universally pervaded," Jizang says that the *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance) possesses ten meanings and is manifested through ten characteristics:

1. It has the meaning of being supreme, symbolized by the crown of the head; 2. It has the meaning of the Middle Way, symbolized by the space between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā*); 3. It has the meaning of luminous clarity, symbolized by the eyes; 4.
It has the meaning of being free from obscuration, symbolized by the *ūrṇā-roma* (white tuft of hair); 5. It has the meaning of destroying darkness, symbolized by...
Sixth, the meaning of non-duality is indicated by the number one; seventh, the meaning of the fundamental source is indicated by the eastern direction;
eighth, the meaning of the perfection of the fruition vehicle is indicated by ten thousand; ninth, the meaning of the incompleteness of the causal vehicle is indicated by eight thousand;
tenth, the meaning of the exhaustive realization of the principle of cause and effect is indicated by pervasiveness. Now...
This means that although this explanation is extensive, it does not fully exhaust the underlying principles. The first and second [verses] merely express the quality of permanence (*nityatā*);
the third, fourth, and fifth merely express the quality of purity (*śubhatā*). Compared to the present commentary, they lack the two qualities of self (*ātman*) and bliss (*sukha*).
The sixth and seventh merely express the sense of "beginning" as the stage of abiding; the eighth and ninth already express the sense of cause and effect, which is identical to the tenth.

"If that were so, since the East has already manifested the complete illumination of cause and effect, what further would it manifest regarding the other directions? This cannot be accepted as a refutation, as stated in the *Shu* (Commentary), and so forth.
[The *Shu*] states, "If one divides the text to assign it to this land," etc.; the *Shu* contains two intentions: first, it addresses the ancients from the point of "At that time" (*er shi*).
The "Light of Ultimate Characteristics" is the sixth auspicious sign of this land; it first illuminates the East and then extends downward to encompass other lands.
Generally speaking, if one distinguishes the section from "At that time, the Buddha... down to "...eighteen thousand [worlds]," it constitutes the sixth sign of this land.
If one distinguishes the section belonging to other lands, from "At that time, the Buddha lowered his hand" onwards, it constitutes the general sign of those other lands. Therefore...
Regarding the further classification: if it were not so, for what reason would this text exist? As for what is called the "general characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*):

among the six matters in the other land, all are caused by the emission of light; this light is the illuminator, while these six are the illuminated. Because they proceed from the illuminator, they are collectively termed "Auspicious Light. Since the "Auspicious" (*śubha*) is one, it is called "general.
Furthermore, because it applies to both [this land and that land], it is also considered general. Within the record, the text is divided here in this land.
Regarding the passage stating that "extending throughout other lands from below down to the hells" refers to those other lands, I now fear this may contradict the original text;
for the commentaries cite ancient masters as holding that [the realm of] Nitala belongs to this world-system.
[Commentary: To say that there is no specific refutation and that the matter simply depends on the person’s judgment is not acceptable.
If one takes all six auspicious signs from the other land and attributes them to this land as the sixth, why not take the other five as well?

If one attributes them all to the other land, why not take everything from the point of illuminating the eastern direction onward and attribute it entirely to the other land? Therefore, it cannot be said that the matter depends on the person.
(Reflect on this. The current commentary states that regarding the respective lengths, one uses the textual divisions of Zuoxi:
from the Eastern [Mountains] to Nitala, two matters belong to the upper [category], while this land’s sixth belongs to the lower;
the first of other lands uses the ancient [reckoning] where reaching Nitala constitutes the sixth phase of this land. Therefore, the Record says: "It encompasses both long and short" (and so forth).

[Commentary] Next, regarding the passage "the light illuminates others" and below, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the six auspicious omens; second, from "furthermore, this and that" and below, the clarification that the paths of all Buddhas are identical.

Regarding the first [the six omens], there are four sections: first, the heading; second, from "first" and below, the enumeration; third, from "since these three already exist" and below, the arising of the sequence;

fourth, from "if this" and below, the clarification of what is symbolized: self-awakening and awakening others. Next, within the section on the identity of the path, there are again two parts: first, the brief explanation; second, the extensive explanation (as recorded in the *Ji*).
[The text continues with various differing views].

[Commentary]: Regarding the first point, "seeing the six destinies" (*ṣad-gati*), the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Nyāyānusāra* differ on whether they combine or separate them to establish four, five, or seven paths (*mārga*) and seven stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).
As for the specific explanations of each destiny: "Naraka" is translated as "hell" (*naraka*); "man" (*nara*) is translated as "human" (*mānuṣya*).
Evil persons frequently commit evil deeds and fall into that state of perversion; for this reason, it is called *naraka*. Alternatively, because it is near to humans, it is called *nara*;
since those who have committed grave offenses go there quickly, it is so named. Or again, *ka* is a synonym for pleasure (*sukha*), *na* means "non-", and *ra* means "to give";
thus, it is called *naraka* because it is characterized by the non-giving of pleasure. Furthermore, it is also [so called].
The term *ārṣa* (rescuer) refers to that which cannot be rescued; the term *naraka* (hell) refers to that which cannot be rescued. Regarding the term *tiryag-yoni* (animal realm):
it is so called because for the most part those beings in that destiny dwell horizontally, or because within that destiny there may be a small portion that does not move horizontally.
The commentary explains: "Dwelling horizontally" refers to those such as donkeys and oxen; "dwelling upright" refers to those such as monkeys. This is stated in contrast to them.
Therefore, it is said that they are "mostly" [so]; furthermore, there may be a small portion of those who move horizontally. Bipedal beings walk upright like birds;
quadrupedal beings move horizontally like oxen, horses, and so forth (*etc.*). As for what are called *preta* (hungry ghosts), they mostly seek much in order to sustain themselves.
As for what are called humans, they mostly possess much deliberation (*etc.*). As for what are called devas (gods), they are honored and sublime spirits.

They are called "devas" (heavenly beings) because they are prayed to by those who possess mastery; as for the term *asura*, it is said [in the scriptures] that they are subsumed within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*), and so forth.

Regarding the "seven stations of consciousness" (*sapta-vijñāna-sthiti*), the treatise states: the humans and devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the three dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the three heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

It is said that the seven places of rebirth constitute the essence of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*); therefore, they are described as "diversity of body and diversity of perception" (*nānātva-kāya-nānātva-saṃjñin*), "diversity of body and unity of perception" (*nānātva-kāya-ekātva-saṃjñin*), and the reverse of these, "unity of body and unity of perception" (*ekatva-kāya-ekātva-saṃjñin*). As for the three lower formless realms (*ārūpya*) and the remaining states, they do not exist because they lack the capacity for deterioration [of the basis of consciousness]. The Treatise says:

Regarding "diversity of body and diversity of perception," the Sūtra states that there are sentient beings with form (*rūpin*), such as humans and certain classes of devas; this is the first station of consciousness. (Commentary: "Certain classes... refers to...)
The gods [of] the desire realm and those of the first dhyāna, excluding those who arise at the beginning of a kalpa (and so forth), constitute the second station of consciousness:
sentient beings with diverse bodies and a single perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-group who arise at the beginning of a kalpa (and so forth).

The third station of consciousness consists of sentient beings with a single body and diverse perceptions, such as the gods of the Ābhāsvara realm (and so forth). The fourth [station of consciousness] consists of sentient beings with a single body and a single perception.

For example, the Śubhakṛtsna gods constitute the fourth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*); the three lower formless realms (*ārūpya*) are named according to the sūtra as the [remaining] three stations of consciousness.
These constitute the seven [stations of consciousness]. (And so forth. Regarding the nine abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*), the verse says:

One should know that these include the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*); these are the nine abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*). As for the others, it is because they do not dwell there with pleasure.

The commentary states: "The seven previous consciousness-dwellings (*vijñānasthiti*), together with the Peak of Existence and the non-percipient beings, constitute the nine; that is, the seven consciousness-dwellings [plus the two aforementioned]."

Above these are the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and the Heaven of Non-Perception; thus nine abodes of sentient beings are established because they are places where beings dwell happily.

Regarding the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), one should know that the four aggregates exist only within their own respective levels. As the Sūtra says: "Consciousness dwells following form;
consciousness dwells following feeling; consciousness dwells following perception; consciousness dwells following formations" (and so forth). The verse says:
Among these, there are four modes of birth; sentient beings are said to be of the egg-born and so forth. Humans, animals, those in the hells, and the various devas possess all four;
the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is exclusively of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*). Ghosts (*preta*) admit of both womb-born and miraculous birth. The treatise says:
"The classes of sentient beings—namely, the egg-born, the womb-born, the moisture-born, and the miraculously born—are designated as the four according to correct reasoning."

The treatise states: "Ghosts (preta) extend to include non-sentient things" (this means that while the four realms [dhātu] are broad, the four modes of birth [yoni] are narrow); "the destinies (gati) consist only of sentient beings," yet it does not say they are universally inclusive (because they do not include the intermediate state [antarābhava], they are narrower than the modes of birth).
Since the modes of birth are universally inclusive, there are also cases where that which is not a sentient being is nonetheless called a "sentient being" (sattva).

Based on this, the term "sentient being" (sattva) applies to those who possess sentience, whereas non-sentient things are not called "sentient beings. In older translations, the term "sentient being" (sattva) was used for what is here termed "sentient beings" (sattva).
These two names correspond to one another: first, according to the Mahāyāna, because they possess the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*), they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*);

second, because they possess the four types of birth—meaning birth as a category—among all sentient beings, although other categories are intermingled, the term "birth-category" and so forth refers to the meaning of "sentient beings," for there are many such birth-categories, as explained extensively below in the section on the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and in the treatise itself (etc.).

[Commentary] Regarding the statement, "First, it generally clarifies that the paths are identical; they shall be identical in the future, and thus [the present] is hidden": this refers to the manifestation of the six auspicious signs as being "identical in name" now, while [the future] is hidden.
It is merely that later people erroneously changed the character *xiàn* (manifest) to *dāng* (shall). The *Jì* (Commentary) explains:

"If what is seen below is taken as 'hidden' and 'identical in the future,' then both the present and future identities would be hidden" (consider this). Below, the two identities of "present" and "future" have been erroneously altered.
Regarding the phrase "should be made manifest," both the characters "should" (dāng) and "manifest" (xiàn) must now be removed.

[Commentary: The statement that "past goodness serves as the cause and the present teaching serves as the condition" refers to the planting of seeds through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Dharma heard by the prince as the cause;

the subsequent maturation through various expedient means serving as auxiliary support as the remote condition; and hearing the current teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the immediate condition.
By means of these conditions, one immediately attains the realization of opening, showing, awakening, and so forth;
that which is produced as the dharma is called "liberation. [Commentary] Regarding "spiritual transformations," the first record of the *Zhiguan* cites the *Mahāvikurvāṇa-sūtra*:

when the Buddha had finished manifesting the eighteen transformations, the Devaputra Śreṣṭhin asked the Buddha, "Is there any spiritual transformation that surpasses this? The Buddha then commanded Mañjuśrī...
In the extensive explanation of transformations, Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha:

"Such supernatural manifestations as these, which subdue evil Māras and cause Bodhisattvas to abide long in the world, are not yet considered supreme. If one speaks thus throughout the eighteen realms—without name, without sign, without sound, and without letter;
without the three liberations yet speaking of the three liberations—even until Śāriputra questioned the Devaputra."
[Mañjuśrī] asked, "Do you not feel fear upon hearing of these divine transformations? The Devaputra replied, "I am myself a divine transformation; why should I fear?

Mañjuśrī said, "All that is good or evil, moving or unmoving, is the mark of divine transformation. The unmoving is the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), while the moving is the divine transformation of phenomena (*dharmas*).
Therefore, whether through two conditions or three conditions, there is nothing that is not divine transformation."

[Commentary: "The one in the position of succession does not know the supreme pinnacle" means that the one in the position of succession according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao) does not know the Sublime Enlightenment (miaojue) of their own teaching.
[Commentary: "Even at the ultimate stage, he does not know" means that the Sublime Enlightenment of the Separate Teaching does not know the Perfect Sublime Enlightenment (yuan miaojue);
it is called "also" (*yi*) because, like the one in the position of succession, they do not know the supreme pinnacle. If one follows the provisional [teaching],...

If one does not even know the true power of the initial stage of the Perfect [Teaching], how much less can one know the Subtle Enlightenment? This is because the Subtle Enlightenment of the Distinct [Teaching] is compared to the Subtle Enlightenment of the Perfect [Teaching]; thus, it is said here that this is the case.
[Sūtra] states: "These are the marks of the Buddha’s radiance and supernormal powers. Here, "radiance" specifically refers to a single auspicious sign of Subtle Enlightenment.
"Supernatural powers" (*abhijñā*) is a general enumeration of the six auspicious omens.
[Sūtra] "The adornment of the realm": this is merely called "adornment" because it is illuminated by light; it is not a pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*). Regarding "verse" (*gāthā*):

the old translation says "verse" (*jie*), which is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term. One should know that "gāthā" is a corruption of the Sanskrit; consider this, and hereafter follow the correct form.

The term *gāthā* should be translated as "verse" (*sòng*). A verse consists of thirty-two syllables. The commentary notes that these verses of praise are like the "songs" (*yǒnggē*) of this [Middle Kingdom].
"Song" refers to the singing of the manifestations of majestic virtue; "verses of praise" refer to the extolling of the essential characteristics of ultimate truth.
The Sanskrit term *gāthā* is translated as "verse," meaning "to praise" or "to sing. The phrases within a verse are exceedingly beautiful.

Because they are elegant, they are praised in song; thus, these *gāthās* advance in expressing the meaning of the essence [of the teaching], yet they are inferior to names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*), as they have receded to the status of being the basis for them and do not equal the phonemes (*vyañjana*).

Among the one hundred dharmas, they are not established as a separate category; rather, their essence consists of the inflections upon sound, which are themselves nothing other than the nature of names, phrases, and phonemes.
Furthermore, it is said that there are two kinds of verses (*gāthā*): first, the *śloka*, and second, the *dharma*.
At the beginning of a sentence, there are five types: first, the intermediate-length sentence; second, the initial sentence; third, the final sentence; fourth, the short sentence;
and fifth, the long sentence. Regarding the intermediate-length sentence: if eight syllables form a name, it is called an intermediate-length sentence because it is neither long nor short.
Thirty-two syllables form four such sentences, and these four sentences constitute a *śloka*. The compositions of the sūtras and śāstras generally rely upon this [meter].

Regarding this number [the commentary says]: "If one speaks of the eight syllables from birth up to cessation, these eight syllables do not exceed the eight syllables; reaching twelve syllables is called a 'not-long' phrase; not exceeding these eight and reaching the preceding four syllables is called a 'not-short' [phrase], and so forth.

Second, regarding the first phrase: if it consists of six syllables or more, it is called a first phrase [the commentary says: from six syllables upward, up until the seventh syllable, is called a first phrase; for example, 'Just as a lotus in the world' is a six-syllable phrase;
'Because of pure cultivation, as broad as a blue lotus' is a seven-syllable phrase; reaching eight syllables belongs to the middle phrase and is not a first phrase]. Third, the final...

Regarding "phrases" (*pada*): those consisting of twenty-six characters or fewer that give rise to a name are called "subsequent phrases. (The commentary states: Verses may consist of twenty-five characters, twenty-four characters, and so on down to nine characters;

all of these are subsequent phrases. If they reach eight characters, this is a "middle phrase," not a subsequent phrase. Regarding "four short phrases": if six characters or fewer give rise to a name, they are called "short phrases. (The commentary states:

For example, in the words "able to act" (*neng zuo*) and "coexistent" (*ju you*), everything prior to the character "you" (*you*)—according to the first interpretation, everything up to the character "neng" (*neng*)—is a short phrase. According to the second interpretation, there is no phrase of one character, and it begins from two characters onward.)

All are short verses (*laghu-pada*). Regarding what is called a "one-character verse," there are three factors—text (*vyañjana*), name (*nāman*), and phrase (*pada*)—that arise together. A "three-character verse" is, for example, the words "Pure" (*śuddha*) and "Truth" (*satya*).
As for a "five-character verse," it refers to those from twenty-seven characters upward, with no fixed limit on the number.
Question: Since four characters constitute a verse, this should be a short verse; why then is it called "intermediate"? Answer: [Because it is intermediate between the short and long categories.]

Eight characters in Sanskrit are translated here as four; for example, *Bodhidharma* consists of two characters each, which are translated as the two characters "Awakening" (*bodhi*) and "Dharma" (*dharma*).
As for the statement regarding thirty-two characters: eight characters constitute one sentence in Sanskrit, and four such sentences make thirty-two.
Whether in prose or verse, it need not be questioned—thirty-two characters constitute a *śloka*.
Regarding the *Gāthā-dharmapada*, a verse must be complete with four lines before it is considered a *gāthā*;

one need not inquire whether they consist of four words or even seven, for it is essential that there be four lines. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states, "Four lines constitute a *gāthā*," which is precisely this point.
Furthermore, *gāthā* refers to a "solitary" verse, while *geya* refers to a verse that follows upon prose (*gadya*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "preaching the Dharma and entering meditative concentration can guide others," it is as the scripture says: "Adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom, one delivers sentient beings by means of this.

As for the phrase "sentient beings are those who are able to proceed [toward rebirth]," the Sūtra states: "that which is proceeded toward is birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Birth-and-death is the general term for the three paths of afflictions, karma, and suffering;
therefore, "that which is proceeded toward" refers specifically to the distinct result, namely the six destinies (*ṣadgati*). It is for this reason that [the text] is composed in this way.
The commentator explains that birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are the cause, meaning the three paths (*trivartman*) by which one proceeds; these are the result, meaning the six destinies (*ṣadgati*).

Furthermore, it is said that the essential nature of the destination—the result—is birth and death, while the path by which one proceeds is the cause. Because afflictions (*kleśa*) and the provisional entity of the sentient being (*sattva*) are what proceed, the commentary states:

"The conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma are the cause by which one proceeds; the receiving of retribution, whether good or ugly, is the result of the destination. [These are] the conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma."
This is because, with wholesome factors such as the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action serving as the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*),
one encounters afflictions as the contributory conditions (*pratyaya*) to receive the general retributive fruit of the three evil realms and their coarse manifestations.
[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "Furthermore, he beheld... to "...the scriptures," the eight thousand worlds are designated as the "Buddhas, Holy Lords, and Lions.

This is analyzed according to four permutations: first, those who are holy but not lords, such as the followers of the Three Vehicles; second, those who are lords but not holy, such as various national rulers; third, those who are both lords and holy;
and fourth, those who are neither holy nor lords, such as ordinary worldlings. The present case corresponds to the third permutation.
The teaching that can express the One Vehicle is called the "Sūtra"; the principle expressed therein is called "subtle and profound," "sudden exposition," "pure and great," and "foremost.
That which is articulated through the eightfold voice without confusion is called "pure sound"; that which skillfully accords with the capacities of sentient beings is called "gentle and soft";
that which contains no mention of the Two Vehicles is called "teaching for Bodhisattvas"; and that which expresses without error is called "Brahmic sound" (*brahma-svara*), where "Brahma" means...
It is pure; it speaks only of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and because this profound Dharma-realm is all-encompassing and harmonious, it is called "wondrous.

Because it accords with the capacities of beings without error, it is said to cause people to delight in hearing it. Eighteen thousand principal and attendant teachings are spoken together, each within its own world, and because they are free from crookedness and deviation, it is called the "Right Dharma.
Because the principles are revealed without concealment, it is called "Illumination. One takes these qualities as the name, and thus it is called "Buddha."

In the true principle of the Dharma, there are indeed distinct Bodhisattvas; for those two types of capacities, they are called "enlightening sentient beings," though the text omits the demonstration of their entry [into the stages], as these are extensively detailed in the *Xing*, *Zhu*, *Xiang*, and *Di* [stages].
Furthermore, it says: "The Buddha’s awakening is unturbid, hence it is called 'clear'; the Buddha’s awakening is uninterrupted, hence it is called 'pure';
the Buddha’s awakening reaches the ultimate benefit, hence it is called 'gentle'; being free from rigidity, it is called 'soft'."
[Sūtra] Question: Why do many sūtras frequently use the Ganges sands as a metaphor? Answer: There are five meanings for this explanation: first, because the sands are numerous;
second, because it is a practice common among worldly people to perform meritorious acts by entering the water to wash away sins forever and, upon death, be reborn in heaven;

third, because although the kalpa of destruction passes, the name [of the Ganges] remains constant; fourth, because the Buddha often resorts to this location to proclaim the sublime Dharma; fifth, [because the sands represent the vastness of the teachings].
Because all people entrust themselves to it, many analogies are used. When first emerging from the lake, it is forty *li* on each of its four sides, eighty *li* in length, and forty *li* in width;
in the center, it is twenty *li* wide, ten *li* long, and one cubit deep. There are no places where it is not reached by sand, and there are eighty thousand distinct varieties.
It is as fine as flour—these are the analogies used.

[Sūtra] Or there may be those who practice giving and so forth. First, having seen others in other lands practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), [the text] provides a general explanation of their names.
Question: What is meant by "perfection" (*pāramitā*)? Answer: In the Sanskrit language, this is called *pāramitā*, which means "reaching the other shore.

It refers to reaching the shore of the principle of enlightenment (*bodhi*) and nirvāṇa. Because the sense of "that which is reached" is the same, they are collectively named *pāramitā*. Next, the names are explained individually.
Regarding the first, giving (*dāna*), there are three types: material wealth, fearlessness, and the Dharma. Material wealth benefits the bodies of others; fearlessness benefits their minds;

and the Dharma benefits them by nourishing their roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*). Thus, all three benefit others. If one considers the retribution for oneself, they result in the attainment of great wealth in future lives.
Among these, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) comprises all six types of wealth, while fearlessness is subsumed under both giving and ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is material wealth, while the other four perfections consist of the dharma of fearlessness;
the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the perfection of giving encompasses all six, which is precisely this same meaning.

"Giving" takes as its intrinsic nature the three types of action (*trikarma*) arising from non-attachment (*alobha*). (The commentary explains: regarding the practice, the essence is derived as non-attachment together with the associated volition (*cetanā*) and the three types of action, taking the benefit of others as its essence.)

buried for a long time it does not change, and even after a hundred refinements it does not become light. The *Shuji* (Commentary) says: "The character 'jin' (gold) is a pictographic character (*xiangxing zi*).

It signifies that earth can produce gold. This character is simple; now, by placing two 'earth' radicals on the left and right, it clarifies that gold is contained within—this is its pictographic nature."

During the time of the Xia dynasty, they were created by Xi Zhong. It is also pronounced as *jū*; in antiquity, "carriage" (*chē*) was pronounced like *jū*, because the vehicle is that in which people reside.

[Commentary] Regarding the second precept for bhikṣus who uphold the discipline, there are three aspects: the restraint of conduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), the gathering of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and [the welfare of sentient beings].
The *abhidharma* on benefiting sentient beings states that the "vow of restraint" (*saṃvara*) is so called because it sustains body and mind and prevents the commission of various evils;

the "vow of gathering virtuous dharmas" (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) is so called because it sustains the causes of bodhi; and the "vow of benefiting sentient beings" (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*) is so called because it sustains great compassion.
Regarding the etymological explanation: guarding, abiding, and being free from faults is termed "vow" (*śīla*); the rules of conduct (*vidhi*) are termed "dharma. Furthermore...
"Discipline" (*vinaya*) refers to the discipline of the Dharma; because it is the ethical conduct of the Dharma, it is called "Dharma-discipline.

Regarding its essence, the *Abhidharma* also takes the three vehicles as its essence. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 42, states: "The essence of the seven classes of *prātimokṣa* discipline consists of those who are householders and those who have gone forth.
This refers exclusively to the two karmas of body and speech. As for the essence of wholesome phenomena, there are... [text continues].

This means that after a bodhisattva has received the vows, all the accumulation of wholesome dharmas through the three types of action for the sake of great enlightenment constitutes the essence of the *śīla* of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-śīla*).
Furthermore, the essence of the *śīla* of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*) also consists of the three types of action. As this sutra states:

"Going to the place where the Buddha is to inquire about the unsurpassed path" constitutes the *śīla* of wholesome dharmas; "thereby abandoning [attachment to] pleasant lands and so forth" constitutes the *śīla* of benefiting sentient beings.
The shaving [of hair] and so forth constitute the *vinaya-saṃvara* (precept of restraint); this is followed by the detailed classification of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), and so forth.

[Sūtra]: "To be clad" (pī; according to the *Fangyan*, it means to spread out or to dishevel). Here, it also carries the meaning of "to wear. The correct term for "one who is clad in the Dharma robes" is "one who wears" (pí;
according to the *Yi* gloss, it means to use, to wear, or to gird on).
[Commentary: Regarding the *Pañcarājaka-sūtra*, there were once five kings who questioned one another and each set forth what they cherished:
first, a garden with flowers and fruits; second, a beautiful woman of fine complexion; third, excellent chariots, horses, and weaponry; and fourth, the pleasures of hunting and sport.
One great king then spoke in succession of the defects of these things: that the flowers and fruits would soon wither, decay, and break off; that the woman... [would likewise perish].
There is the suffering of separation from those one loves; there are battles involving chariots and horses where beings kill one another; and there is the injury and harm caused by hunting.

Since these are contrary to compassion, it is better to weary of old age and death and seek the eternal Nirvana. Upon hearing this, the Four Heavenly Kings all went to the Buddha’s dwelling, left the household life, and practiced the Way.
[Commentary] Question: Regarding the "three types of patience" mentioned in the *Śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (唯識) also speaks of three patiences:
first, enduring enmity and harm (*kṣānti-āghāta-marṣaṇa*); second, accepting suffering (*duḥkha-adhyavasāna-kṣānti*); and third, discerning the Dharma (*dharma-pravicaya-kṣānti*).

If one cannot endure enmity, one abandons those [beings], and thus it is not called "patience. Because one is able to endure, one does not abandon sentient beings. Explanation: This refers to the patience of enduring enmity (*āghāta-marṣaṇa-kṣānti*).

Because one can accept oppressive circumstances with composure, it is explained as "the patience of acceptance" (*anupaghāta-kṣānti*). Because one thoroughly examines phenomena, it is explained as "the patience of examining phenomena" (*dharma-nidhyāna-kṣānti*).

By observing that phenomena are non-dual in terms of being adverse or favorable, and by taking non-aversion, diligence, careful wisdom, and the three types of action—of body, speech, and mind—as its essence, one endures the harm of enemies;
this is the "patience toward beings" (*sattva-kṣānti*) arising in the present text, which is characterized by acceptance.
