though they differ in form, their essence and principle are no different. "Fundamental" refers to the dharma-nature of a single thought-moment, while "derivative" refers to the three worlds.
In terms of phenomena (*dharma*), there is a beginning and an end; in terms of principle (*li*), there is neither beginning nor end. This is merely an interpretation based on my own understanding;

I shall not trouble you with further elaboration (and so forth). [Commentary]: Regarding this explanation, from "single, shallow, solitary, and unique" onwards, the intent of the commentary is to explain the ten pairs of provisional and real [teachings].

If the first five pairs—the causes—are absent, then it is single, shallow, solitary, and unique. If the latter five pairs—the fruits—are absent, then it is likewise single, shallow, solitary, and unique.

Even if many dharmas are enumerated, it is difficult to distinguish between the provisional and the real, or the Great and the Small; this does not mean that practice and understanding do not coexist.

To label something merely "provisional" or "real" is not profound, and to call it "shallow" is a biased preference. To speak of "only samādhi" or "only wisdom," or of "only emptiness" or "only existence," is inconsistent with the Mahāyāna teachings. Let those with eyes behold this!
[Commentary] That the teaching for worldly people is established as the cause is the position of Cien (Ci'en). Furthermore, it differs from others regarding the "three and four":

Guangzhai [asserts] that the three are provisional and the one is real; others say that the three are bondage and liberation while the four are cause and effect—this is likely incorrect (and so forth).
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "capable of [attaining] up to the sudden," this gives rise to one member of the sixth pair of "essence and function" among the five subsequent pairs.

[Record] As for the statement that these are the "functioned upon" (the objects), and that the remaining four pairs all derive their names by being contrasted with the "capable of" (the subject), this is to be understood according to the section on "gradual and sudden" below.

It is said: "Now, it is known that the arising of function and the functions themselves are gradual and so forth; therefore, function belongs to the 'capable of using' (the subject), while the four pairs below belong to the 'used' (the object).
If one considers function in relation to the essence (*tattva*), function is the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) and the essence is the *dharmakāya* (dharma body); thus, function is the object.
If one considers the four functions such as the gradual and the sudden, then function is the subject, because the *saṃbhogakāya* preaches the sudden and so forth (reflect on this).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the phenomena are mind, thought, and consciousness," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains "mind" (*citta*) as the eighth consciousness because it "accumulates" (*cita*) all seeds and gives rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

It explains "thought" (*manas*) as the eight consciousnesses in their totality because they "discern" (*ālambana*)—that is, each discerns the objects of its own respective aspect of appearance (*nimittabhāga*) and seeing (*darśanabhāga*).
It explains "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) as referring specifically to the seventh [consciousness] because it "thinks" (*manana*).
The eighth consciousness is termed *manas* because it constantly and deliberatively reflects upon itself as an internal self;
it is called *manas* because it serves as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the subsequent arising of the seven consciousnesses.

The first six consciousnesses are termed *vijñāna* (cognition) because they individually cognize their respective objects; that is, the six consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and so forth—are called "cognizing consciousnesses" because they can cognize objects such as sounds.
Because the six objects are clearly distinguished, "discernment" (*vijñapti*) refers specifically to the differentiation of objects; this is a general name for the eight consciousnesses.

The eighth [consciousness] takes its own self-characteristics and the two divisions of the seen and the seeing as its object; the seventh takes the seeing-division of the eighth as its object; the sixth takes the image-aspect of the eighth's seen and seeing divisions as its object;
and the first five take the image-aspect of the eighth as their object—all are capable of discerning their respective objects extensively.

As the treatise states (and so forth), what is now called "pure and impure karma" refers to the seventh [consciousness], which clings to the eighth [ālayavijñāna] as being the self through the four afflictions of self-delusion, self-love, self-view, and self-pride;
this is the innate clinging to a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*), which is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) and does not create karma.

The sixth [consciousness], however, possesses both the discriminative and the innate types of the two kinds of clinging to a self—the self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*) and the self of persons—and it creates both general and specific types of karma. The former [the seventh consciousness]... [as previously stated].
The five consciousnesses are associated only with greed, hatred, and delusion; they are co-nascent with dharmas and the self, and thus I do not create karma.
If one says that what is impure is entirely of the nature of parikalpita (imagined), it is called "impure. All eight consciousnesses are of the nature of paratantra (dependent).

The essence of the eighth consciousness is vipāka (maturation), unobscured and indeterminate, and is therefore called "pure" and does not create karma. The sixth consciousness takes the teachings of the Three Vehicles as its object and is untainted (anāsrava).
The seeds perfumed by these [factors] are called "pure karma. Among them, the first seven are the perfumers (*vāsaka*), while the eighth is the perfumed (*vāsya*).

Perfuming that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is called pure karma; perfuming that which is tainted (*sāsrava*) is called impure karma. Impurity and so forth belong to the nature of parikalpita (imagined), whereas pure karma is untainted.
Based on the nature of the eight consciousnesses, both the perfumer and the perfumed are seeds; being tainted, they belong to the nature of paratantra (dependent).

The general name is "expedient means" (*upāya*), while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is "reality" (*tattva*). Therefore, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) within the *Vijñaptimātratā* are subsumed here as the dyad of expedient means and reality in this present sutra.

[Commentary] Regarding the expedient means and reality of teaching and practice, the *Ji* (Record) states: "The teaching that manifests the stages of practice for oneself refers to the forty-two stages, which are profound."

The "shallow" [teachings] differ in name as they specifically explain practice; the "small difference" refers to those teachings that explain principle, which lack any progressive advancement. [Commentary:
The various sprouts are a metaphor for the various gradual and sudden [practices] of one's own cultivation; the capacities of others to be transformed are likewise gradual.
The sudden [approach] is not the same.
In the *Commentary*, regarding the cultivation of causes and realization of fruits, there are both gradual and sudden aspects. Within the pair of one's own practice of cause and fruit:

that which proceeds from the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) into the perfect fruit is called "gradual"; that which proceeds from the initial generation of the bodhicitta to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is called "sudden. From... [the text continues].
Because within the section on the gradual and sudden arising of essence and function, there is both the real and the provisional, the Record states that "the meaning is inclusive.

[The *Shu* (Commentary) says: "The gradual is inherently incompatible," etc.; the Record explains that because the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) vehicles do not abandon the Small Vehicle, they are also incompatible with the Sudden.

Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas of the three teachings have not yet entered the reality, I now say: it is not that they do not abandon the Small, nor is it that they have abandoned the Great; it is not that they are not Bodhisattvas... [text continues].
[Saṃghabhadra] alone does not enter the ultimate [truth], as even the Small Vehicle enters it; therefore, one must not speak of it in a partial manner (reflect on this).

[Commentary on the *Śū*]: Regarding the specific and general benefits, the *Jì* states: "Among the preceding gradual and sudden [teachings], there was 'half-and-half' present at the beginning of the gradual.

Now, the 'half' that extends to the subsequent refers to the fact that while previously [the teaching] was restricted to the beginning of the gradual—the Deer Park—it now generally includes the Deer Park as well as the Vaipulya [sūtras]; thus, it extends to the subsequent."

[Commentary]: "All three are worldly" means that the four flavors of the three preceding teachings are all subsumed within the three *siddhāntas*, because they are viewed in relation to the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth) of the *Lotus Sūtra*;
however, if considered according to their respective divisions, they are not the same.
[Commentary: Regarding the "principle of the quiescence of all phenomena," the Record states that both the two principles of the ultimate and the conventional are ineffable. This is as it says:
"The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding," which means the conventional principle is ineffable; and "the true mark," which means the ultimate principle is ineffable.
Both are non-dual.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding those who seek the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions, the prediction [of their future attainment] concerns these various causes and conditions of the past and present.
That which was the cause and condition of the seven expedient means in the past is precisely the cause and condition for the teaching of the present.
[Commentary: Regarding all phenomena, principles, objects, and wisdom up to the provisional and the ultimate, there are two kinds:

first, wisdom; second, the gates of wisdom. The Treatise states that there are two types of profundity: first, the profundity of realization, which refers to wisdom; second, the profundity of scripture (*āgama*), which refers to the gates of wisdom.
*Āgama* is translated as "teaching" (*jiao*) or "transmission" (*zhuan*), meaning the transmission of the teachings of other Buddhas.
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of "wisdom" (*jñāna*): it refers to the meaning of the "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākāra-sarvajña-jñāna*).

"Explanation" means that the wisdom of the Omniscient One is called the "knowledge of all aspects. Its essence encompasses both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and is thus termed "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*).

This refers to the state of *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi* at the stage of Buddhahood. Now, as for "all aspects," according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin), it corresponds to the "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The single category of "all-aspect omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is that which is realized. Regarding the term "all-aspect omniscience": "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) refers to the person;
"second knowledge" refers to the knowledge realized by that person. Thus, it is called "knowledge of knowledge. Regarding the statement that its essence encompasses both nature and characteristics:
this means the essence of what is realized encompasses both the two fruits of *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*. *Nirvāṇa* is the nature, while *bodhi* is the characteristic.
Now it is said that both *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi* possess both provisional and ultimate aspects. As it is said that *nirvāṇa* has three natures:

"pure by nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*) is the ultimate, while "purified through expedient means" (*upāya-viśuddha*) is the provisional. The three types of *bodhi* are likewise so; because the provisional is subsumed under the gate of wisdom (*prajñā*), it should be distinguished [from the ultimate].

Next, regarding the explanation of "omniscience" (*sarvajña*): this is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is precisely the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). The word "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is repeated for emphasis.

This refers to the object of the term "subsequently attained wisdom" (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). Now, I maintain that subsequently attained wisdom is provisional and should be subsumed under the category of "wisdom-gate" (*jñāna-mukha*);
it should not be used to explain actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). Furthermore, there are five kinds of wisdom that exhaustively encompass all phenomena, termed "all-aspect" (*sarvākāra*):
first, the essence of wisdom, which is *tathatā* (suchness)—now I maintain this is the substance of wisdom itself; second, the aspect of wisdom...

This means that the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) are what is meant here; the fundamental is the ultimate (*tattva*), while the subsequently attained is the provisional (*upāya*).
The three wisdoms, accompanied by sands-of-the-Ganges virtues, the ten powers (*daśabala*), and the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), are also merely provisional wisdom.
The causes of the four wisdoms—namely, the teachings that express them and the myriad practices—are also merely provisional. The objects of the five wisdoms refer to such characteristics as these.
Now, it is said that the objects [of cognition] encompass both provisional and ultimate realms.

Although this master claims that all phenomena are fully subsumed within these current ten pairs, he only includes three pairs—phenomena and principle, teaching and practice, and cause and effect—while the remaining pairs are entirely missing; how, then, can this be called "complete"? As for the three pairs:
the nature of wisdom is principle, while its characteristic is phenomena; wisdom is the result, while its companion is the cause; and wisdom is the teaching, while its companion is practice.

Because wisdom (*jñāna*) and its object (*viṣaya*) encompass both phenomena (*artha*) and principle (*tattva*), they subsume the three pairs [of profundities]. The present text cites them as "all phenomena" and so forth:
"phenomena" refers to the profundity of meaning; "principle" refers to the profundity of essence; "object" refers to the profundity of the basis;
and "wisdom" refers to the profundity of internal realization. Therefore, all are described as "real."

[Commentary]: Regarding the "opening and closing" of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision through their being fully realized, the Record states: "The provisional realization is the opening, and the full realization is the closing.

This is likely an error; rather, it should be understood that the first two knowledges and four eyes represent the opening, while the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the Buddha-eye represent the closing. Therefore, it says "all have been [realized]."

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "if one's own benefit is complete, benefiting others is necessarily so," this means that if one’s self-benefit is complete in both the provisional and the real, then the transformation of others is likewise complete in both the provisional and the real.
[Treatise]: As for the Buddhas attaining the benefit of the Great Matter (*mahā-kṛtya*), the Commentary states: "The Great Matter arises from the distinct; yet each must ultimately be integrated."

This means that although the Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of the Great Matter, sentient beings were unable to bear it; therefore, he differentiated and taught the One Vehicle as three.
It is called "previously common" because it was common to both the four flavors and two teachings of the Two Vehicles, as well as the three teachings of the Bodhisattvas.

[Commentary] Quoting the treatise on the five kinds of profundity: first, profundity of meaning, because it is the meaning of differentiation; second, profundity of essence, because it is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
third, profundity of internal realization, because it is known internally by correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and cannot be attained by other forms of knowledge;
fourth, profundity of reliance, because the *dharmadhātu* and *dharmatā* are the fundamental basis of all Buddhas; fifth, unsurpassed profundity, because its essence is supreme—namely, Great Bodhi.
"Ti" (提) refers to the fruit of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment that is realized. Its profundity of meaning is the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*);
its profundity of essence is the nature of True Suchness; its profundity of internal realization is because it reveals the inner True Suchness of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).
Its profundity of reliance is that it further reveals True Suchness itself. In sum, this "unexcelled profundity" is simply the nature and characteristics of wisdom.

Regarding the first, second, fourth, and sixth [of the six meanings], these are the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*); the third and fifth are the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), which are the characteristics of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).

To state the meaning: the meaning is profoundly deep. As for the meaning of differentiation (*prabheda-artha*), it refers to the various names contained within True Suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding the meaning of differentiation:

as it is said, "the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of quiescence," "the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)," "the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*"), "the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*"), "the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*"), "the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*"), "the non-falsity (*amṛṣā-dharmatā*"), and so forth.
Regarding the "three jewels as one essence" (*ekasvabhāva-triratna*) in terms of their various meanings, it is said that their meaning is profound.
To speak of the profundity of the essence (*svabhāva-gambhīra*) means that True Suchness (*tathatā*) serves as the foundational essence for all phenomena; this is called "profound.

Regarding "internal realization" (*pratyātma-vedya*), although both the subject that realizes and the object realized are called profound, here we take the object realized and not the subject that realizes. Regarding "reliance" (*niśraya*): *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "言依止" (regarding reliance).*
Suchness (*tathatā*) serves as the basis for both delusion and awakening: through delusion regarding suchness, one undergoes the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);

through awakening to suchness, one attains the realization of *nirvāṇa*. Here, we take it as the basis for awakening, not the basis for delusion. Regarding the term "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*), it applies generally to both *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *nirvāṇa*.

When contrasted with what precedes, it is described as unsurpassed. If we distinguish between cause and fruit, *bodhi* is the cause and *nirvāṇa* is the fruit; thus, [this term] specifically excludes *bodhi*.
Regarding the title *The Treatise on the Gate of Wisdom*: this gate is profoundly deep and possesses two meanings: first, its essence is wondrous; second, it is difficult to comprehend.

As for the wondrousness of its essence, the treatise cites a sūtra which says: "This gate of wisdom is difficult to see, difficult to awaken to, difficult to know, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter.

It enumerates these five difficulties. Regarding the term "difficult to see," it is because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not know it; this is due to the fact that it is the object of expression (*abhidheya*).
1. Because the meaning is profound, its gateway is difficult to see; 2. because the essence of wisdom is profound, its gateway is difficult to awaken to; 3.
because wisdom is realized through internal realization, its gateway is difficult to know; 4. because the basis of wisdom is profound, its gateway is difficult to understand;
5. because wisdom is unsurpassed and profound, its gateway is difficult to enter. Thus, the five difficulties of the teaching are now correlated with the five kinds of profundity of wisdom.

The intent of the Commentary (*śāstra*) is that because the wisdom of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is profound, it is difficult to understand; and because the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are profound, they are difficult to enter and difficult to perceive.

Regarding the "three great masters" who do not provide a corresponding record [of this], the view that they correspond to the three types of wisdom prior to the stages is likely incorrect (and so forth).

[Commentary] Regarding the "Gate of Wisdom" up to "Principle, Teaching, Expedient Means, and Reality," the treatise states that while eight types are manifested, the scriptural text contains only six phrases:
(1) receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the profound sutras; from "having previously drawn near to the Buddha" downward is (2) practicing the profound sutras;
from "practicing them to the end" downward is (3) the profound practice of the fruit, starting from "valiantly."
The fourth is the *Sūtra on the Profundity of the Mind of Increasing Merit* (Catur-vṛddhi-guṇa-citta-gambhīra-sūtra), beginning from the section on "Universal Gate" (*Samantamukha*).

The fifth is the *Sūtra on the Profundity of the Mind of Delightful and Sublime Matters* (Kṣipra-manojña-vastu-citta-gambhīra-sūtra), beginning from the section on "Accomplishment. The sixth is the *Treatise on the Unsurpassed Profundity* (Anuttara-gambhīra-śāstra);

regarding the addition of the "difficult-to-understand dharma," it refers to the Tathāgata’s ability to know [it]. The seventh is the "Profundity of Entry" (*Praveśa-gambhīra*); the sūtra states that the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of what was taught according to suitability is difficult to understand.
Regarding the explanation of these eight [qualities], they are not shared with Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;

because the profound discourse on the maintenance [of the Dharma] is unknown to all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, these eight points are established to reveal that the expressive teaching is called "profound.
The first point reveals that the Buddha, throughout incalculable eons, made offerings to various Buddhas and received, maintained, read, and recited [the teachings] from those Buddhas.
Because this Dharma-gate is thus, it is profoundly deep. Regarding the second phrase, "exhaustively practicing the immeasurable path-dharmas of all Buddhas," the practice is profound.
In the present text, these are combined as "the profundity of practice" because receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting constitute both the benefit of merit and the benefit of wisdom;
therefore, they are unified into one. If one follows the subsequent passage, it says: "Externally, one encounters many Buddhas and receives their teachings."

The essential point is that the first phrase refers to the depth of wisdom (*jñāna*), while the second phrase praises the immeasurability of true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*). If one correlates this with the provisional and the real, it constitutes the "teaching of reality" (*śāsana-tattva*).
The third phrase, "the profound practice of the fruit through courageous diligence," refers to the "fruit" (*phala*) as being decisive, pure, and valiant;

it denotes the capacity to endure toil and fatigue so that all actions are accomplished, which is termed "decisive fruition. Alternatively, by means of diligence, all that is undertaken is brought to completion.

Having attained [this state], one now obtains the supreme fruit; this name is profoundly deep. The first interpretation concerns practice alone; the second interpretation holds that the fruit is induced by practice.

Regarding the fourth phrase, "one whose fame is widely renowned": because one's merit increases, the mind is profoundly deep. Because the name resounds afar, it is heard universally by both the mundane and the noble.
Encouraging oneself, one applies oneself diligently to cultivation; thus, the mind rejoices as its own merit further increases, or [the same occurs] for others.
To cause [the roots of goodness] to increase: if one follows the explanation in the subsequent commentary, this explains provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*);
if one follows the "Duality of Wisdom" section, this constitutes the practice of expedient means (*upāya-caryā*); if one follows the intent of the *Śāstra*, all four phrases explain the teaching;

if one follows the intent of the *Sūtra*, the first two phrases represent the teaching and practice of the initial vehicle, while the latter two represent the practice and teaching of the subsequent vehicle. Therefore, they are now combined as the "Expedient Means of Teaching and Practice."
It is indeed so.
[Commentary] The treatise explains the accomplishment up to the provisional and the real regarding essence and function, stating:
"The fifth is the accomplishment of profound and unprecedented dharmas. This refers to the mind of wondrous and sublime matters being profound because the dharmas accomplished are unprecedented.
The mind capable of accomplishing swift, wondrous, and supreme matters is also called the "Swift, Wondrous, and Wondrous Mind Teaching" because it explains those matters.
The commentary states: The principle to be accomplished, being endowed with myriad virtues, is named "Swift and Wondrous Matter";

the mind capable of accomplishing that wondrous matter is named the "Swift and Wondrous Mind Teaching. According to its essence and function, its provisional and ultimate aspects, this is the mind capable of accomplishment. This is...

The phrase "using the name 'wondrous and marvelous matters'" refers, according to the subsequent text, to the establishment of the actualized principle; as this follows the treatise (*śāstra*), it is still considered scripture (*deśanā*), hence it is called "spoken.
Regarding the difficulty of understanding the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) and so forth, it is said that they are "unsurpassed, most profound, and deeply entered.

As for the "difficult-to-understand dharmas" mentioned in the sixth line of the treatise, these are known by the Tathāgata; they are unsurpassed and most profound precisely because they are extremely difficult to understand.

Because the Tathāgata is able to know this, this Dharma-gate achieves the state of being unsurpassed; or rather, the essence of the dharma that is difficult to understand is itself unsurpassed, for it can be known only by a Buddha, and is therefore profound.
Regarding the seventh phrase, "that which is spoken according to what is appropriate": for those who reach understanding, they enter the profound.
For those who enter the profound, names, chapters, and phrases are established as difficult to attain; thus, the Buddha himself maintains and upholds them so that others may enter and understand.
The intention differs from that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others; there are two meanings to this "entry": first, it is difficult to enter because the Buddha himself has realized it;

second, what is taught according to suitability causes others to enter the Dharma. Thus, the fact that the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) is difficult to understand is called "profound" (*gambhīra*).

These two phrases, according to the following text, merely conclude the provisional [teachings] as being suited to the capacities of sentient beings; they do not refer to skillful means (*upāya*), which is why it is said to be "difficult to understand" in relation to this passage.
This is because it takes as its essence that which is entered; "according to what is appropriate" refers to the function of transforming others.
Regarding the eighth phrase, "all śrāvakas up to those who do not know," the *Xuanzan* explains that this is not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
It states that because their activities differ from those of the two vehicles—specifically, because they perform external benefit and maintain internal benefit—it constitutes profundity.
This passage does not exist in the sutra; the phrase "all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know" is absent from the initial praise of virtues.
[Commentary] The *Śāstra* explains that from "attaining Buddhahood" up to "the provisional and the real are identical," the sutra says:

"Śāriputra, since I attained Buddhahood, I have used various causes and conditions and various parables. This refers to the preceding praise of what has been realized and the Dharma that has been taught.

"Excellently Wondrous" (勝妙) below is an exclamation praising the Tathāgata as the Teacher capable of realizing and expounding the Dharma. This "Excellently Wondrous" refers to the treatise (*śāstra*) which cites the Sūtra;
next below, it should state: "For what reason, Śāriputra? Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have achieved mastery in their exposition.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata has achieved various skillful means (*upāya*), various knowledges and insights (*jñāna-darśana*), various mindfulnesses and contemplations (*smṛti-vipaśyanā*)," and so forth.

Regarding the words [of the treatise, etc.], the introduction of the treatise itself explains: Because the Tathāgata has accomplished four kinds of merit, he is able to transform and deliver sentient beings.

First, accomplishment of going: by means of various skillful means, from descending from Tuṣita Heaven until his parinirvāṇa, he is able to go to the ten directions and manifest inconceivable transformations such as the eight major signs. Second, accomplishment of transformation: namely, the planting...
The third is the ultimate accomplishment of the three qualities, which refers to various forms of mindfulness and contemplation;

it is by means of these that the causes for accomplishing those dharmas are explained. This is because, through possessing such knowledge and vision, one is able to manifest within the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) the presence of all causes of defilement that can summon suffering, as well as all causes of purification that can realize cessation, and so forth. (etc.)

Because it accords with the Dharma through conditions, it is called "concordant" (*saṃprayukta*), which carries the meaning of harmonious union and realization. Regarding the fourfold exposition of accomplishment:

it refers to various modes of expression by means of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and so forth. In the present text, "going toward accomplishment" (*yāna-siddhi*) is contrasted with cause and fruit, and with the provisional and the real.
[Commentary] Regarding the citation of the treatise from "explaining through countless skillful means" to "the intent is the same," the commentary states:

"The 'transforming and bringing to maturity' corresponds to the second 'accomplishment' in the treatise, while the 'accomplishment of preaching the Dharma' corresponds to the third 'accomplishment' in the treatise."

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the meaning of gradual and sudden is the same," this refers collectively to the teaching and preaching of the Dharma, which generally belong to the Tathāgata’s application of gradual and sudden transformations.
The accomplishment of the preaching of the Dharma is precisely the third merit of ultimate perfection within this treatise; therefore, the treatise says:
Furthermore, regarding the various modes of mindfulness and contemplation, the *Śāstra* explains the attainment of the past as follows:

"There is another meaning concerning 'various skillful means,' which demonstrates the manifold faults of the heterodox teachings of non-Buddhists and the manifold merits of the true Dharma of the Buddhas.
As the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded verbal teachings through countless skillful means to guide [beings]."
Regarding the phrase "guiding sentient beings," since it speaks of manifesting equality externally, it refers to the accomplishment of their transformation and edification.
Furthermore, the explanation of "innumerable skillful means" consists of four further points: first, causing them to enter wholesome dharmas; second, severing all doubts;
third, causing them to enter superior and transcendent wisdom; and fourth, gathering sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) so that they may attain liberation.

Therefore, within this explanation of the four phrases, one turns away from the heterodox to enter the orthodox, advances in goodness and destroys evil, enters superior wisdom oneself, and brings others to liberation;
these are assigned in sequence, even unto causing them to be free from all attachments, as explained at length in the treatise (etc.).

[Commentary] The citation from the treatise explaining that the Tathāgata’s skillful means reach "deeply into the boundless" and so forth refers to the third section of the treatise on the accomplishment of teaching and transformation, specifically the ultimate accomplishment of the third merit. The second explanation therein states:
"Furthermore, regarding the various forms of knowledge and vision: these are the inconceivable realms accomplished by oneself, which are not shared with Śrāvakas or Bodhisattvas."

Because they are identical, as the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, because the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision reaches the further shore through skillful means, he who has reached the further shore excels all other Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the third phrase of the Treatise, it says: "Furthermore, regarding various forms of mindfulness and contemplation, as the Sūtra says:
'Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision is vast, profound, far-reaching, unobstructed, and unimpeded.'"
[The Commentary] states that the two types of accomplishment (*siddhi*) mentioned here—namely, "fear" (*bhaya*) and so forth—are collectively designated as "benefit" (*artha*).
[The Commentary] further cites the treatise’s various classifications of what pleases the minds of the multitude, concluding that this constitutes "benefit.

This refers to the fourth section of the *Siddhiviniścaya-śāstra*, which explains that there are seven kinds of accomplishment. First, "various accomplishments" (*nānā-siddhi*), as in the Sūtra: "Śāriputra, all..."
Because the Buddha-Tathāgata has deeply entered the boundless and accomplished all unprecedented dharmas, the treatise states:
"From 'deeply entering the boundless' in the sutra downward is the discourse on the various accomplishments. It says:

"Second is the accomplishment of speech, whereby he attains five kinds of exquisite and beautiful voices to preach the Dharma, as the sutra says: 'The Tathāgata skillfully distinguishes and expounds all dharmas in various ways.'"

This is most pleasing to the hearts of the multitude; the present commentary combines these [points] for the sake of benefit. That is to say, "benefit" (利益) has the same meaning as the *Śāstra*, which states:

"Third, accomplishment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-sampad*); fourth, accomplishment of capability (*bhavyatva-sampad*). The present commentary combines these into the four *siddhāntas* (the four purposes): those who can be transformed and those who cannot.

Regarding what the *Śāstra* calls "accomplishment of characteristics," the *Śāstra* says: "Because there are sentient beings who are vessels for the Dharma whose minds are already satisfied, it is called 'characteristics'."
Accomplishment is further of two kinds: first, for those who are ready (the *pratibhū*), and second, for those with whom a karmic connection is established (*pratyaya-bandha*).

Śāriputra was one who was ready through his superior pride (*adhimāna*). Regarding those ready through a karmic connection: for those who delight in the wondrous Dharma, he manifested signs by chanting "Stop" to cause them to invite him; for those ready through a karmic connection, he remained silent.

For those who did not delight in hearing extensively and had not yet departed from their seats, he manifested signs by chanting "Stop" to cause them to rise and leave; therefore, this is called "Signs."

Regarding the treatise on the four types of those capable of accomplishment: one who is capable of accomplishment is so called because all sentient beings to be converted know that the Tathāgata has accomplished rare and marvelous qualities and is capable of preaching the Dharma. Thus it is said: "Śāriputra, whose faculties have matured, is termed 'one capable of being converted.'"
[Commentary] The passage from "Only Buddhas and Buddhas... to "...achieve immeasurable merit" refers to the fifth phrase of the treatise, which is titled "Achievement of Immeasurable Kinds.
The current text says "merit" (fú), which is likely an error for "inexhaustible" (bù kě jìn).

Because the Buddha’s wisdom fully knows the essence of this true reality (dharmatā) to its ultimate source and foundation, it is called "ultimate" (jiūjìng). It does not merely achieve the myriad conditioned virtues and the myriad unconditioned [virtues].
Because the Buddha’s virtues are also thoroughly exhaustive, it is said that they are accomplished in immeasurable ways and cannot be fully described.
[Commentary] The passage from "The Buddhas are able to know" to "accomplishment through self-realization" refers to the sixth, the accomplishment of the essence of awakening (*bodhi*).

In the sutra, the single phrase "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) refers to the essential nature of the Tathāgatagarbha and the Dharmakāya; because this nature is immutable, it is the essence of awakening.
"Accomplishing the Tathāgata’s capacity to know all dharmas" means that because the Buddha has personally realized them, it is called "accomplishment through personal realization.
[Commentary] Regarding "being able to accord with sentient beings": this is the seventh point, which refers to teaching the methods of practice according to the inclinations of sentient beings.
It signifies accomplishing the Tathāgata’s ability to expound all dharmas; thus, what is stated in this sutra—namely, that "all dharmas are suchness," and so forth—is this very meaning.
These five, six, and seven are collectively categorized as phenomena (śa), principle (li), provisional (quan), and real (shi). Of these, the first two are principle and the latter one is phenomenon.

[Commentary] Regarding the fifth point, the summary of the provisional and the real, the *Ji* states: "The 'one hundred and sixty' refers to the twenty divisions within the combination of self and other—ten from the side of the self representing the provisional, and ten from the side of the other representing the real. When separated, they form two sets of twenty; when combined, they constitute ten."

Question: What is the reason for the two aspects of provisional and real? Answer: There are ten pairs. From the third phrase onward, these are immediately the provisional and real within the essence of the body (*tǐ*).

Now, corresponding to each of the four teachings, there are ten pairs, which constitute the three expressions—following others, following oneself, and following both self and others—for each of the four teachings.
Furthermore, there are those that are able to penetrate, those that are penetrated, and those that are neither able to penetrate nor penetrated. This is it.

Within the teachings established by the Buddha, there are methods that correspond to the words of others (*paravāda*), meanings based on gates that correspond to the intentions of both self and others (*svaparābhiprāya*), and secret, wondrous meanings that correspond to one’s own intention (*svābhiprāya*). Each of the ten pairs consists of these three types of speech;

likewise, the separate conclusion regarding the four teachings relative to one another consists of these three types of speech, and the same applies to the conclusion regarding the four phrases. All provisional means are methods, while all realities are the ultimate truth.
This secret and wondrous [reality] is both provisional and real; this is the meaning of "gate. That which is neither provisional nor real is the substance of the third phrase.
If one encompasses the two within the three, these two are likewise the internal skillful means of the three.
If it were otherwise, it would be the aforementioned method and gate, and not the intent of this chapter; therefore, there is this concluding passage.
[Reflect on this. [Commentary:

Regarding "each according to principle and teaching," etc., it means that verifying the principle and giving rise to the teaching—from the unified to the differentiated—is all termed "transforming others. [Commentary:

Furthermore, the sub-commentary at the end of the *Sanzang Shiji* (Record of the Three Baskets) states: "The former refers to the differentiation of the teachings, yet within the Dharma there are both the general and the specific."
The preceding discussion on the differences between the four teachings regarding names and doctrines was explained in terms of ten pairs;

these are further categorized into three types—general and specific—in relation to oneself and others. Now, while this teaching is general, the dharmas are specific: in the *Zang* (Tripitaka) teaching, there is only "other";

in the *Yuan* (Perfect) teaching, there is only "self"; and in the *Tong* (Shared) and *Bie* (Distinct) teachings, both are considered "self" and "other," with three variations for each through progressive and regressive analysis.

This explains the general nature of these four teachings in their mutual relationship; thus, they are called "general in terms of teaching. However, as for the "particularity of the Dharma," the Perfect Teaching does not communicate with the other treasuries, and the others do not communicate with it.

The Distinct and Shared Teachings communicate only with themselves and others respectively, whereas the Single Self and Single Other do not communicate with each other; this is what is meant by the "particularity of the Dharma."

[Commentary]: Regarding the sixty types of self and other, both general and specific, the *Ji* (Record) states: "In the first stage, self and other are established by means of the general and the specific;

these remain specific self and other. In the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), there are both common and uncommon aspects; in the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), there are the two paths of teaching and realization.

Although this constitutes a single teaching, there is both self and other, appearing as if they were general and specific self and other. Now, however, it is not so; 'self' is exclusively [the former]."
Because they equally perfect others and are consistently identical with the treasury [of the Dharma], it is said that this is precisely the distinct characteristic of self and other.

[Commentary: Regarding the analogy of milk, curd, and clarified butter: in the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings, attaining the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle is called "milk"; being rebuked on that very seat is becoming "curd"; and [attaining the fruit of] the Great Vehicle is "clarified butter."

[Commentary]: "If one follows from the Buddha’s traces," etc., refers to the single basis; this is the secret and wondrous single trace. When self and other are made to correspond, it constitutes the meaning of a "gate.
Therefore, it says: "Following the Tathāgata’s use of skillful means. Next, "following from the introduction" refers to the phrasing concerning both self and other.
As for "one's own practice," it does not mean a solitary practice of the self alone. Since it says "the practitioner follows from cultivation," [it implies that practice is necessarily relational].
This is precisely what leads from the provisional to the real, all culminating in the present sutra as the realization within the body [of the Dharma]. Question:
Why does it not state that the four propositions constitute the "Chapter on Expedient Means"? Answer: The four propositions are themselves the three practices, such as self-cultivation;
since they are already subsumed under the two categories mentioned previously, there is no need for a separate conclusion.

[Commentary] Regarding the question of what constitutes the essence of the "skillful means" (*upāya*) cited by some, there are those who say it refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) following the five perfections (*pāramitā*) of the *Vijñaptimātratā* [system].
Thus, the *Enshū* states: "The *Vijñaptimātratā* speaks of the latter five. There is also an interpretation that the four [perfections] are *Vijñaptimātratā* and does not make this claim;
the *Ryūshū* states: "This refers to the last among the ten perfections in the *Abhidharma-kośa*."
The four [perfections] are comprised solely of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), while the sixth perfection is comprised solely of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*);
however, if one considers the first five perfections, they encompass both fundamental and subsequently attained wisdom, which differs from that commentary.
[Commentary]: The statement that "no one can startle or awaken the Tathāgata when he has entered meditative concentration" distinguishes him from those of the Two Vehicles.

When those of the Two Vehicles enter concentration, they can only emerge upon being startled; for example, when Śāriputra was in concentration, he was struck by a malevolent spirit who had subdued him, and Maudgalyāyana emerged from concentration only after hearing the sound of an elephant king entering the water.
[Commentary: Regarding "the four *siddhāntas* up to mastery": first, when the Buddha enters *samādhi*, the world moves or remains unmoved, because there is a distinction between these states;

second, regarding the observation through the two kinds of *yathābhūta-jñāna*, it is because the principle of phenomena is inherently good; third, regarding arising from *samādhi*, it is to refute others' claim that there is no wisdom apart from *dhyāna*;
fourth, regarding manifesting the Tathāgata’s attainment of mastery, it is because he realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and possesses freedom in both entering and emerging [from it].
Because he possesses the four *siddhāntas*, he is said to be "sovereign" (*svatantra*) in possessing the four *siddhāntas*.

[Commentary: Regarding the mention of Guangzhai among the "Immeasurable" [masters], since the previous reference to the "Old Man" was Guangzhai’s interpretation, it says "the Liang dynasty did not recognize [him]," and so forth.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The reasons for the exclamation are twofold according to the text," the phrasing here is incomplete.

It should read: "The text has two parts: first, the reasons for the exclamation; second, the actual exclamation itself. Within the first part [the reasons], there are two sub-sections: first, clarifying the reasons for the exclamation;

second, from "Taking the essentials" onwards, identifying the object of the exclamation. Within the second part [the actual exclamation], there are again two sub-sections: first, the actual exclamation itself.
Next, the meaning of the exclamation of transcendence is explained. [The Commentary] states:

"The four immeasurables of the Buddha-ground" refers to loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Regarding the term "immeasurable," there are three senses:

first, they take an immeasurable object, for these four arise by taking the *dharmadhātu* and sentient beings as their objects; second, they initiate immeasurable practices, pervading the *dharmadhātu*; [and third, they result in immeasurable fruits].

Because one practices these four within the realms and conducts, three bring about immeasurable fruits: one attains the merit of a Great Brahmā and becomes a Tathāgata. Regarding the characteristics of these practices:

within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and among sentient beings, there are generally three categories. First, for those who lack happiness, giving them joy is called "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*); its essence is non-aversion.

Second, for those who suffer, removing their suffering is called "compassion" (*karuṇā*); its essence is non-harming. Third, for those who possess happiness, assisting in their joy is called "sympathetic joy" (*muditā*).

The essence of this is the root of goodness characterized by joy and freedom from envy. Furthermore, regarding the first [object], one gives rise to the perception of being free from delusion; regarding the second, one gives rise to the perception of being free from hatred;

and regarding the third, one gives rise to the perception of being free from poverty. Moreover, there are three types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*): those with sentient beings as the object (*sattvālambana*), those with phenomena as the object (*dharmālambana*), and those without an object (*anālambana*).

"With sentient beings as the object" refers to forming the perception that all sentient beings obtain happiness. "With phenomena as the object" refers to [forming such a perception] toward those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). "Without an object" refers to... [the perception of] non-arising.

Regarding the statement that the perception of phenomena associated with outflows (*āsrava-dharma-saṃjñā*) is "without an object" (*anālambana*), it means that its object is *tathatā* (suchness), which is free from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-saṃjñā*). The remaining three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) should be understood accordingly.

Here, within a single [state] of the Buddha-ground, these three are present: sentient beings are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); phenomena are the objects of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
and non-objectification is the Middle Way of the primary ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that it "cannot be spoken of" because one has attained the supreme Dharma through cultivation, the *Ji* (Exegesis) explains:
"The term 'attained through cultivation' applies generally to the object, wisdom, practice, and stages; 'self and other' is restricted specifically to the fruit.

As for the four excellences of the object, wisdom, practice, and stages being the causes for attaining [the fruit], the object is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), wisdom is the Prajñā-attribute, and practice is the Liberation-attribute (*vimuktikāya*). These three attributes are first illuminated.

This stage begins with the initial illumination and ends with the ultimate fruit; therefore, the wondrous response and transformation, supernatural powers, and the preaching of the Dharma constitute the two wondrousnesses for the benefit of one’s own retinue.

Because these are what is transformed for others, they pervade the ten wondrousnesses; yet, as they are restricted to the fruit and are termed "attained through cultivation," they are specifically situated therein.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "profound realm," the Record states that while it generally applies to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*) throughout their beginning and end, as well as their retrogression and progression, it is specifically restricted to the Buddha.

"Ordinary beings" refers to the six destinies; "sages" refers to *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and *bodhisattvas*. "Buddha" refers to the ten realms of existence. "Beginning" refers to the initial mind of the four types of sages;

"end" refers to the resultant stage of the four types of sages. "Retrogression" refers to the four miserable destinies; "progression" refers to the human and heavenly realms. Although these are all...
This principle and its scope are termed "universal" because the provisional [teachings] of the nine realms are identical to the reality of the Buddha-realm; thus, it is termed "restricted. Question:

What is the difference between the previous "restriction to the fruit" and this "restriction to the Buddha"? Answer: The former is explained from the perspective of realization (*pratyātmavedya*), while this is explained from the perspective of the nature of the Buddha-realm.
Although there is a distinction in terms of cultivation and nature (*śikṣita* and *prakṛti*), their essence is fundamentally without difference.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage in the *Shu* (Commentary) that begins with "The dharmas... and explains the profound realm, it states: "This is the fundamental principle of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

This means that the realm of principle (*li-jing*) serves as the foundation for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and the starting point for all other teachings. It further explains that within the path of the One Vehicle, the three vehicles are taught through differentiation;

thus, the One Vehicle is the starting point for the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). As for the key to interpreting the meaning: if one were to explain the provisional and the real (*upāya-tattva*), [this text provides the essential framework].
The meaning of this is that this principle serves as both the joints and the keys to the gates.
That which sentient beings rely upon refers to the fact that the beings of the ten realms rely on this principle; it is the foundation for generating the aspiration for enlightenment.

As for its being the "leverage" (píngzhàng), it is because within the Unconditioned Four Noble Truths, one seeks the Way above and transforms suffering and its accumulation below. Thus, it is called the substance of the application of skillful means (quánmó).

The nature and principle (*xingli*) inherently possess the three thousand [realms]. Because one realizes this principle, one is able to transform throughout the ten directions of the world without deliberation;

thus it is called the "substance" (*ti*). Regarding the root source of delusion and enlightenment: "delusion" refers to the six paths of existence, while "enlightenment" refers to the four types of sages;

the principle is used as the fundamental origin. As for the principle that is the basis of the fruition-virtue: the fruition of the three virtues employs this rational nature of the three thousand realms.
It is the foundation. The perfection of a single transformation—that which exhausts all things—is the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
The application of this principle is pervasive and reaches its ultimate limit; that which concludes the five periods of teaching never departs from this principle.

Just as a single mote of dust contains a great chiliocosm of sutras, these ten points all take the principle as their essence; therefore, they are called the "Inconceivable Realm. Now, [the author] says that these ten points are cumbersome...
The reliance of sentient beings upon [the Buddha] is identical whether in delusion or awakening; expedient means and the merit of the fruit are no different;

and the single transformation and the five periods are likewise the same. For example, just as the great earth alone can produce various sprouts, how could it be limited to only ten meanings? (and so forth).
To speak directly of "correspondence" (*pratibimba*) is to explain by way of correlating and contrasting [the concepts] to refute [misconceptions regarding] grace.

[Commentary]: "If one illuminates the nine realms" and below is explained as follows: if it is "self," then the nine realms are the Buddha-realm; if it is "other," then the Buddha-realm is the nine realms;
if it is the cause, it is a single thought-moment; if it is the fruit, it is the realization of wondrous enlightenment—all do not depart from the mental substance of a single thought-moment.
Regarding the statement "within the one, there are the immeasurable," there are nine pairs of examples, following the aforementioned pair of provisional and real.

Since the provisional and the real cannot be definitively established—because one is not fixed as one, yet many are said to be one, and ten are one because one is ten—it is neither one nor ten, yet it is both one and ten;
this is called "the unconditioned. One should reflect on the eight pairs of analogies:
since the ten realms are fully present within the cause, such is the nature of the resultant retribution; therefore, one cannot speak of the cause as the fruit, nor speak of the fruit as the ten.
Because there are causes, it is called "well-spoken"; because it possesses the six paths, it is called "evil-spoken.

Because it possesses the ten suchnesses, it is the "emptiness-speech"; because within one [reality] there are immeasurable [phenomena], it is the "existence-speech. Because in a single thought-moment nothing can be apprehended, it is the "ordinary-speech";

because within the four noble truths there are ordinary beings, it is the "noble-speech. Because within the noble there are ordinary beings, it is the "gradual-speech"; because a single thought-moment possesses [all stages], it is the "sudden-speech," which is the sequential.
Because they arise [simultaneously], it is explained that the ten are mutually inclusive; because they are combined, it is explained that the ten realms are distinct;

because the mind explains that it possesses the dharmas of the ten realms, it is explained that the ten suchnesses of these dharmas are all one mind; because the support explains the existence of the primary retribution, the primary retribution explains that it possesses its support.
Since two thousand worlds constitute the primary retribution and one thousand constitute the support, and as both are identical within a single thought-moment, they cannot be explained in isolation.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "the delusion regarding the phenomena that are the fruits of afflictions [obscures] the principle that is their cause": those who lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* see only within the scripture that the ten directions mutually interpenetrate as dust-motes and lands, all being harmoniously fused, and they claim this is "unspeakably unspeakable.
They do not realize that this phenomenon already exists inherently within the rational nature (*dharmatā*) of the causal stage.

If this principle did not exist inherently from the beginning, then the "three thousand realms in a single thought" (*ichinen sanzen*) and the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants (*shoji funi*) could not be realized. When one realizes this principle, one simply speaks of it as such.

Regarding the contemplation of the aspect of the fruit’s merit, it is said that this refers to the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Since the principle of the fruit is thus, how is the principle of the cause?
If the cause were not fully present, it would be a case of "non-existent now having come into existence," which would not differ from impermanence.

If one says that Mount Sumeru entering a mustard seed is called the gate of karmic function—whereby such a function arises through untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*)—this too would be a case of "non-existent now having come into existence."
Because the principle is not yet complete, the intention of the Great Master here is that this inconceivable function exists precisely because the principle is complete.

The true nature track (*dharmatā-naya*) is the essence, which is eternally constant; the track of following conditions through expedient means (*upāya*) is the function. Contemplate how essence and function are non-dual.

[Commentary]: The reason why "the one contains the immeasurable" refers to the ten realms is as follows: ordinary beings constitute the six destinies; the two vehicles constitute the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha realms;
and the Bodhisattvas of the three teachings constitute the remaining nine realms. The Tathāgata’s thorough penetration of these constitutes the Buddha realm. Below [is the explanation].

[Commentary]: Regarding the explanation based on the stages, the statement that it "penetrates both good and evil" means that because this principle follows conditions, it does not sink even when in evil;
this is because it is unchanging. Thus, it constantly follows conditions while remaining unchanging, and is eternally unchanging while following conditions (reflect upon this).

[Commentary: Regarding the difference in the conditions for conversion between the two Buddhas in the prose section: the "difference in persons" refers to the fact that the various Buddhas and Śākyamuni differ as individuals;

the "difference in dharmas" refers to the fact that the provisional and real teachings of the two Buddhas are each praised separately. In the verse, the two Buddhas are combined; however, this merely combines the "persons" by referring to them collectively as "World-Heroes," while it does not combine their two wisdoms with the dharmas.
As for the combination of persons and dharmas, it occurs when the two Buddhas and the two wisdoms are not distinguished [from one another].
Because these dharmas are consistent, it is said that the principle of the two wisdoms is identical.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the second part opens with praise, etc.": this is similar to the previous explanation concerning the differences in the conditions for conversion;

however, as for the term "different dharmas," because the provisional and real dharmas of all Buddhas differ from the provisional and real dharmas of Śākyamuni, they are called "different dharmas. Therefore, the prose section must open [with a new exposition]. If...
The individual praises of the provisional and the real are also called "opening" (kai). What is now termed "total" (zong) refers to the integration of the two Buddhas without distinction;
it is also called "total" because there is no differentiation between person and dharma, and is thus referred to as "synthesis" (he).
[Commentary]: Regarding the "wish-fulfilling jewel" (*cintāmaṇi*), the *Zhiguan ji* (Record of the Stopping and Contemplation) explains the inconceivable realm as follows:
"The form of the jewel is like that of a mustard seed, yet it possesses great efficacy; according with one's wishes, it provides abundance or scarcity and rains down grain in profusion.

It neither increases nor exhausts, and it even provides the five pure and wondrous desires and the seven treasures of lapis lazuli and crystal. It is neither stored within nor enters from without; it does not deliberate on sequence, nor does it discriminate."

To what extent even insentient things that are neither coarse nor subtle—being merely material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*)—can still function in this way, how much more so the spirit and mind, which are numinous and wondrous;
how could they not possess all dharmas? Therefore, it is called the "Inconceivable Realm. In the *Commentary*, the inconceivable mind is explained in detail:

in a single moment of thought (*kṣaṇa*), the three thousand worlds are present, where the one and the many are sovereign, transcending the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), and being neither internal nor external; their essence is neither vertical nor horizontal, yet they are perfectly integrated.

Spontaneous bestowal and transformation without prior deliberation is called "conformity" (*he*); establishing [teachings] according to capacities is called "conformity" (*he*) without discrimination;

whether responding to the occasion or the capacity, it is neither provisional nor ultimate, which is called "conformity" (*he*); not making distinctions between the coarse and the subtle, but responding to conditions, is called "conformity" (*he*);
providing for beings with abundance or scarcity as desired so that their benefit is inexhaustible is called "conformity" (*he*), like rain falling in profusion—*rang-rang* (profuse) meaning blessing.
[Sūtra] It says: "Those who wish to contemplate the Buddha’s true wisdom—this Dharma of the seven expedient means—is called 'the Buddha’s true wisdom' for these seven types of persons.
Those who do not realize this is an expedient means cannot know even a small portion of it."
[Sūtra] Those who do not understand the direction of this meaning have three types of doubt: first, doubt regarding the teaching; second, doubt regarding the person; and third, self-doubt.

Regarding "doubt regarding the teaching," this refers to mutual contradictions between former and present [teachings]. For example: formerly it was taught that what is attained through the Three Vehicles is identical, whereas now it is taught that the Great and Small Vehicles differ;

formerly it was taught that the Great and Small Vehicles are equally real, whereas now it is taught that the Great is real while the Small is provisional. These constitute four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There are four types of discrimination: first, not knowing that what was previously wrong is now right; second, not knowing that what was previously right is now wrong; third, not knowing whether it was right or wrong both in the past and present;
and fourth, not knowing whether it is right or wrong both in the past and present. Therefore, it is said that "one does not know where this meaning leads. The current commentary states:
"One suspects for oneself that the Three Vehicles one has attained are all provisional; when has it ever been said that the Great [Vehicle] is real? (and so forth). Second, doubting the person.
If the teaching spoken contradicts the person who speaks it, then that person is a Māra. Third, self-doubt:

as Śāriputra said, "I now have doubts regarding my own wisdom and cannot comprehend it," etc. [This refers to] questioning the aforementioned three movements of attachment to the Three Vehicles and the arising of doubt regarding the Three Vehicles.
The Buddha then showed him the teachings of the Three Vehicles; subsequently, when the Bodhisattvas heard this Dharma, their net of doubts was severed.
[Question: Since all [categories] have already been eliminated, why is it now stated that only those of the Two Vehicles harbor doubts? [Answer:

Jizang criticizes Guangzhai for being biased by raising the objection that there are Bodhisattvas who practice the Six Perfections separately; he asks how it is that the doubts of such Bodhisattvas are not clarified.

Furthermore, by inferring from this, since there are no Bodhisattvas who practice the Six Perfections [separately], Cien (Yuanze) combines the two [meanings] according to the interpretation of Jizang.
If even Ear-Whorl (Karṇa-guṇa) did not know that the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles were provisional, how could he have known their reality?
Furthermore, it is said that the "net of doubt" for a bodhisattva does not mean they cling to the past as ultimate and then give rise to doubt upon hearing of the present expedient means;

rather, it is simply that they doubt why the Tathāgata previously taught the three [vehicles] but now teaches only the One Vehicle. If this is so, then before the bodhisattva had heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, what...
Therefore, it is said: "Is this not called failing to practice the Bodhisattva path well?

[Sūtra] The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, has two meanings: first, he can extinguish the darkness of the five stages of dwelling; second, he can manifest the principle of the single reality.
He is named the Sun of Wisdom. Regarding the term "Holy Honored One," among the three types of sages, he is the most honored, being a seer (ṛṣi) possessing the five supernatural powers.
Because among the three vehicles, the Buddha is the greatest of all, he is called the "Great Holy Honored One" (Mahā-ārya-guru).
[Sūtra]: "All shall be struck with alarm and doubt. The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that throughout the entire beginning and end of this single sūtra, there are five kinds of "alarm":
first, "alarm of diminution," which refers to clinging to the parinirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna as ultimate and slandering the parinirvāṇa of the Mahāyāna, thereby diminishing the meaning of "Great."

1. Fear of loss and fear of many activities: This refers to those who have entered the Mahāyāna; when they hear of the Buddha-way, their minds give rise to extensive grasping for the fruits of the Hīnayāna over a long period of practice.
2. Fear of inversion: This refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who calculate the existence of a self and what belongs to a self;

upon hearing this sūtra concerning the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena—they give rise to fear. 3. Fear of regret: This refers to one who regrets [their past actions] with their body and mind.
Realizing the Lesser Vehicle is precisely this mind of regret, which is called "fear of being deceived. Fifth is the fear of being deceived:

those with overweening pride think to themselves, "How can the Buddha deceive us? This is called the fear of being deceived. These five encompass all matters—Great and Small Vehicles, ordinary and noble, internal and external.
[Sūtra] Regarding "those about to fall into a great pit," there are three meanings: first, the pit of wrong views consisting of slandering the Dharma;
second, the pit of karma consisting of slandering the Dharma—these two serve as the causes; third, the Avīci Hell—this one serves as the result.

[Sūtra] Regarding "those with sharp and keen faculties": the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, are "sharp" because they remove defilements, and "keen" because they illuminate without forgetfulness.
[Sūtra] Regarding "clear and lucid wisdom": to comprehend phenomena externally is called "clarity," and to be without delusion internally is called "lucidity."
[Sūtra] Regarding "the mind that is able to revere and believe": to look up toward with veneration is called reverence (*gaurava*);

to have no doubt is called faith (*śraddhā*). [Sūtra] Regarding "stop, stop": in the prose (*gadya*), a single instance of "stop" expresses the intention of what is about to be said; in the verse (*gāthā*), the repetition of "stop" further articulates the startling nature of the teaching.
This is merely a matter of varying the weight of the words.
[Commentary: The fourth section, "Briefly Summarizing Prajñā," uses the single term *prajñā* to refer to the beginning, from form and mind up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is called "extensive. Regarding the record of the intermediate stages up to the Buddha-way, it follows what is said in the section on "Maturation, Ripening, and Liberation":
it means that all [beings] are matured through various skillful means (*upāya*), and does not mean that the Buddha acts as the one who matures them.

[Commentary]: Regarding those who hold biased views that deviate from the sutra, according to the *Ji* (Record), Guangzhai maintained that because this present sutra still contains real śrāvakas, it therefore only teaches and transforms bodhisattvas.
I now say: Guangzhai pointed out that both the teachings of the present and the past contain real, practicing śrāvakas;
whereas Kaishan held that both the present and the past consist only of provisional śrāvakas. Why is this? According to the correct interpretation, if one follows the elder [Vimalakīrti], then...
If there were no "hired servant" (the lowly person), then there would be no one of true practice either in the past or the present.

If [the servant] refers to the impoverished son—that is, the lowly person—then he existed in the past but does not exist now. How then can there still be an impoverished son even after the opening of this sutra?
According to the view of Guangzhai, based on the four types of śrāvakas in the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra), he maintains that such a person truly exists.

[Commentary] The fifth section, "Furthermore," below, judges the prediction for Mahāyāna śrāvakas, stating that it differs from other interpretations. Within the Mahāyāna, [the author] establishes his own view regarding śrāvakas.

According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the four reliances (*catuḥpratisaraṇa*) are called the four fruits; furthermore, in the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) include śrāvakas.
This refers to śrāvakas based on the Mahāyāna. Now, it is said that the four reliances collectively propagate both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, being provisionally entrusted [to them].
Those with minor results are not merely base individuals; they are not called Mahāyāna Śrāvakas. [Commentary:
For example, as stated below regarding the "three knives," the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue* cites that one turns from faith in the Dharma through sixty-four cycles of faith-practice.
These are the two faculties: faith and wisdom. When hearing is predominant and reflection is slight, it is... [the faculty of faith].
When the Dharma relies on faith and listening while reflection is minimal, this is called "faith relying on the Dharma" (the two faculties).

Alternatively, when faith transforms into the Dharma and the Dharma transforms into faith, this is called "reciprocal transformation" (the two faculties). Regarding the cultivation of the faculty of faith, there are four *siddhāntas* for each of concentration and wisdom, totaling eight;

the same applies to the practice of the Dharma, totaling eight. Reciprocal reliance consists of eight for each, and reciprocal transformation likewise consists of eight for each; furthermore, these transformations are mutually [interdependent].

The "resources" (sambhāra) each consist of one-eighth, totaling sixty-four parts. Since that [text] follows the practice of Dharma (dharmānusārin) while this sūtra follows the practice of faith (śraddhānusārin), it refers back to that passage. [Commentary:

To say that it "transversely points to the fundamental Dharmakāya" means that at the first stage (prathamabhūmi), one partially attains the Dharmakāya and further gives rise to the eight types of corresponding bodies (nirmāṇakāya).
Because both bodies are present in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), they are called "horizontal.

[Commentary: The phrase "neither self nor other can destroy" intends to clarify that only through the harmony of causes and conditions can destruction occur; thus, neither the solitary self nor the solitary other, nor the absence of causes, can effect destruction.
When seeking destruction through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), it is found to be unobtainable.
[Commentary] To dismiss [the Śrāvakas] at first glance, as in the third chapter of the *Mohe zhiguan*, is because they do not mention time and place; thus it is called a "dismissal" (*yiwang*).

Since even the Śrāvakas themselves have already resolved their minds [for enlightenment], how much more so should Bodhisattvas avoid taking the Lesser Vehicle? Regarding the two meanings of knowing the eternal (*nitya*):

first, it refers to the sixteen princes who previously heard the Mahāyāna and thus knew [it]; second, it refers to those who, at the Deer Park, knew the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Based on the minor names [of the precepts], one knows that these two do not exist; since all those who take refuge and receive the precepts are likewise incomplete, this dismisses their arbitrary citations.

[Commentary] "Spear" (*máo*) and "shield" (*shǔn*) refer to weapons, as recorded in the *Zhìguān Jì* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation). A spear is twenty feet long and is mounted at the rear of a war chariot; a shield is...
It is like the story from the state of Chu, where there was a man selling spears and shields.
To one who came to buy a spear, he said, "This spear can pierce through a thousand shields. To one who came to buy a shield, he said, "This shield can withstand a thousand spears.
The buyer of the spear and shield then said to him, "Use your own spear to pierce your own shield. Like the seller, he had no reply, for his own words were mutually contradictory.

[Commentary] The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (Dafangdeng Daji Jing) cites twenty-three pairs of cases where it is said that "they do not understand my intent. This refers to those who were in the small vehicle (*hīnayāna*) in the past, as well as those for whom the teaching was reserved to guide future conditions;
in all such cases, it is stated that they shall not attain Buddhahood. Therefore, the commentary notes that one must say they do not achieve [Buddhahood].

However, when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (Fahua Jing) opens up the provisional and reveals the real, even those who were not present at this assembly—such as those mentioned in the passage "you should proclaim it for them"—are included. Thus, although the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* speaks of not attaining Buddhahood, it does not contradict the *Lotus Sūtra*, as the former concerns the period prior to the revelation of the ultimate truth.
Because they conceive the thought of attaining *nirvāṇa* yet hear this sutra in that land, the Record states: "They exist now" and "they will certainly achieve it. [Commentary:
Regarding the opening and non-opening of the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings across the three periods of time, the "opening" occurs in the *Lotus Sutra* and not elsewhere.

"In the past and in the future" refers to the small [teachings], while "in the past and in the future" refers to the great [teachings]. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the opening and non-opening of both the small and the great are discussed in relation to the three periods of time.

[Commentary] states: "Those who have lost their provisional attachments and cling to the real are still few. This means that it is only now, after the *Lotus Sūtra* has completed its revelation, that one knows the past teachings were merely pointers.
Since Quan did not recognize the underlying principle (*ji*), he merely stated that all things are real and not false; thus his transgression was still slight.

[Commentary] Regarding the "Minor Sections" (*Kṣudraka*) which differ and are clearly easy to eliminate: among the twenty-three pairs, there are differences within the Hinayana sections, such as speaking lightly of what is heavy or speaking heavily of what is light.
These are merely differences in capacity (*ji*), and for this reason it is said they are "easy to eliminate. Others [interpret this differently].
The claim that the *Kṣudrakavāda* (Minor Treatise) is invalid is an error (reflect upon this).

[Commentary] Regarding the protection of those with the capacity for the [Śrāvaka] path and the non-protection of Pratyekabuddhas: if one were to protect Pratyekabuddhas, it would cause them to remain stationary and not move forward;

because they do not receive the teaching, they are contrary to those with the capacity to receive the teaching. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not act for the sake of Pratyekabuddhas; thus [the objection] is in vain.
[Commentary]:
Regarding the phrase "Listen attentively," this is an admonition and a grant of permission. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The listener gazes intently at the Dharma as if hungry or thirsty, enters single-mindedly into the meaning of the words, and hears the Dharma with a heart leaping with joy and moved by both sorrow and delight. To such a person, one may preach."
