After four Buddhas have appeared during the *vivartanī-kalpa* (the kalpa of formation), the tenth *kalpa* sees the appearance of Maitreya Buddha;
then, through the fifteenth *kalpa*, nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas appear. Therefore, it is said that [this period] is difficult [to encounter]. Another interpretation states:

first, regarding the temporal limits, two *kalpas* of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—totaling one hundred and ten *kalpas*—constitute one "Auspicious Kalpa" (*bhadrakalpa*). Second, regarding the names...
The reason for this is that at the time when this kalpa first began to form, a thousand-petaled lotus suddenly appeared in the world, its brilliant radiance illuminating all the celestial palaces.
At that time, the devas, following the light, arrived there and saw this Way-lotus;
upon each and every petal, there were sages and saints who said to one another, "In the future, there will surely appear a thousand worthies to bring it to fulfillment."
Because he attained the fruit of Buddhahood, he is known as the second Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Aeon). Regarding the Bodhisattva who appeared during his time:
during the previous eighty kalpas, there were twenty periods of formation, twenty of abiding, twenty of destruction, and twenty of emptiness.

Within the twenty kalpas of abiding, during the sixth kalpa of abiding when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, a Buddha named Krakucchanda appeared. During the seventh kalpa of abiding, the human...

When the lifespan was forty thousand years, there appeared one Buddha named Krakucchanda. During the eighth abiding kalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared one Buddha named Kanakamuni.
During the ninth abiding kalpa, when the human lifespan was one hundred years, there appeared one Buddha named Kāśyapa.
During the tenth abiding kalpa, when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, there appeared one [Buddha].
The Buddha’s name is Maitreya. In the fifteenth kalpa, nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas appear simultaneously in the world;

together with the preceding one, this makes nine hundred and ninety-nine Buddhas appear in the world. From this point onward, until the twentieth *vāsakalpa*, no Buddhas appear, and the world immediately enters the period of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*).
This lasts for twenty empty kalpas, followed by twenty kalpas of formation (*vivarta-kalpa*), after which another twenty kalpas pass.
Within this kalpa, there was one Buddha named Ruci who appeared; he alone remained for eighty kalpas, so that including the preceding ones, the total reached one thousand Buddhas.
It is said that his teaching was difficult to encounter: Kāśyapa Buddha appeared and remained in the world for seven days, yet did not preach the Dharma;

and as for the present Buddha, it has been more than forty years since he first preached the Lotus Sutra. Thus, it is said that hearing the Dharma is difficult because one constantly dwells within these eight [difficulties].

It is difficult to encounter [such a person] and difficult to have them listen to the teaching. Although one may encounter such a person, they hear only the Lesser Dharma (*hīnayāna*) and do not rejoice in the Great [Dharma];
thus, it is difficult for them to listen. *Tiantai Fahua shuyi zuan*, Fascicle Three (End).
*The Compendium of the Meaning of the Tiantai Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Composed by the Eastern Spring Śramaṇa Zhidu.
The Chapter on Parables.

[Commentary] Some say "the Great Nine" refers to the *Yuanjing shu* (Commentary on the Perfect Mirror). Generally, whenever the phrase "some say" (*you yun*) occurs, it is the interpretation of Dharma Master Yanxiu from the *Yuanjing shu*.

[Commentary] "Whether now or in the past" refers to all four *siddhāntas* (teachings) in contrast to the present and the past; specifically, the three carts of the past versus the one cart of the present.
[Commentary] "Many gates" refers to the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates; every Dharma-gate possesses a parable, which is likewise like a round mirror.

[Commentary] In the previous section on the broad explanation, within the clarification of the purpose for coming, it was stated: "Although the capacity [of the sentient beings] has already [ceased], it still awaits [the Buddha's response] without end.

This is because the compassionate and wise one fears that [beings] might fall into error. One should state that during the middle and lower periods, the capacities did not awaken to the teachings of the upper period; what was previously called "already" refers to the Buddha’s wisdom.

Since [the previous explanation] was not yet sufficient, he further employs the metaphors of "moving a tree" and "raising a fan" for the middle and lower capacities to illustrate his teaching and principle (*dharmatā*).

Because the Buddha’s instruction is inexhaustible, the Commentary states: "It causes them to awaken and understand," which is precisely this point. Although this teaching and principle are termed "manifest" for those of superior capacity and "hidden" for those of middle and lower capacity, in reality there is no such thing as hidden or manifest;
it is only in relation to the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) of the recipients that they appear hidden or manifest. This remains true even when speaking of the "teaching" alone.

"The principle is also complete, while the person is twofold. [Commentary: Since their severance and realization are identical, the formal refutation is omitted. This refers to the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), which are called "identical in severance and realization"; it merely refutes the two vehicles and does not mention Bodhisattvas because their severance and realization are identical, and thus their principle is also identical.

The current text is simply abbreviated. Question: *Note: The term "xing" (形) here refers to the specific forms or manifestations of the refutation; "tong" (同) means "identical" or "the same"; "chong" (斥) means "to refute" or "to exclude"; "sheng" (乘) means "vehicle" (yāna); "duanzheng" (斷證) means "severance and realization" (prahāṇa and sākṣātkriyā).*

Question: Since the Bodhisattvas of the Three Piṭakas have not yet realized the same [truth], why is it not said that they are excluded? Answer: Because they are the same as those in the stage of the four roots of goodness (catur-kuśala-mūla) of the Two Vehicles, in that they have not yet severed their afflictions (kleśa), they are likewise omitted.

[Commentary] "Not yet fathoming the remaining fragrance" means that although one knows the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* differ in being extensive and concise, one has not yet fully fathomed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
This is the continuation of "The Meeting of the Three Vehicles Opening the Distant Original Fragrance.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the three joys, each section contains a repentance. First, regarding the joy of the body: one feels a sense of urgency and lamentation, repenting for the loss of what was known, and realizing that by losing it, one has missed the Great [Vehicle], thus giving rise to repentance.
Second, regarding the joy of speech: "This is our fault" refers to repenting for having taken up the Lesser Vehicle; if one had not taken it up...
That which is small yet without fault is precisely the "evil" referred to as "regret" (kaukṛtya) for what was previously done; this is the third interpretation.

Regarding the phrase "joyful regret" (*anumoda-kaukṛtya*), it need not wait for an explanation of its cause. As for "doubt" (*vicikitsā*), it refers exclusively to the minor [vehicle], as the text asks:
"How can the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna? Now, I say that when the Sūtra speaks of severing all doubts and regrets, it does not refer solely to the Hīnayāna.
They give rise to doubt.

[Commentary: Those who are suspicious within and disdainful without see the Buddha’s inconceivable body and the inconceivable deeds of the bodhisattvas, and thus they hold them in contempt and do not accept the sutra.
Regarding those who see various bodhisattvas receiving predictions of Buddhahood, the Commentary states that this refers to the predictions found within the Vaipulya (fangdeng) scriptures.

Regarding the "Cloud" (Yun) [section], it encompasses both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras: first, from the *Prajñāpāramitā* up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, all [disciples] were granted the prediction of bodhisattvahood;
second, in the *Āgama* sūtras, there is a record that Maitreya would become a Buddha, which caused Śāriputra to witness this and give rise to remorse in his present life.

[Commentary: "Constantly dwelling alone" is named according to the capacity for dwelling; if it were from the perspective of the place where one dwells, it should be called a "dwelling-place" (chù, departing tone).

This clarifies the former doubts. Having previously clarified the time of being in the assembly, this now clarifies the days of dwelling alone. "Every time he has this thought" correctly brings forth what was doubted.
As for the statement "entering together into the Dharma-nature," one asks: "Where does Śāriputra enter the Dharma-nature? The answer is: "There is."

In three instances, Ājñātakauṇḍinya encountered [the Buddha] once and heard the Dharma of emptiness; thus it is said that he "stilled his mind and reached the fundamental source," where the fundamental source is precisely the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature).
Second, after Śāriputra attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), he heard the discourse of Aṅgulimāla and attained arhatship.

Third, having attained arhatship, he traveled through the various directions and heard the *Vaipulya* and *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* sūtras; in all cases, he heard of the Three Vehicles and equally attained the *dharmatā*. However, the names for this dharma are identical.
There is a difference in scale [between the two], yet one does not reflect upon one's own faults but instead suspects that the Buddha was partial.
[Sūtra]: When those who first heard the Buddha’s Dharma asked why the Buddha first delivered the Four Noble Truths to the five disciples, why is it said that Śāriputra was the first to hear it?
Answer: This does not mean he was the very first among the five; rather, it simply means he was the first to hear what was preached by Aśvajit.
Question: Do doubt (*vicikitsā*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*) apply to both the present and the past? Answer: Doubt applies to both the present and the past; regret, however, pertains only to the past.

This is because the fault of the past is great, whereas one who realizes in the present that there has been no loss has no regret. As for doubt applying to both the present and the past: it arises from doubting the relationship between principle (*li*) and teaching (*jiao*).

Since principle is singular, the teachings should not be threefold; thus, one doubts the teachings of the past and present, which appear as two distinct rains [of Dharma], and resolves them through analysis (and so forth).
[Sūtra] The two lines following "Golden color, thirty-two [marks]" clarify the loss of one's own virtuous fruits; there are two verses regarding these fruits.

In the first verse, the two bodies—the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*)—of the Hīnayāna are presented. In the second verse, the two bodies—the birth-body and the dharma-body—of the Buddha’s Mahāyāna are cited.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Hīnayāna, it is not taught that the birth-body possesses the eighty minor marks, nor is it taught that the dharma-body possesses the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*)."
Regarding the "shared dharmas," the present [text] uses the categories of "great" and "small" to clarify that Śāriputra has lost both.
Furthermore, it states: first, citing the thirty-two marks as external virtues and the ten powers as internal virtues briefly praises the Buddha’s two types of virtue—external and internal;
next, citing the eighty secondary marks as external and the eighteen unshared [dharmas] as internal extensively praises the Buddha.
Inner and Outer.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "people of the world" and so forth, the *Record* cites the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which states that in the world above, beyond Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a land named *Saṃghagandha* (All Fragrances). All...

There are pavilions made of incense, walkways, and fragrant grounds; the name of that Buddha is "Accumulation of Fragrance," and the fragrance of that land is the foremost among all the ten directions.
In that land, there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only a pure assembly of great bodhisattvas.
The Tathāgata of that land does not preach by means of written words, but causes all humans and devas to attain [realization] through various fragrances.
They were fully endowed with all the practices of the Vinaya up to their various merits.

Those nine hundred trillion bodhisattvas from that land, having seen the emanated bodhisattva sent by Vimalakīrti arrive to receive the fragrant food, all followed him there to make offerings to Śākyamuni and Vimalakīrti.

Upon hearing the discourse on the difficulties of the five realms of existence in this land and the fact that beings born therein are stubborn, difficult to transform, and hard to discipline, their minds were moved.
Just as it was said regarding the ten unwholesome paths and so forth, those bodhisattvas marveled at what they had never before experienced:
the cultivation of the path of transformation and the gate of the contemplation of emptiness, which are called the "practice of the two together.

[Sūtra] The verse says: "Those who first hear what the Buddha has taught" refers to those who, upon first hearing the brief opening of the three to reveal the one, have their attachments shaken and give rise to [faith].
At the time of doubt, one wonders whether it might be a Māra manifesting as a Buddha. Having already given rise to such doubt, one secretly thinks in one's mind that the Buddha is indeed a Māra.

For the nature of a Māra is to claim existence where there is non-existence, and non-existence where there is existence; to claim there is "one" where there is "three," and "three" where there is "one.
Now, [the teaching] that the "three" are a skillful means (*upāya*) and that the "three" previously taught are the ultimate truth is identical to what the Māras say. Thus is the question asked.

"What distinguishes this new category of doubt from the old? The answer is: the old refers to doubts arising regarding what is correct, while the new refers to doubts arising from the conflation of the heterodox and the orthodox.
Regarding doubts arising regarding what is correct: in the past, both principle and teaching were spoken by the Buddha, yet one used principle and teaching to doubt each other;
thus, it is called 'doubt arising within the correct. As for the present case of doubts arising from the conflation of the heterodox and the orthodox: Śāriputra [regarded] the three vehicles..."

Regarding the teaching: the present One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teaching is that which the Buddha preached; it is that within birth-and-death there is nirvana, while the three vehicles taught [by others] are all that within birth-and-death one regards as nirvana.
[Sūtra]: "His mind is as peaceful as the ocean" means that his peace is like a mountain and his vastness is like the ocean; when the spirit is thus unified, it is the same.
Regarding "mountains and seas," one knows they are not demons; thus, doubt is severed. [Sūtra]:

"Those who hear the Buddha’s gentle and soft voice"—the following three phrases conclude the section on the joy of speech. His Brahma-voice is called "gentle and soft" because it is perfectly chanted.

It is called "profound" because it vertically traverses the Three Truths. It is called "far-reaching" because it horizontally pervades the Dharma-realm. It is called "sublime" because the vertical and horizontal dimensions are non-dual.
That ignorance is non-defiled is called "purity," which explains the subtle principle of the One Vehicle.
[Sūtra] "I shall certainly become a Buddha" praises the preceding passage, "Today I know for the first time that I am truly a son of the Buddha," which concludes the perfection of the body.
"Being honored by devas and humans" praises the preceding passage, "born through transformation from the Dharma," because within one is no doubt.
That he is revered by devas and humans externally, and that he immediately forms the resolve to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, is a verse from the Buddha’s own mouth;
it is formed through the mouth. This signifies obtaining a portion of the Buddha-dharma and serves as a summary of the realization of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
[Commentary] That which is accomplished through the function of eliciting retribution refers to my certain attainment of Buddhahood as the retribution;
that which is accomplished through the function of being honored by devas and humans refers to the turning of the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.

[Sūtra]: Regarding Puṣpamitra (Flower-Light), some say he was named so because he beheld flowers raining down with his eyes and heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* with his ears. If it is the light of wisdom, why are other people not also named Puṣpamitra? Answer: Śāriputra received his name from the very beginning; others who attained realization later received different names. This is analogous to Ājñātakauṇḍinya (“One-Who-Knows”), whereas other people are not so. The commentary states: [The case of] Puṣpamitra is like this. He was named Puṣpamitra because he first beheld the rain of flowers and heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As for the others, they were named according to their respective attainments. It is not that everyone who attains the Way must be named Puṣpamitra. Furthermore, the Buddha bestowed names upon them at the time of their initial awakening. Because Śāriputra’s awakening was the foremost, he was given a name based on that initial event. Other people attained awakening later; therefore, they received different names. For example, Ājñātakauṇḍinya was named because he first understood the Dharma. Others did not do so. Thus, it is not the case that all who hear the Dharma are named Puṣpamitra. It is simply that Śāriputra was named based on his initial attainment. This is the meaning. The commentary further notes: “As for the others, they were named according to their respective attainments. This means that because their attainments differed, their names differed accordingly. It is not that everyone who hears the Dharma is necessarily named Puṣpamitra. It is simply that Śāriputra was named based on his initial attainment. This is the meaning. The commentary further notes: “It is not the case that all who hear the Dharma are named Puṣpamitra. This means that although there are many who hear the Dharma, they are not all named Puṣpamitra. That which is the source of the various jewels is called "Flower" (puṣpa); that which illuminates all ten thousand things is called "Light" (prabhā).
[Sūtra] The land named Vimala—some say this is because it was never a pure land made impure by sentient beings;

rather, it is pure or impure only because the minds of sentient beings are pure or impure. Śāriputra formerly possessed the impure mind of an ordinary person, but now he has awakened to the One Vehicle. Furthermore...
Having departed from the defilements of the two vehicles, when one attains Buddhahood by being doubly free from these two defilements, that land is named "Free from Defilement" (*Vimalā*).

(The above is the name of the land. That land is level and upright: its substance is free from elevations and depressions, hence it is called "level"; it is not small or large, nor is it slanted, hence it is called "upright.
It is pure because it is free from filth and evil; it is adorned with various jewels. The following clarifies that the inhabitants are secure and free from the calamity of weapons (*śastra-yuga*).
Therefore, it is peaceful and secure because it is free from the kalpa of famine; it is abundant and joyful because it is free from the kalpa of pestilence;

and it is magnificent because its ground is made of lapis lazuli. This specifically clarifies the adornment of the ground. Regarding the eight intersecting roads, this specifically clarifies the adornment of the paths.
Proceeding from the broad to the narrow: first, the land is explained in general; next, the ground is explained in detail; and finally, the paths are explained in detail.
[Sūtra] Regarding the statement that the Three Vehicles were taught by virtue of his original vow: Śākyamuni taught the Three Vehicles in this defiled age in order to eliminate its turbidity;
in that land, there is no turbidity, yet he vowed to teach the Three. Question: What was that vow? Answer:

While Śāriputra realized the One Vehicle within the context of the Three Vehicles, Śākyamuni taught the Three Vehicles. As for the eon being named "Great Treasure," it is not because pearls and jade are considered precious therein.
They take wisdom as their treasure.
[Sūtra] Regarding those Bodhisattvas who arrive in the land, there are first ten virtues: (1) the virtue of being difficult for those on lower stages to conceive;
the text says, "Those Bodhisattvas cannot be known by anyone except through the power of a Buddha's wisdom"; (2) the virtue of having auspicious flowers supporting their feet.

The seven kinds of pure flowers represent the virtue of having long since aroused the three great minds; "these bodhisattvas" and below represent the virtue of the four internal practices being flawless;
"immeasurable" and below represent the fifth, the virtue of being praised by Buddhas externally; "constantly" and below represent the sixth, the virtue of constantly seeking true wisdom;
and as the text says, the seventh represents the virtue of external transformation through great supernormal powers—possessing great supernormal powers is the eighth, the meaning of the teaching.

Pervasive and universal virtue is the quality of thoroughly knowing the gateways to all dharmas; this is the ninth. Nature of purity and freedom from crookedness is the quality of being upright and sincere without hypocrisy;
this is the tenth. Firmness of mind and non-retrogression is the quality of having steadfast resolve and mindfulness; it is called "firm" because one is not moved by afflictions.
In brief, the essential meaning does not go beyond making vows and practicing the cultivation of concentration and wisdom.

[Sūtra]: It is said that the Buddha’s lifespan is twelve minor kalpas while the lifespan of sentient beings is eight minor kalpas. Question: Why is it that in the Sahā world the Buddha’s lifespan is short while the lives of sentient beings are long, whereas in the Vimala world the Buddha’s lifespan is long while the lives of sentient beings are short? Answer: Sentient beings in the Sahā world have brought about this defiled land through the gravity of their delusions regarding birth and death; thus, their capacity to invoke the Sage is [proportionate to] their heavy afflictions. In contrast, those in the Vimala world have purified their lands through the lightness of their afflictions; thus, their capacity to invoke the Sage is [proportionate to] their light afflictions. Therefore, the lifespans of the Buddhas and the lengths of the lives of sentient beings correspond to one another. Furthermore, the Sahā world is a place where the Dharma is difficult to encounter, and its sentient beings are deeply steeped in ignorance and delusion; therefore, the Buddha’s lifespan is short so that he may frequently appear and manifest his passing away, thereby inspiring awe and reverence in sentient beings. In the Vimala world, the Dharma is easy to encounter and the sentient beings are pure and upright; therefore, the Buddha’s lifespan is long so that he may remain for a long time, allowing sentient beings to dwell securely in the bliss of the Dharma. This is why the lifespans of the Buddhas and the lengths of the lives of sentient beings differ in these two worlds. Furthermore, the Sahā world is a place of great suffering, and its sentient beings are weary of the cycle of birth and death; therefore, the Buddha’s lifespan is short so that he may frequently manifest his parinirvāṇa, causing sentient beings to feel grief and longing, thereby increasing their desire for liberation. In the Vimala world, there is little suffering and the sentient beings are not weary of the cycle of birth and death; therefore, the Buddha’s lifespan is long so that he may remain for a long time, allowing sentient beings to gradually cultivate the roots of goodness for liberation. This is why the lifespans of the Buddhas and the lengths of the lives of sentient beings differ in these two worlds. Furthermore, the Sahā world is a place of great suffering, and its sentient beings are weary of the cycle of birth and death; therefore, the Buddha’s lifespan is short so that he may frequently manifest his parinirvāṇa, causing sentient beings to feel grief and longing, thereby increasing their desire for liberation. In the Vimala world, there is little suffering and the sentient beings are not weary of the cycle of birth and death; therefore, the Buddha’s lifespan is long so that he may remain for a long time, allowing sentient beings to gradually cultivate the roots of goodness for liberation. This is why the lifespans of the Buddhas and the lengths of the lives of sentient beings differ in these two worlds. Furthermore, the Sahā world is a place where the Dharma is difficult to encounter, and its sentient beings are deeply steeped in ignorance and delusion; therefore, the Buddha’s lifespan is short so that he may frequently manifest his parinirvāṇa, causing sentient beings to feel grief and longing, thereby increasing their desire for liberation. This is why the lifespans of the Buddhas and the lengths of the lives of sentient beings differ in these two worlds. Because [the defilements] are not dense, the Buddha’s lifespan is short while the lifespan of sentient beings is long. Sentient beings who are free from defilement attain a pure land;

this must surely be due to the fact that their attachment to life and death is thin, while their affection for the Way is increasingly profound. Thus, human life is brief while the Buddha’s lifespan is extended.
The premature end of his manifested traces is merely due to the varying degrees of depth in the dispositions of sentient beings.

[Sūtra] "Flower-footed and Peaceful-conduct" means that the multitude of true practices serve as the cause; because the myriad practices are all fulfilled, they are the "flowers"; because the various things are not in error, they are the "feet";

and because the manifold transformations are circulated for the sake of peace, they are the "conduct. Furthermore, it is said that when the bodhisattvas of that land walk, precious flowers receive their feet;
therefore, it is called "Flower-footed. The Sanskrit original says *go-vṛṣabha*; since in India the noble ox is highly esteemed, this is used as a metaphor.
Since the term *bhū* (earth) does not honor the ox, it is changed to *anuvṛtti* (peaceful progression).
[Commentary]: Regarding *Bhagavat*, Nāgārjuna explains it in four ways: first, the ability to destroy afflictions; second, the possession of merit; third, skillful discernment;

and fourth, having a good reputation. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states: "The word *bhaga* means 'merit' (*guṇa*), and *vat* means 'possessing' (*asti*); thus, it is called 'Possessing Merit' (*Guṇavat*)."

Virtue is the second meaning. Furthermore, *bhaga* means "discrimination" (*vibhāga*) and *bha* means "skillful" (*kauśalya*); because one skillfully discriminates the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena, this is the third meaning.
Furthermore, *bhaga* means "sound" (*śabda*) and *bha* means "existence"; that which possesses existence is called "sound," as in the case of the Buddha—this is the fourth meaning.
Furthermore, *bhaga* means "destruction" (*bhaṅga*) and *bha* means "ability"; it refers to the ability to destroy lust, anger, and delusion.
Therefore, he is called Bhagavat; this is the first [meaning].

[Sūtra]: Regarding the "greatest wheel of Dharma," as stated in the second fascicle of the *Xuánwén*: "It is explained in general across various sūtras that [the teaching] awaits the transition from the 'half' to the 'full,' as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
'From the moment he sat beneath the Bodhi tree, by his power he subdued Māra, attained the extinction of ambrosia, and realized the path of enlightenment.'"
Regarding the statement that the former was half-luminous and now fully luminous: the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra says that the second turning of the Wheel of Dharma is seen in Jambudvīpa;
this refers to the Deer Park as the first [turning] and the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the second. Both the *Nirvāṇa* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtras state:
"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, I first turned the Wheel of Dharma; now, in the city of Kuśinagara, I turn the Wheel of Dharma. This present scripture is as stated in the text.
Generally speaking, in comparison with the ancient views, each respective division may be considered either "half-full" or "full.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "not yet healed," and so forth: this fully explains that in all lands—just as in the Land of Common Residence (*sāṃbhogika-kṣetra*) there are those with *dṛṣṭi-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* afflictions; in the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-kṣetra*) there are those with *rajas* (dust-like delusions);
and in the Land of True Reward (*dharmatā-niṣyanda-kṣetra*) there are those with ignorance (*avidyā*)—the provisional person manifests in all these cases as being both ill and healed. Furthermore...

Superficially, they appear to be adversaries; however, if one discusses this from a fundamental perspective, those dwelling in the stage of Expedient Means (*upāya*) share three afflictions—view-delusions, thought-delusions, and the dust-and-sand-like delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*).

There are two types of removal for those at the Expedient Means stage: the first removes view-delusions and thought-delusions, while the Real Reward (*sambhoga*) stage removes view-delusions, thought-delusions, and dust-and-sand-like delusions, leaving only ignorance.
Because the highest grade of tranquility is the abode of the Radiant Buddha (*Prabhāsa*), it is free from illness.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "obtaining the prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*), etc., below: the four sections concerning the parable and the four sections concerning the causal conditions (*nidāna*) are what are being referred to here;
thus it says, "all are based on the parable. This means that both the four sections of the parable and the four sections of the causal conditions are based on the causal conditions alone;
it does not mean that the sections on "accepting the understanding" (*anujñāna*) and "confirming the realization" (*anuparindana*) are omitted. Therefore, it notes "etcetera" (*yathā*).
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, beginning the second cycle of teaching by describing his own [realization of] the two views of existence and non-existence;

"existence and non-existence" refers to the extreme views of annihilationism and eternalism, as well as the false views of *dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa* (clinging to views), *śīla-vrata-parāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and rituals), and other dull underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "if a kingdom, city, etc.," some say that "kingdom, city, village" refers to the meaning of the word *yadi* (if).
Furthermore, *yadi* means "like" (*yathā*); it is spoken according to how things are. A "kingdom" (*rājya*) refers to a bounded territory or domain.
Quoting the *Śāstra-vyākhyā*, it says: "There are generally four places ruled by a single Buddha; the first is called one world."
Section Two: Clarifying the World-Oceans; Section Three: Clarifying the World-Systems; Section Four: Clarifying the Portion of Beings to be Saved within a Single World. Regarding "a single world":
ten billion suns and moons and so forth are called one Great Trichiliocosm (*mahāsāhasralokadhātu*).

When there are as many such Great Trichiliocosms in each of the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, this is called one Buddha-world. Regarding "the world-ocean": it refers to such Buddha-worlds [assembled together].
A number equal to the sands of one Ganges River is called an ocean of worlds (*lokadhātu-samudra*).
What is called a world-system (*lokadhātu-jāti*) refers to such oceans of worlds numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions; this is called one world-system.

What is called the portion of worlds to be traversed refers to such world-systems, infinite in the ten directions; this is called the portion of worlds to be traversed. These four types, taken together, constitute the totality.

The city-state ruled by a single Buddha-king serves as the primary analogy for the divisions of the world-system; the townships correspond to the secondary level, representing the various clusters of worlds;
the distant outskirts correspond to the ocean-like assemblies of worlds; and the nearby villages correspond to a single world.
It is said that among these four, the first is the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), while the latter three are the Land of True Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*).
Because it lacks the land of skillful means (*upāya*), it is not employed here. Regarding the term "village" (*grāma*):

the *Guoyaya* states that a village is a dwelling, a gathering of many people, and that the place where people reside together is called a "village," while the outer courtyards are also called "villages. It is said that people call a district (*xian*) an "inner town" (*yi-nei*), while the clusters outside the villages and the outskirts are called "villages" (*luo*).
Now, when one speaks of a "neighborhood" (*lin-lu*) as a "village" (*ju-lo*), this refers to the collective of the outer outskirts and boundaries as a "village."
[It] falls [into this category].

[Commentary] states that "the horizontal and vertical mutually interpenetrate" means it is like being situated in the center while encompassing the remaining three lands. "Horizontal" implies that it encompasses the "vertical," such that they are non-dual yet dual.

Apart from the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka*), there are separately the other three lands—Convenience (*upāya*), etc.—while the Land of Peaceful Light (*śānta-prabhā*) is exclusively ultimate. This is what is called [the "horizontal"].
Vertically pervading the three lands, each is immediately the Land of Peaceful Light; this is called "the two yet non-dual," meaning that within the vertical there is the horizontal.
[Commentary] For details regarding the Left Aide and others, refer to the seventh fascicle of the *Zhi guan* commentary (as noted, etc.).

[Commentary]: Regarding "a sable fur on the left and an ornament inserted on the right," the *Hanguanyi* by Ying Shao states: "The Attendant Councillors (*shizhong*) wear the golden cicada and the sable fur on the left.

Gold is taken for its vertical hardness; even after a hundred refinements, it does not diminish. The cicada dwells high and feeds on purity. The sable fur is internally vigorous and fierce, yet externally warm and lustrous.

During the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, Wang Tanshou, Dianzhi Ren, and others were all appointed as Attendant Councillors; their positions were established to be close to the sovereign.

The Benevolent Emperor sat with him knee-to-knee and conversed; the sable fur brushed against the Emperor’s cap, so the Emperor reached out his hand, moved the sable to the side table, and when the conversation ended, he returned it to its place by inserting it back into his hand.

[Sūtra] Regarding the phrase "virtue has both internal and external aspects," the first part indicates the nature of his virtuous deeds—namely, praising those deeds—and the subsequent section provides an explanation, which is further divided into two parts.

First, the explanation of virtue; next, the explanation of karma, beginning with "童" (tóng). Regarding virtue, there are two parts: first, the indication of internal and external aspects; second, the explanation of these. Regarding the explanation, there are two parts:
first, a brief explanation; second, an extensive explanation. The brief explanation begins with "Internal refers to... and extends to "...wealth and property. The extensive explanation has two parts:
first, the internal; second, the external. Regarding the internal, he first explains his age, saying: "His years are advanced, and he is profoundly learned in both the ancient and the modern."

In the commentary on the sutra, the term "years" (*nian*) refers to a worldly elder whose years have long passed; he is widely learned in the foundational classics and historical records of both past and present.

This serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue—the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real—whether in terms of phenomena (*shi*) or principle (*li*). Regarding phenomena, there is nothing among the three thousand worlds that is not understood;
regarding principle, it is the realization of emptiness (*kong*). Next, concerning the term "advanced in years," it says "the faculties and resolve are matured. Here, "faculties" (*gen*) refers to...

The phrase "the will releases decay" (*zhì shì shuāi*) explains "matured transcendence" (*chúnshú shì mài*). "Mài" (transcendence) means "far-reaching," signifying that one who is decaying encounters the far-reaching [state] and returns to quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*);

it is a metaphor for the Buddha’s virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), the principle of *nirvāṇa*, and its pure nature. Next, from the passage beginning with "wealth and property" (*cáifù*) downward, the external virtues (*bāhirdharma-guṇa*) are explained in two parts:
first, a general explanation, and second, a detailed explanation, as the text indicates.
[Sūtra]: "A great multitude of people" refers to the fact that the number of sentient beings within the three realms is vast and manifold; thus it is said, "a great multitude of people.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that the seeds of the five destinies are differentiated by the various types of karma summoned through the perfuming of names and phrases (*nāma-pada*).

These are called the "five" according to their respective correspondence. Those who possess the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma—meaning those who have them—are what are termed "seeds," namely the five [aggregates].
The seeds of the aggregates are not distinct across the five destinies; it is because they are summoned by wholesome and unwholesome karma that they differ, and thus the five paths are distinguished.

Regarding the statement "five hundred," some say that what is summoned and experienced by the ten courses of action is called "five hundred. This means that within each of the ten courses of action, there are [the factors of] doing it oneself, inciting others, encouraging them, and rejoicing in their success;

these may be performed to a small degree, a great degree, or in full, and at a short duration, a long duration, or for a lifetime. It is through these variations that the number five hundred is derived.

For a long time, as well as at the exhaustion of one's lifespan, the ten types of aging and cultivation arise individually through their respective conditions; these are established with five hundred names.

These various kinds reside within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which is called the "dwelling. Because these seeds exist therein, the manifold sufferings of the cycle of existence in the five destinies do not cease.
Now, regarding the causes for the three miserable realms, they are summoned by the ten non-virtuous actions; one such action serves as the basis, while the others follow.
The nine [factors] assist in completing the ten; as each of the remaining nine is likewise so, they constitute one hundred.

If the karma of breaking the precepts constitutes the hundred [types] of hell-beings, shamelessness constitutes the hundred [types] of animals, and stinginess and greed constitute the hundred [types] of hungry ghosts; as for humans, devas, and asuras, they arise from the three grades of the ten wholesome actions mutually adorned, each numbering one hundred.

This does not refer to those who have been converted through teaching and so forth. Question: Why is it that only five hundred are cited? Answer: [Because... (Note: The final answer is omitted as the provided text ends with the question).

Regarding the statement "one or two": the answer is that one refers to the devas and two refers to humans, as these are singled out because they are capable of receiving transformation through teaching.

Since those in the three miserable realms rarely receive such transformation, they are included collectively; thus it says "up to a hundred," excluding the asuras, which is why the phrase "up to" is used.
As for the term "abiding": this refers generally to the five destinies (*gati*) and specifically to the forty-eight abodes, including the eight hells along with the hungry ghosts and animals.
There are fourteen states of existence (*dhātu*), ten realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) consisting of the six desire realms and the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), totaling forty locations.

[Sūtra]: "The halls and pavilions have reached a state of collapse. Some say this is a metaphor for the five aggregates (*skandha*); that the hall is dilapidated refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), which is the body-faculty.

The "main hall" represents the primary [consciousness], to which the sense faculties (*indriya*) are attached; the "body" is like the pavilion. "Arising and ceasing" is called "decay," meaning rotting away.

"The collapse of walls and partitions" is a metaphor for the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): that which wards off the external is the wall, and that which resists the internal is the partition.

The external transformations of appearances are like the wall, while the internal transformations of images are like the partition. Being empty and unreal, and migrating and passing away from afar, is called "collapse. The commentary explains: "External..."

The transformations of mountains, rivers, the great earth, and sentient beings—whereby one feels desire upon seeing the pure and aversion upon seeing the foul—are such that when the internal transforms into images, it gives rise to desire and aversion based on the internal body.
The rotting of the pillar’s base is a metaphor for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);
within this aggregate of formations there are four categories of phenomena, and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the most preeminent master of the body, as well as being non-dispersing.
One should practice the Dharma as follows: when the pillars of a house have rotted, it is called "decayed. Furthermore, it is said that the stability of a house depends on the support of its pillars;

likewise, the existence of karmic retribution depends on the sustenance of life. When life is about to end, the body of retribution is about to perish, just as when the base of a pillar fails, the hall and house are about to collapse.
Regarding "the ridgepoles and beams are tilted and perilous," the "beam" (dōng) refers to the vertical support, while the "ridgepole" (liáng) refers to the horizontal beam.

This is a metaphorical comparison: internal matured experience (*vipākavedanā*) is like the ridgepole as the root; external dominant-result experience (*adhipatiphala-vedanā*) is like the rafters as the branches.

Just as rafters and ridgepoles depend upon pillars, so too do experiences depend upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because karma exists [as their basis]. Therefore, being on the verge of collapsing, it is called "tendency toward ruin.
Sustaining a single body necessarily depends upon the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*); sustaining a single house necessarily relies upon the rafters and ridgepoles. Now, the Commentary...
The intention [of this analogy] is as follows: first, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the walls; next, in the contemplation of dissolution, they are used as a metaphor for skin and flesh.

Regarding the "formless realm" (*ārūpyadhātu*), according to certain Hīnayāna schools there is form, while in Mahāyāna there is "meditative resultant form" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*); since both can serve as skin and flesh, they pertain to all three realms.
If that is so, since the burner (fire) already pervades the three realms, how could the burned (the fuel) be restricted to the desire and form realms? This is now the metaphor of the walls.

The analogy of the four great elements (mahābhūta) is as follows: the outer courtyards represent the walls, while the inner partitions represent the interior walls; this illustrates how the skin constitutes the exterior and the flesh constitutes the interior, thereby forming the physical form (*rūpa*) of the body.

Now, according to the Mahāyāna, if even the subtle delusions persisting up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) can act as both the burner and the burned, how could it be that only the two realms of desire and form lack anything to be burned, while the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has nothing at all to be burned? Furthermore, although the sensation (*vedanā*) aggregate is omitted in the present text...
If one considers the two aggregates [of sensation and perception] as being analogous to the three [remaining] aggregates, it accords with the sequence of the aggregates:

the four great elements are the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Thus, by means of these three phrases, the three aggregates are illustrated.

Since there is already the aggregate of consciousness, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) must necessarily be accompanied by mental factors (*caitta*); therefore, the five aggregates are also sufficient. Furthermore, the present intention is that the four great elements constitute both form and the life-faculty.

The three—consciousness (*vijñāna*), warmth (*uṣman*), and life-force (*jīvitendriya*)—are so called because they are the three seeds at the time of initial conception in the womb; thus, these are correlated with the three realms.
Some say "palaces and pavilions" (*kūṭāgāra*); this refers to the dwellings where beings gather as their halls, which are stacked one above another and thus called "pavilions.

The retributive fruits of the three realms are possessed by all sentient beings who congregate therein, which is likened to a hall. Furthermore, the heights and depths of the retributive fruits within the three realms correspond to the relative status of those beings.
The difference is that the analogy of the "piling up of houses" refers to the three realms as the supported basis (*āśraya*), like a hall;

whereas the analogy of the "multi-storied pavilion" refers to the resultant retribution of the three realms as the supporting [beings], like the pavilion itself. This is an explanation based on the two types of retribution: the environment and the inhabitants.

[Commentary] To address the objection raised by some who maintain that both the primary (the person) and secondary (the environment) retributions are fully present: "Just as for humans and terrestrial devas, the primary retribution does not correspond to the secondary;

or, when a human dies, the secondary retribution is not extinguished. If, according to the Consciousness-Only school, the secondary retribution is the *nimittabhāga* (image-part) of the eighth consciousness, then when the primary retribution perishes, the secondary retribution should also perish, because the *nimittabhāga* is not separate from the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part) of the mind. Now, [this argument] relies on the perspective of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).

The vehicles do not perish; the desire realm’s empty abodes, as well as the form and formless realms, along with the hell, hungry ghost, and other realms of dependent retribution (niśraya-vipāka-bhūmi), all exist in accordance with the primary retribution (mukhya-vipāka). One might say they are mutually inclusive. But since humans are not like this, how can they be mutually inclusive?

Now, according to the explanation of the *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) system, that the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) does not depart from the mind is precisely what is meant by "inclusion. Therefore, the present text follows this principle throughout.
[The text discusses] the primary retribution (as detailed above).
[Commentary: Regarding the passage "surrounding" and below, which clarifies the fire that burns, someone asks:

"If the triple world always exists, if there are always manifold sufferings, and if there is always the burning house with fires constantly ablaze, why was the burning house explained first and the fire explained later?"
When asked, Yaśas replied: "It possesses both general and specific meanings. Generally speaking, it refers to the three realms and the universal experience of the suffering of change and sensation.
Specifically, regarding the meeting of craving with the three roots, 'suffering' implies the sense of having a temporary cessation of transformation;
yet once the Buddha has passed away, afflictions arise again. Therefore, the house was explained first and the fire is now being analyzed. He asked: "I understand this through this analogy."

Does it possess both the general and specific meanings? Answer: First, five hundred people are listed; next, thirty sons are clarified. The five hundred represent the general meaning, while the thirty sons represent the specific meaning.

Furthermore, it is said that this sutra causes all sentient beings to leave behind the stage of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), and subsequently to leave behind the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Therefore, it describes the faults and afflictions of the triple world (*traidhātuka*) so that they may not be greedily attached to them; this constitutes leaving behind the stage of ordinary worldlings. Subsequently...

It clarifies that when the sons went out seeking carts and failed to find them, the Buddha immediately bestowed upon them great carts to cause them to transcend the stage of the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*).

Now, it is said that the burning house was originally taught as the Dharma for those of medium capacity; because they did not awaken to it, the Buddha created this parable to extensively clarify the five destinies (*pañcagati*) of the burning house’s cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
He cites five hundred people as a metaphor for the very basis of this cycle of rebirth—those who are originally children of the True Cause (*samyak-hetu*). Furthermore...

This is the place where the mechanism of birth arises and from which suffering emerges like a burning house; by leaving behind the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), one attains liberation from the limited continuity of existence (*paricchinna-bhava*).

Now, by causing them to leave behind the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), they attain liberation from the transformation of existence (*pariṇāmi-bhava*); therefore, the great vehicle is bestowed equally upon all.
It is not that all sentient beings are merely caused to leave the stage of ordinary beings as a secondary matter.

Regarding the statement that "the cycle extends to the four modes of birth," there is a threefold analysis: first, defining their characteristics; second, distinguishing their scope and application; and third, clarifying their breadth and narrowness.

In the section defining their characteristics, the "four modes of birth" refers to viviparous (*jarāyu-ja*), oviparous (*aṇḍa-ja*), moisture-born (*saṃsveda-ja*), and transformation-born (*upapāduka*).

As for the viviparous, beings such as humans who receive retribution by being entrusted with and dependent upon the union of semen and blood are called viviparous. The oviparous are those such as various birds that depend upon an egg-shell.
Regarding those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), such as the various devas and others, they arise suddenly without any basis or support; this is called "transformation birth. Question:

If there is no basis or support, how can birth occur? Answer: As explained in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), birth occurs in dependence upon karma. The characteristics of birth have been explained above.

Next, regarding the distinction between the general and the specific within the five destinies (*gati*), among the four modes of birth, the single category of transformation birth fully encompasses two [of the five destinies].
Regarding the "two [births] fully encompassed by the destinies and three parts": all heavens, hells, and one part of the human destiny are exclusively born by transformation (*upapāduka*).

As for the "three parts," humans, ghosts, and animals possess them in part; for instance, at the beginning of a kalpa, humans, ghosts, and animals were all born by transformation, but since they mostly do not exist now, they are called "parts.
The single type of birth from a womb (*jarāyuja*) belongs in part to humans, ghosts, and animals.
Among the other destinies, there are no beings born from eggs or moisture; these two modes of birth exist only among humans and animals. In the other destinies, there are none.
Regarding egg-born humans, such as the mother Viśākhā, who had thirty-two sons within a single egg—beings of this kind are egg-born humans.
As for moisture-born humans, such as King Mūrdhaja (Crown-Born), there was once a king named Śubhavyūha (Well-Abiding) who gave rise to Mūrdhaja.
A child is born from a fleshy sac when ten months have been fulfilled; because he was thus born, he was named Mūrdhaja. Such as these are moisture-born beings (*saṃsvedaja*).
Within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*), those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*) and those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*) may be known accordingly. Next, to distinguish their breadth and narrowness:

the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* asks, "Does birth encompass the destinies (*gati*), or do the destinies encompass birth? The treatise itself explains: "The four modes of birth encompass the destinies, but the destinies do not encompass birth. Why is this?

Therefore, since all five destinies (*gati*) are not outside the four modes of birth (*yoni*), the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the five destinies is entirely of apparitional birth (*upapāduka*).
Because the five destinies do not encompass [all] four modes of birth, the four modes of birth are not subsumed within the five destinies. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Humans and animals possess all four [modes of birth]," and so forth, as explained in detail below in the commentary on Rejoicing (*anumodanā*). (etc.)
[Sūtra]: "Whether ten, twenty, or up to thirty. Some say: "If it is ten, this refers to the Bodhisattvas [mentioned] in the 'Bhadramukha-parivarta' of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

Since there is a fixed number [of Bodhisattvas], why does it say 'or'? Answer: There are three meanings: 1. "Or" indicates that the two vehicles may be either expanded or subsumed within the Lesser Vehicle;
thus, the expansion and subsumption are not fixed. 2. It refers to the indeterminate nature of the faculties of those belonging to the three vehicles of the past.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, six thousand bodhisattvas regressed; Kāśyapa, who was originally a pratyekabuddha, encountered a Buddha and became a śrāvaka.
Although he possessed the capacities for all three vehicles in the past, he ultimately became a bodhisattva; therefore, it is said that "some" [regress].

[Commentary]: The phrase "suddenly" (*kṣaṇam*) is used as an analogy for that which was originally non-existent but now exists; this is cited from a single passage in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which appears in four locations therein.

In the ninth chapter, the "Chapter on the Distinctions of Bodhisattvas," it addresses the relative nature of principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) through the distinction between difference and non-difference.

In the fifteenth chapter, the "Chapter on Holy Conduct" (*Brahmacarya*), it clarifies that "attainment is non-attainment" and "non-attainment is attainment," based on the attainment of the fruit through the cultivation of causes. This is the twenty-fifth [section]. Master... [text ends].
In the "Chapter on the Lion’s Roar," it is clarified that existence is indeterminate and non-existence is indeterminate, based on the relative opposition of the ultimate and conventional truths.

Twenty-six refutations are made regarding determinate nature to clarify the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Now, first, regarding the explanation of "originally non-existent but now existent" and "originally existent but now non-existent":

afflictions are themselves *tathatā*. From the perspective of the afflictions, they are called "originally non-existent"; from the perspective of *tathatā*, they are called "originally existent. Thus, they are "originally non-existent."

That which is "originally existent" (benyou) is called "originally non-existent" (benwu) from the perspective of the afflictions (*kleśa*). That which is "now existent" (jin you) refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*);
from the perspective of the afflictions, it is called "now existent," while from the perspective of True Suchness, it is called "now non-existent" (jinwu).
Furthermore, that which is "now existent" is also called "now existent" from the perspective of the presence of afflictions; therefore, the afflictions are themselves the original [nature].
That which is non-existent now is *tathatā* (suchness); that which was originally existent but is now non-existent is *tathatā*;

that afflictions are themselves *tathatā*—that such dharmas exist throughout the three periods of time is impossible. To explain this according to the sūtra’s distinction between differentiation and non-differentiation:

the essence of differentiation is *tathatā*. From the perspective of differentiation, it is "originally non-existent"; from the perspective of *tathatā*, it is "originally existent. Now, regarding differentiation...
Since the separate essence is true suchness (*tathatā*), it is fundamentally non-existent within its differentiated names.

To say that it "exists now" means that one is deluded regarding non-differentiation and perceives differentiation; within this non-differentiation there is no limit, whereas within differentiation there is a limit.

Because differentiation now arises from delusion, it is called "existing now. Therefore, the conclusion states: "Differentiation is fundamentally non-existent and exists only now; non-differentiation [is eternal]."

"If that which existed originally is now non-existent, there is a difference; if there is no difference, then it is not different. That a dharma exists throughout the three periods of time—past, present, and future—is impossible;
all other cases are to be understood accordingly.

[Commentary] The Dilun masters say that the essence and function of permanent dharmas are such that Zhanran (Zhang'an) challenges them by asking: "If they were hidden originally and are now manifest, then they are truly [subject to change]."
Just as the essence was previously hidden because it existed within ignorance, it is said to be "manifest" once ignorance has been transformed into True Suchness (*tathatā*).

"Manifest" refers to its constant function, while "hidden" refers to its constant essence. If, now that it is manifest, it were to become ignorance again, it would be said that after being manifest, it subsequently vanishes.
[Commentary]: It should be stated that because afflictions (*kleśa*) are beginningless and their essence is itself bodhi, they are called "without end.

If one were to speak of them separately: because afflictions are the fundamental basis, they are called "beginningless"; because they are severed today, they are called "having an end. When a Bodhisattva first realizes [this], it has a beginning;
because it does not perish throughout the limits of the future, it is "without end. Now, by explaining their mutual identity (*lakṣaṇa-samatā*), they are said to be "separated" [from duality].
Because awakening is free from afflictions, afflictions are the beginningless aspect of awakening;
because there is no awakening apart from the cessation of afflictions, awakening is the endless aspect of afflictions. The same applies to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa: they are the dharma of eternal abiding.

[Commentary] Regarding the citation of Zhanran’s five interpretations, the first three concerning the Three Truths should be stated as follows: the True and the Conventional are "originally existing but now absent," while the Middle Way is "originally non-existent but now present.

That the True and Conventional are identical to the Middle, and the Middle is identical to the True and Conventional—namely, that there is no such thing as a phenomenon existing throughout the three periods of time—is incorrect;

this should be understood by analogy with the other four interpretations. Furthermore, one should reflect that these judgments and explanations do not accord with the first two phrases of the sutra text.
Because they are identical in nature, it is not possible [to distinguish them] (reflect on this).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "body, sensation, mind, and phenomena are identical to the house and so forth," according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, prior to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are five stages of mental abiding (*sthiti-citta*). The verse states:

To treat the four types of craving universally, one first analyzes the visualization of the skeleton; expanding it to the ocean and then contracting it again is called the stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika*).
Removing [the visualization] from the feet up to the midpoint of the head is called the stage of mature cultivation (*kṛtaparijaya*).
Binding the mind between the eyebrows is called the stage of transcending mental attention (*atikrāntamanasikāra*).

The Treatise says: The cultivation of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is specifically for the purpose of counteracting desire. Briefly stated, there are four types of desire: first, desire for color (*varṇa-rāga*); second, desire for shape (*saṃsthāna-rāga*);

third, desire for exquisite touch (*sparśa-rāga*); and fourth, desire for service (*paricaryā-rāga*). One cultivates the contemplation of impurity by taking a livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) and so forth as the object to counteract the first type of desire;
one cultivates the contemplation of impurity by taking food and so forth as the object to counteract the second type of desire; and one [cultivates it] by taking worms and maggots...
Cultivating the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) by focusing on a corpse that does not move treats the third type of greed;

cultivating the contemplation of impurity by focusing on a skeleton (*asthi-śaṅkalikā*) treats the fourth type of greed. The contemplation of impurity based on a skeleton is capable of treating all four types of greed, because within the skeleton there are no objects for those four types of greed.
To explain this: it teaches that the four types of greed and so forth are countered by taking the object of a livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) as the opposite of beauty.

Because the object of "exquisite blue" and so forth is transformed into being devoured by jackals and wolves, it reverses [the perception of] beautiful features; because the object of "worms" is transformed into [a corpse with] maggots, it reverses [the perception of] exquisite touch;
because the object of "the unmoving corpse" is transformed into [an image for] making offerings and so forth—these four contemplations of impurity each remedy one type of craving.

(The explanation of remedying the four types of craving is complete. If one contemplates a skeleton, it can remedy the four types of craving; when seeing the skeleton, at times there is no manifestation of exquisite color, and...

Regarding the marvelous forms, marvelous touches, and marvelous deportment (the commentary on one line of the verse states: "First, distinguish the contemplation of the bone-chain"): One first contemplates the bone-chain extending to the edge of the ocean, and from the edge of the ocean back to oneself;
this is the stage of the beginner (*ādikarmika*). Next, one contemplates one's own body from the feet to the head until half of it is seen as bone;
this is called the stage of the proficient practitioner (*kṛtaparicaya*). Finally, one binds the mind between the eyebrows and emits the eight colors.
The light is called "Transcending the Stage of Mental Application" (and so forth). The verse says:

Entry into cultivation requires two gates: The contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing. Those for whom desire and discursive thought predominate Should practice these in their respective order.

The treatise says: The correct entry into cultivation consists, in brief, of two essential gateways. Since there are many types of essential gateways for entering cultivation, and since the practices of sentient beings are manifold, there are likewise many gateways for entering cultivation.
First, the extensive [method], which is the "multitude. Second, there are five types: namely, those with much greed [practice] impurity;
those with much anger [practice] loving-kindness and compassion; those with much delusion [practice] dependent origination; and those attached to a self [practice] the analysis of the aggregates.

Regarding the six elements (*ṣaddhātu*), vitarka, and vicāra, the practice of breath-holding (*ānāpānasmṛti*) follows the two most concise gateways for the majority of cases: first, the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), and second, the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
Therefore, these two alone are called the "essential gateways. Impurity serves as the antidote to greed (*rāga*), while breath-holding serves as the antidote to discursive thought (*vitarka*);

this is explained according to the majority of cases. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that from the perspective of the gateway of immediate antidotes, it is taught that the meditation on impurity can serve as the antidote [to greed].
The disease of greed is not left untreated; mindfulness of breathing treats discursive thought, and it should be understood that the same applies here. Therefore, the verse says:

"For those in whom greed and discursive thought predominate, [the remedies] are taught according to their strength. Impurity is prescribed as the remedy for greed. To explain this further, the treatise provides a detailed commentary on the verse.

Furthermore, the term "greed" is explained below by means of the three characters for the "contemplation of impurity," while "counting the breaths" and so forth explain the two characters for "mindfulness of breathing" (reflect upon this).
The treatise having thus explained the two gateways for entering cultivation, by means of these two gateways the mind attains concentration.
Once the mind has attained concentration, what further practice is there to be undertaken? The following three verses clarify the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Since the first two verses concern the applications of mindfulness to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), one verse summarizes the applications of mindfulness to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the clarification of the specific characteristics in the first two verses, the stanza says:

Having relied upon the already accomplished *śamatha*, one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) for the sake of *vipaśyanā*. One contemplates body, sensation, mind, and phenomena by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Their intrinsic nature consists of wisdom derived from hearing and so forth; as for the other [associated factors], they are explained as being mixed with the objects of focus and arising in successive order.
They are established as exactly four because they serve to counteract the [four] inversions.
The Commentary states: "Relying on the already cultivated and perfected excellence of *śamatha* to practice the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as *vipaśyanā*.
This is a general explanation of the intent of the foundations of mindfulness. *Śamatha* is translated as "calming" (*zhi*), and *vipaśyanā* is translated as "insight" (*guan*).

According to the correct principle, having already cultivated and perfected calming as the basis, one practices the four foundations of mindfulness so that insight may be swiftly accomplished; it is not the case that one who has not attained concentration is capable [of this].
Seeing things as they truly are, the intent of this treatise explains that the five *sthāpakacitta* (stabilizing mind) contemplations consist of respectfully and diligently cultivating *śamatha*.
At that time, the mind abides in a single sign through the conceptual visualization of the skeleton and so forth; this is called *śamatha*.

The contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) involves grasping the distinct characteristics of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena, and furthermore, grasping various specific characteristics within the body.

Because it eliminates the four inversions and gives rise to vision according to reality, it is called the *Abhidharma* (Treatise). How, then, does one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness? This is the question. Regarding the term "treatise" (*śāstra*):
it refers to observing the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena through their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṇa*).

The individual intrinsic natures of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena are called their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) have the nature of impermanence; all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) have the nature of suffering.
The emptiness of all phenomena and their lack of self-nature is called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) states:

"By means of the specific and common characteristics, one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. This means that the practitioner, with wisdom and a one-pointed mind, contemplates each part of the body individually through its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) while practicing the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), thereby discerning the distinct nature of these phenomena from other phenomena.
To discern that this phenomenon is indistinguishable from other phenomena is called "contemplating the common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) within the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*):

it refers to observing that the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of the ten internal bases (*āyatana*)—from the eye to the tactile organ—are each distinct, for each one possesses its own specific characteristic as a base. Thus, within those respective [bases], there is correctness.
The arising of wisdom is called "contemplation of specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*). When this contemplation of specific characteristics reaches fulfillment, there arises a form of the path;
it is at that time that the designation "application of mindfulness to the body as a specific-characteristic lineage" (*svalakṣaṇa-gotra-kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*) is established.

This also consists in the thorough knowledge of the specific characteristics of those phenomena, because a distinct right wisdom arises for each [phenomenon] rather than a single wisdom arising collectively regarding all objects (and so forth). Next is the application of mindfulness to the body.

Abiding in the contemplation of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) means observing that although the individual characteristics of each part of the body differ, the general characteristic of the body remains the same.
Furthermore, at that time, one contemplates that all ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality bases) are likewise of the nature of form (*rūpa*) without distinction;

that is, they do not transcend being derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). When right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) arises regarding this single category of phenomena, it is called the contemplation of common characteristics.

When this contemplation of characteristics reaches fulfillment, there arises a "path-form" (*mārga-rūpa*); it is at that time that the designation "body-foundation of mindfulness of the shared-characteristic lineage" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-gotra-kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*) is established.

This also constitutes the thorough knowledge of the shared characteristics of those phenomena; thus, there arises a single, unified correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*), rather than a separate cognition arising for each individual object.

(The term "path-form" refers to the object of meditative concentration. Regarding the intrinsic nature of the body, it consists of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*).

Regarding the self-nature of sensation, mind, and phenomena as being manifest according to their names: "excluding the three, the remaining phenomena" refers here to the self-nature of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (and so forth).

It further states: regarding the body, one conceives of it as pure, and craving is its self-nature; regarding sensation, one conceives of it as pleasure, and the grasping of a self is its self-nature;
regarding the mind, one conceives of it as permanent, and a portion of the view of extremes is its self-nature; regarding phenomena, one conceives of them as...
"My view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) constitutes its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); apart from these four, the remainder are either its outflow (*niṣyanda*). The commentary explains:

According to the *Nyāya*, one contemplates the body and so forth through their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the individual contemplation of each, there is the separate contemplation of specific characteristics and the separate contemplation of general characteristics.

First, concerning the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), the distinction between the specific and the general is as follows: first, one contemplates the object of form (*rūpa*) in relation to the other ten [bases].

One first contemplates the distinctness of the individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), observing that from visible form (*rūpa*) up to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), these eleven types are each different from one another.
Next, one contemplates their common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), observing that these eleven kinds of matter all share the characteristic of being obstructive matter (*rūpa-pratighāta*).

Furthermore, one next contemplates the body as being distinct in its essential nature and characteristics from the three [mental aggregates] such as feeling (*vedanā*), which do not possess the quality of experiencing objects.

Next, one contemplates the body separately by its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, one contemplates the body together with other aggregates such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, taking their collective impermanence as their characteristic;

this is called "contemplation by common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-vibhāvanā*). Feeling, mind, and dharmas each have both specific and common characteristics, as explained at length in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (and so forth).
Regarding the verse’s mention of "mixed objects," the treatise states: "Among the four [foundations of mindfulness], three are exclusively nominal and unmixed."
The fourth object-condition (*ālambana*) encompasses both mixed and unmixed objects. If one contemplates only phenomena (*dharma*), it is called an unmixed object-condition;
if one observes two, three, or all four [aggregates] such as the body (*kāya*) collectively, it is called a mixed object-condition. The commentary explains:
there are six permutations for the combination of two, four permutations for the combination of three, and one permutation for the combination of four, totaling eleven permutations.
Regarding the question of why the *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness) with mixed objects is induced immediately after the *smṛtyupasthāna* with non-mixed objects, and what the sequence is:
it is because the treatise holds that one should first contemplate whatever object is coarsest;

or, because various forms of craving (*rāga*) operate upon the body, the contemplation of the body is placed first among the four foundations of mindfulness. Furthermore, craving toward the body arises through delight and attachment.
One experiences delight in feeling because the mind is not disciplined; the lack of discipline in the mind is due to the fact that the afflictions have not been severed.
Thus, one contemplates feeling and the others in this sequential order. The explanation of this sequence is as follows: among the four [aggregates], form is coarsest, so it is contemplated first;

among the latter three, feeling is coarsest, so it is contemplated first; among the latter two, the mind is coarsest, so it is contemplated first; and since phenomena (*dharma*) are the most subtle, they are contemplated last. Question 5.

Regarding the sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*), formations (*saṃskāra*) are coarse and mind (*citta*) is subtle. Why, then, are the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) such as perception (*saṃjñā*) considered subtle, while mind itself is both subtle and coarse?

The answer is: although perception and formations are coarse when compared to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), because they include the extremely subtle phenomena of *nirvāṇa*, they are discussed together with the coarse and the subtle within the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena;
therefore, it is explained last. (And so forth. The verse says: "Because they counteract the perversions, there are only four."

The Treatise says: These four foundations of mindfulness counteract, respectively, those four kinds of inversions—purity, pleasure, permanence, and self—and there are exactly four, neither more nor less. [Commentary]:
Regarding the *Mahāśāstra*, up to the section on "postures," there are four: first, desire for color; second, desire for form; third, desire for speech; fourth, [desire for]...
