The desire for smoothness and softness (*ślakṣṇa-spraṣṭavya*) is subsumed under the two categories of form (*rūpa*); the desire for the five postures (*īryāpatha*) and the desire for the six perceptions of persons (*pudgala-saṃjñā*) are subsumed under the category of form;
this exquisite touch (*sūkṣma-spraṣṭavya*) is subsumed under both form and smoothness; and this service (*upasthāna*) is subsumed under speech and sound (*ghoṣa*).
[The desire for] postures and the perception of persons are excluded, and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the Great and Small [Vehicles], those who must be delivered through the appropriate Dharma are moved by compassion; for the small [vehicle], he extracts them from suffering at the Deer Park, and through the arising of loving-kindness, he brings about the Lotus Sūtra.
Through great compassion, he responds to them by bestowing happiness.
[Sūtra]: Someone asks the Buddha: "If it is certain that those who slander the Mahāyāna will fall [into the evil realms], why do you say 'perhaps' (*vā*)?

Why not say they will definitely fall? [Answer]: In the past, at the sites of twenty thousand Buddhas, this person heard the Mahāyāna to its conclusion; yet from that day forward, he gave rise to malice and took pleasure in being attached to the three realms.

When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he immediately presented the Mahāyāna. Because his great capacity (*mahā-indriya*) was not yet mature, hearing it would have caused him to produce slander. Once slandered, he would have immediately fallen into suffering. It was for this reason that [the Buddha] said "perhaps."

Not teaching [the Mahāyāna] to them because they currently have no fault of slandering it, but rather gathering them in by means of the Hīnayāna to temporarily remove their attachments, and later teaching the Mahāyāna so that they may enter the One Vehicle—there is certainly no possibility of them falling into the three miserable realms. Because whether they fall or do not fall is not fixed, it is called "perhaps" (*vā*).

Furthermore, because both the beginning and the end are Mahāyāna while the middle proceeds toward the Hīnayāna, and because their faculties and natures are indeterminate, it is again called "perhaps."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the fires of the five turbidities burn the house of the five aggregates": one might ask, among the fires capable of burning, why are the *dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya* (turbidity of views) and the *kleśa-kāṣāya* (turbidity of afflictions) called the "burners" of sentient beings' life-span (*āyuḥ-kalpa*)? Since the other three turbidities are not distinct from the five aggregates, how can they be called "burners"?

The answer is that "sentient being" is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), "life" is a provisional construct established upon the mind and form (*rūpa-citta*), and "kalpa" is likewise a provisional construct; therefore, [the distinction holds]. Ten.

Among the four dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), there are three—namely, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), and time—which are conventionally designated as the "burner.

These apply to both the conventional and the real; however, that which is "burned" is exclusively real. Furthermore, the "burner" of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) applies to both the internal and external, whereas the "burned" non-turbid aggregates exist only internally.
Moreover, the fire that acts as the "burner" applies to both cause and effect, while the "burned" house [is the effect].

The fire that exists solely in the fruit and is capable of burning pertains to both natures; the affliction of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*) is of an unwholesome nature, while the other three are of an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature.
This distinction exists because the five aggregates (*skandha*) that are burned are exclusively of an indeterminate nature.
[Sūtra]: This house has already been burned. Regarding the question: "Since it is said that it has already been burned, why then say 'do not let it cause harm'?
[Answer]: This is spoken to describe the matter of fear. These fires of the five corruptions (pañca-kaṣāya) are attached to this house of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha);

their union is called "already burned. Because the attachment [to the world] has not yet been long-standing and the roots of goodness (kuśala-mūla) of the One Vehicle have not yet been harmed by the fire, he now issues this admonition:
"Do not let it cause harm.
[Sūtra] Regarding "having fully informed": was this previously informed or not?
If it had already been informed, then since the One Vehicle has already been expounded, why does the first sūtra say, "I would rather not preach the Dharma," and now say, "having fully informed"?

Yajñadatta replied: "I intended to preach the teaching of the One Vehicle, but because it was merely a provisional expedient devised according to mental inclinations and dispositions for the sake of salvation, I could not continue my transformative work;
thus, I did not truly inform them. Therefore, it is said that the 'Gate of Admonition' refers to such provisional adaptations."

[Commentary] "Not recognizing the eight sufferings" refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging. There are three methods for explaining these eight sufferings:
first, explaining their names; second, defining their characteristics; third, subsuming them under the three types of suffering. First, regarding the explanation of the names: (1) Birth...

That which is suffering as the initial arising of the retribution-portion is called "birth"; because there is suffering at the time of birth, it is designated by that name, hence it is called "the suffering of birth.

The decline and transformation is called "aging"; because there is suffering at the time of aging, it is named after that state, hence it is called "the suffering of aging. The increase and decrease of the four great elements is called "sickness";

because there is suffering at the time of sickness, its name is made manifest according to that state. The disintegration of the aggregates is called "death"; because there is suffering at the time of death... [it is so named].

Regarding suffering that also arises in dependence on conditions: that which is characterized by the thought of being separated from what one loves is called "separation from the beloved" (*priyaviprayoga*);

because distress arises based on this condition, it is designated as such. That which is characterized by the forced gathering of what one hates is called "union with the hated" (*apriyasaṃprayoga*); because distress arises based on this cause, it is also designated as such.
That which is characterized by the non-attainment of what one seeks is called "unfulfilled longing" (*yad-apicchatā*); because distress arises based on this cause, it is designated as such.
Regarding the suffering of seeking birth, it is also established by way of its conditions and designated as the "suffering of the five aggregates of clinging" (*pañca-upādāna-skandha-duḥkha*).

The five aggregates being in a state of intense flourishing are called the "five aggregates of clinging"; this is a designation established by way of their essential nature. Alternatively, "flourishing" (*skandha*) has the meaning of "receiving" (*vedanā*);

thus, when the five aggregates receive the seven preceding types of suffering, it should be called the "suffering of the five aggregates of clinging. Next, to distinguish their characteristics: what is the suffering of birth? As stated in the *Pañcarājāsūtra*: [text follows].

It is taught that from the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) up until birth from the womb is called "birth" (*jāti*). In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, "birth" encompasses both the beginning and the end, which differs from other sūtras.

This [explanation] is divided into five parts: First, the initial emergence, namely the link of consciousness; because it is the beginning of retribution, it is called the "initial," and its first arising is called "emergence.
Second, reaching the end, namely the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); because the mental and physical factors are fully present, compared to the preceding stage, it is called the "end. Third...
"Development" refers to the prior *nāmarūpa* increasing into the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). "Emergence from the womb" is the fourth.
"Species" refers to the period after emerging from the womb until old age and death; within this interval, the continuous arising of new moments is termed "birth.
What is the suffering of old age? As explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are two meanings: first, it pertains to the entire life, namely the graying of the hair.

The withering of form and the change of complexion is called "aging" (jarā) in its second sense; the continuous succession of transformations from the link of consciousness (vijñāna) up to old age and death is termed "aging" in its first sense. These two—the beginning and end of every moment—are as follows:

the first is "growth," which refers to the continuous transformation from the link of consciousness through the prime of youth; the second is "decay," which refers to the moments following the decline of one's years.
Contemplating the suffering of old age: what constitutes the suffering of illness? As explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are two meanings.

First is physical illness, which refers to the imbalance and fluctuation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as well as other incidental illnesses. Second is mental illness, which refers to joy, sorrow, fear, delusion, and so forth.
What constitutes the suffering of death? As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are three types of death. The first is... [abandonment].

First, death through negligence refers to slandering the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras. Second, death through the breaking of precepts refers to violating the prohibitions of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Third, death through the destruction of life refers to the exhaustion of the body and the end of life. This section of the sutra is divided into two parts: first, death by the exhaustion of the life-span; second, death due to external conditions.

Within the category of the exhaustion of the life-span, the sutra states there are three types: first, the exhaustion of the life-span while merit is not yet exhausted, which pertains to the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
Although the secondary retribution (the environment) has perished, the primary retribution (the body) still remains; this occurs when one’s merit is exhausted but one’s life-span is not.

Although the secondary retribution has vanished, the primary retribution still remains; this is also generally termed death by the exhaustion of life. Third, when both merit and life-span are exhausted, both the primary and secondary retributions perish;
this is what is called death due to external conditions. The Sūtra states that there are three types: first, self-inflicted harm; second, harming others; and third, being harmed by both.
What is the suffering of separation from the beloved? It is divided into two types: first, internal; second, external.

The internal refers to relatives and kinsmen; the external refers to assets and property. What is the suffering of encountering the hated? There are two types: first, internal, which refers to retribution in the evil realms;
second, external, which refers to conditions such as swords and staves. What is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks? There are two types: first, the cause; second, [the result].

Within cause and effect, there are two [aspects]: first, one seeks to be free from unwholesome dharmas but cannot attain it; second, one desires to seek wholesome dharmas but cannot attain them. Within the effects, there are also two:
first, one seeks to be free from suffering conditions but cannot attain it; second, one desires to obtain pleasant conditions but cannot attain them.

Regarding suffering conditions, there are two: first, internal; second, external. Seeking to be free from the retribution of suffering in the three miserable realms is called internal; [suffering from] weapons and the like is external.
Regarding the causes of external pleasure, there are two types: internal and external. When one seeks the fruits of pleasure from humans and devas and does not obtain them, this is called internal;
when one seeks the exquisite objects of the five sensory realms and does not obtain them, this is called external.

As for the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, these [eight types of suffering] collectively comprise the seven preceding categories as the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging. Regarding the inclusion of the three pairs within the three types of suffering, among the eight [types of suffering], the first...

The seven [types of suffering] are individually assigned to the three types of suffering, while the last one subsumes all three collectively. Regarding the former seven, there are both general and specific applications:

"suffering upon destruction" (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) and "suffering due to conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) apply generally to all seven. Birth, old age, sickness, and death are subsumed under "the suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkha*).

Furthermore, if one experiences affliction and harm by way of the loss of physical form through old age, the loss of strength through sickness, or the loss of life through death, these are subsumed under "suffering upon destruction."

Separation from the beloved is subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*); meeting with the hated involves the retributive suffering of the two or three miserable realms (*durgati*), where one is forcibly assembled through external conditions such as blades and staves, and is thus subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*); the activity of seeking is forcibly manifested before one and is therefore subsumed under the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*);

and within the failure to obtain what is sought, the meaning encompasses all three types of suffering; specifically, when one fails to obtain what is sought through evil seeking, it is subsumed under the suffering of suffering.

When one seeks union with what is pleasant and fails to obtain it, this is subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*); when one seeks to avoid what is unpleasant and fails to do so, this is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
The five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*) possess all eight of these sufferings.
The passage beginning with "He addressed them, saying... refers to words of rarity, which are expressions of praise; the words concerning what is difficult to obtain are exhortations.

The phrase "If you do not accept [them]... means that if you do not follow my exhortation to leave the burning house and take the carts of the three fruits, you will inevitably be scorched by the fire of thirst and give rise to sorrow and regret.

[Sūtra]: "Various rare treasures and extraordinary objects" refers to the three skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*): they are considered rare treasures within the Hīnayāna, yet extraordinary within the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The commentary states: "The three carts are the rare treasures; the realms of humans and devas are the extraordinary objects."

[Sūtra] Regarding these various sheep-carts and so forth: among the three vehicles, those at the lower level—the human and celestial realms—are said to have different fruits of retribution for their precepts and wholesome deeds;
thus they are called "various. Bodhisattvas who transform the world and Śrāvakas who follow teachers both dwell among humans, and such types are likened to sheep.
Pratyekabuddhas, who advance without transforming the world and retreat without following a teacher, are compared to deer to represent this.
Furthermore, in the mountain forests, sheep are slow-witted by nature, which is like the śrāvaka; deer are swift and agile by nature, which is like the pratyekabuddha;

and oxen are strong and robust, which is like the bodhisattva. Moreover, the body of a sheep is small, which represents the Hīnayāna; the deer occupies a middle position, which represents the Madhyamāyāna; and the ox is large in form, which represents the Bodhisattva.
[Commentary]: From "At that time" up to "according to the sons' wishes," the term "suited wishes" (*shiyuan*) refers to a state of joyful and delighted mind.
Since it says they "heard what their father said," this is the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "Each mind was courageous and keen" means courageous progress and sharp acuity;
because the three vehicles (*triyāna*) differ, they are called "each. "The mind moved with deliberation" explains the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the preliminary skillful means (*pūrvaprayoga*); its vigor and sharpness constitute the initial deliberation. Regarding "mutually pushing and displacing":

"pushing" refers to contemplating the principles of the Four Noble Truths through the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), as one first treads upon the path of the Four Noble Truths; hence it is called "displacing. When the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox has not yet been resolved, it is termed "mutual.

For example, when contemplating the object of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*)—namely, suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity—one [erroneously] labels them as permanence, pleasure, self, and purity.

To regard purity as impure is called "error" (*mithyā*) regarding this; or, failing to discern it, to reject the impure as pure or to reject the pure as impure is called "mutual [confusion]," because of immaturity in contemplation.
The other three truths should be understood by analogy (and so forth).

[Commentary] Regarding the statement "contemplating the thirty-two truths," the *Ji* (Record) points to the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), which explains this in detail. Here, we shall briefly understand the general meaning. There are three grades of patience (*kṣānti*).

In the lower grade, one contemplates all eight truths, with four aspects (*ākāra*) for each. First, one contemplates the suffering (*duḥkha*) of the desire realm; next, the suffering of the two higher realms;
and so on, up to the path (*mārga*) of the desire realm, followed by the path of the two higher realms. Thus, there are sixteen aspects for each of the upper and lower realms.

This is called the thirty-two-fold contemplation of the truths (*satya-vipaśyanā*). Next, during the stage of medium patience (*madhyama-kṣānti*), there are twenty-four cycles of reducing the aspects (*ākāra-prahāṇa*) and seven cycles of reducing the objects (*ālambana-prahāṇa*).
Each cycle of reducing the aspects consists of three [aspects], while each cycle of reducing the objects consists of only one aspect; these are further termed "reducing the objects.

There are seven such cycles of reducing the objects, and for each of the eight truths, there are three cycles of reducing the aspects. All these reductions proceed from the higher stages back toward the lower ones, until reaching the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-duḥkha*).

The second moment of mind within the stage of the Truths (satya-adhigama), observing a single object and a single mode of activity, is called the fulfillment of medium patience (*madhya-kṣānti*). The text states that this involves "contracting the contemplation," which refers to this.

The next moment of mind, observing a single object and a single mode of activity, is called the fulfillment of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). The remainder is as explained in the *Shu-chi* (Commentary on the *Jie-shen-tong-zhi-lun*), etc. (as indicated by "and so forth").
[Commentary]: In the preceding section on the teaching by Dharma, first the arousal of the capacity was shown, followed by the removal of obstacles and the Buddha’s joy and fearlessness.
Regarding this, the Sūtra says: "Those who aspire to seek the Buddha-way" refers to the great arousal of the capacity. Next, regarding the removal of obstacles and the Buddha’s joy:

if the obstacles were not removed, they would not escape the calamity of fire, and the Buddha would consequently give rise to sorrow and fear. Only when the sons' obstacles were severed did [the Buddha] reach the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to preach.
When the Buddha’s wisdom arises, the Buddha gives rise to joy and is without fear; thus, the Buddha’s joy manifests that his sons’ obstacles have been removed.

Now, regarding the analogy, first is "escaping the peril," as the sutra says, "no longer having any obstructions. This is the escape from peril. "Rejoicing and leaping for joy" refers to the sons' joy.
Each then addresses their father, which immediately follows as "requesting the vehicle. According to the characteristics of the scriptural text, these two points correspond to these two sections.

Regarding the sequence of "before" and "after," if one considers it from the perspective of the person, one must first eliminate the obstacles and only then will the capacity [for understanding] arise.

[Commentary: As for the phrase "those who seek the Small [Vehicle]," the intention of this master is that the statement in the *Lotus Sūtra*, "We pray you grant us the three kinds of precious chariots," constitutes a request for the fruits of the Small [Vehicle].
This master does not realize that they had already attained those fruits at the time of the Deer Park; it was not the case that they were seeking them in the past.
Not having yet attained [the ultimate], today’s seeking arises simply from slightly opening the provisional and setting aside the expedient;
although one now seeks the Small Vehicle, the intention actually aims for the Great, which is why it is said that the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been awakened.

[Commentary]: "Outside the gates of the fruits of the two vehicles" means that even if one has severed the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and exhausted them to attain the minor fruits, the Buddha-fruit remains outside the gate of the hindrance of residual habituation and ignorance. "Residual habituation" refers to the remaining traces of those very afflictions;

"ignorance" refers to the hindrance of *rajas* (dust-like obscurations), which is the failure to comprehend the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is what is termed "ignorance."
[Commentary: "Now, from 'for you' up to 'the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching'—these refer to the Bodhisattvas of the four teachings, each attaining one phrase.
When discussed in their full completion, the Bodhisattvas of each teaching possess all four phrases: seeking, not seeking, both seeking and not seeking, and neither seeking nor not seeking.
Regarding the four [phrases] of the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) Teaching: first, the stages of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred *kalpas* are called 'not [seeking]'."
The stage of severing twenty-three or twenty-four moments of mind is called "severing the three pairs and grasping. Furthermore, it is called "both severed and not severed.

Fourth, setting aside the aforementioned characteristics and considering them according to principle, it is called "neither severed nor not severed. These four [categories] were all "not sought" in relation to the past;

this constitutes the first phrase. In relation to the present, they are all "sought"; this constitutes the second phrase. When the present and the past are contrasted, it is called "both sought and not sought"; this constitutes the third phrase.

Excluding the aforementioned characteristics and according to principle, this is termed "neither seeking nor not seeking. These four propositions constitute sixteen propositions. Regarding the four types of abandonment in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*):

first, the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) and the stage of nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) are termed "non-abandonment"; second, from the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*) up to the eighth ground is termed "abandonment";

third, the bodhisattva grounds where habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted are termed "both abandonment and non-abandonment"; fourth, excluding the aforementioned characteristics and according to principle...
The principle is named "neither severed nor unsevered. These four [positions] were called "not seeking" in the past and are called "seeking" in the present;

taking both the present and the past together, they are called "both seeking and not seeking. Excluding the previous characteristics, according to the principle, they are named "neither seeking nor not seeking," forming four sets of four, which constitute sixteen phrases.
Regarding the four severances of the Separate Teaching: first, the ten faiths are named "unsevered"; second, the ten abidings...

Entering emptiness is called "severing," which consists of thirty practices; emerging into the provisional is called "severing the sands of dust," yet because ignorance is not yet severed, it is called "both severing and not severing," which constitutes forty [practices].
The ten dedications cultivate the Middle Way, and the ten stages realize the Middle Way; these are called "neither severing nor not severing.

These four pairs are called "not seeking" in contrast to the past, while in contrast to the present they are called "seeking"; taking both together, they are called "both seeking and not seeking," thereby eliminating the previous characteristics.

Regarding the principle, the names "neither seeking nor not seeking" constitute sixteen phrases. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there are four stages of severance: first, the stage of names (*míngzì-wei*) is "not severed";
second, the stage of contemplative practice (*guānxíng-wei*) is called "severed"; third, the stage of semblance (*xiāngsì-wei*) is called "both severed and not severed";

fourth, from the ten abodes (*shizhu*) upward, it is called "neither severed nor not severed. These four pairs, when contrasted with the single [stage] of "not seeking," are established according to their nature (*xing*).
Second, regarding the "seeking" (suo) [of the fruit] through cultivation, there are three cases: first, seeking; second, not seeking; third, both seeking and not seeking taken together;

and fourth, neither seeking nor not seeking, which excludes the preceding characteristics. Based on principle, this constitutes sixteen phrases. For a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), "seeking" refers to advancing to subsequent stages according to their own vehicle.

If one calculates these across the four teachings, they form four sets of sixteen phrases. There are general similarities and specific differences; within the Perfect Teaching, there are... [the following].
First, regarding whether they enter gradually, suddenly, or indeterminately—these four types of bodhisattvas in the four teachings are common to all five periods;

because this is discussed in terms of both the hidden [teachings] at the Deer Park and the manifest [teachings] that follow, it is called the "grand framework and great synthesis. One should reflect that even for those of the two vehicles who entered in the past, there was likewise a hidden entry, as well as sudden, gradual, and indeterminate modes.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "Worldly people cling to," the Record states: "This is all due to not explaining whether the Buddha-vehicle and Bodhisattva-vehicle are combined or separated, or their initial and final stages, up until the point of non-meeting.

This refers to the fact that in the Deer Park [the *Āgama* period], the cause was named the Bodhisattva-vehicle and the fruit was named the Buddha-vehicle; thus it is said they were "combined at the beginning.

From the Vaipulya [period] onwards, they are called "separated at the end," which refers to the Bodhisattvas of the three teachings of the *Ekayāna-gate*. Question: What is meant by the Perfect Vehicle?
Question: What are the similarities and differences between the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the Mahāyāna, the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*), the Bodhisattva Vehicle, and the Buddha Vehicle?

Answer: Their names differ while their essence is the same; they are distinguished by what they contrast with. When contrasted with the Three Vehicles, it is called the "One Vehicle," as the text says:

"From the One Buddha Vehicle, three are taught through differentiation. When contrasted with the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), it is called the "Mahāyāna. When referring generally to the four teachings, it is the Bodhisattva Vehicle. When contrasted with the Middle and Lower [vehicles], it is called the "Supreme Vehicle."

Regarding the term "Buddha Vehicle" (buddhayāna) when applied to the Bodhisattva Vehicle, and "Buddha Vehicle" when applied to the cause [of Buddhahood], both are common to all four teachings; however, in the present context, the former three are excluded, and only the Perfect [Teaching] is intended, as it does not involve [the other modes].

[Commentary on the *Huayan jing*]: Regarding the passage from the eighth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* beginning with "below," the *Ji* (Commentary) states that the first three [stages] follow the Response [of the Buddha], while the second follows the Capacity [of the sentient beings]. I fear this may be so.

All erroneous interpretations of the text stem from failing to recognize that it is taught according to the capacities [of the audience]. For instance, when it says "those of inferior capacity who are weary and submerged," this refers to dull faculties;
"sharp" and so forth all likewise refer to capacities.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the dharma of the three liberations issues forth from the Śrāvaka vehicle and so on," "issues forth" (*niṣkrānti*) has the meaning of "cause"; that is, it refers to proceeding from the cause to the fruit.
"Name" means emergence; it is also said that the characteristics of the Śrāvaka-yāna are precisely the characteristics of practicing the practice.

[Commentary] Regarding Guangzhai’s taking the two knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) as the essence, the *Abhidharmakośa* asks: "What is the difference between the two aspects of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising? The verse says:

Regarding the four noble truths, the wisdom that "I have known what was to be known" and so forth—namely, that there is nothing further to be known—is, in due order, the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.

As stated in the *Tathāgata-śāstra*: "What is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)? It is when one in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) correctly perceives and knows: 'I have already known [what was to be known].'"

"I have known suffering, I have abandoned its origin, I have realized its cessation, and I have cultivated the path"—the knowledge, vision, clarity, awakening, understanding, wisdom, light, and observation arising from this is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).
The commentary states: These are alternative names for the same knowledge, distinguished as general and specific. To decisively sever [delusion] is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*);

to investigate is called "vision" (*darśana*); to be free from darkness is called "clarity" (*vidyā*); to awaken to the principle is called "awakening" (*buddhi*); to penetrate thoroughly is called "understanding" (*avabodha*); and to discern is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

The Dharma is named "Wisdom-Light" (*prajñā-āloka*); "illumination" refers to its observing and "examination" refers to its scrutinizing. This indicates that while the names differ, their essence is one. The *Śāstra* states:
"The Buddha’s knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) means that through right vision he knows: 'I have already known suffering; it need not be known again,' and so forth, up to:

'I have already cultivated the path; it need not be cultivated again. This is called the knowledge of non-arising. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "It refers to whether there is or is not non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
Because [the path] arises, this wisdom attains the wisdom of arising; because it relies upon non-arising, it is named the "wisdom of non-arising" (and so forth).

If one were to take the wisdom of non-arising alone, it would apply generally to the Mahāyāna. However, what is here termed "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) and so on is restricted solely to the Hīnayāna and cannot serve as its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, since the cause does not contain the myriad virtues, why speak of the fruit alone?

[Commentary: Regarding "the cause is primary and the fruit is secondary": if one follows the direct cultivation of the cause, the fruit is primary and the cause is secondary; however, since we are now following the practice of cultivating the cause out of a longing for the fruit, it is said that the fruit is primary.

[Commentary: Regarding "if the internal cause severs the fetters," etc.: the question is, as for the conditioned capacity to sever, does "severing" mean the very act of severing the fetters, or does it mean attaining the state of having severed the fetters?

Question: Since the fruit beyond the vehicle has already been realized as the ultimate, how can it be said to be subsumed within the vehicle? Answer: Conditioned phenomena are called "vehicles" because they rely on principle and their essence is capable of transporting [the practitioner];
True Suchness is the nature of the vehicle and is likewise called "subsumed within the vehicle. Question:

Since the Buddha-fruit has ceased its transport, and that which has ceased transporting is not called a vehicle, how can it still be called "subsumed within the vehicle" upon reaching the fruit? Answer: Although transport has ceased upon reaching the fruit...
To personally attain [enlightenment] is called the vehicle that transforms others; to cause others to progress until the end of the future is called the vehicle that gathers [beings].

[Commentary]: Regarding "transporting them into the remainderless," the *Prajñāpāramitā* says, "I shall cause all to enter nirvana without remainder," which means causing sentient beings to enter the remainderless state.
Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "I establish all my children within the secret treasury," which refers entirely to this.

Regarding this example: if one asks how those śrāvakas of fixed nature who enter the nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa can be said to be "subsumed by the Vehicle" (yāna-saṃgṛhīta) within the context of the gate of benefiting others through self-realization—given that they have entered final extinction—the answer is as follows:

In the Mahāyāna, both forms of benefit [self-benefit and benefit for others] are termed "carrying" (vāhana). Therefore, because they possess the capacity to transform others, they are designated as being subsumed by the Vehicle;
whereas those [śrāvakas] lack the capacity to transform others, and thus their "carrying" is categorized as being of the same type as their own personal practice (svārtha-pravṛtti).

[The section on] "Vehicles and Inclusion. [Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the three vehicles encompass both the upper and lower [stages]," this refers to the *Yuanjing shu* (Commentary on the Perfect Mirror) which explains that within the house of the two vehicles they are called "upper vehicles," while outside the house they are no longer seen and are thus called "lower vehicles" (as stated in the *Ji*, etc.).

[Commentary: Regarding the second point, "the carts are equal," although the carts prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* were equal, the children were not; because the children were unequal, the carts appeared unequal.
If we reach this present sutra, however, both the children and the carts are equal. As for the statement that "Buddha-nature is the same":

if one refers to the principle (*li*) prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is already fused and harmonious, such that there was never a time when it was not equal—so why wait for today? This is said in reference to the teaching according to the capacities of beings (*jì*).
The previous teachings did not speak of the equality of nature; today, as the teachings are opened up, both the practice and the principle are called "equality. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "because the dharmas are equal," this refers to the five vehicles and seven stages of expedient means, all of which are the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm and none of which are not equal.
The *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) states: "Contemplate that every thought-moment is nothing other than the dharma-nature and true reality; this is called equality."
[Sūtra] It says, "That the carriage is high and broad. These four characters precisely clarify that the body of the carriage represents the three causes of intrinsic virtue (*svabhāva-guṇa*).

"High and broad" signifies non-duality: the non-duality of the two [causes] is the direct cause (*dharmatā-hetu*); being non-high yet high is the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*), and being non-broad yet broad is the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
Thus, the oneness within the three is the three causes of intrinsic virtue. If contrasted with the virtues of cultivation (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), however—

The general name is the "True Cause" (*samyag-hetu*). That which is below "the carriage body made of various jewels" refers to the "Condition-Cause of Cultivated Virtue" (*bhāvanā-kuśala-pratyaya-hetu*);

the "great white ox" refers to the "Revealing-Cause of Cultivated Virtue" (*pariniṣpanna-kuśala-niḥsyanda-hetu*). If one were to distinguish between the essence (*tattva*) and the possession of the perfections (*pāramitā*), one should punctuate [the text] from below "various jewels.
However, in the present text they are combined because both the Condition-Cause and the True Cause are that which is led, while the white ox is that which leads; therefore, [they are joined here].

When [the two natures] are opened, each nature has three aspects of cultivation; when they are combined, there are two aspects of cultivation and one nature. Therefore, they are combined to form the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the extensive explanation of the vehicle and so forth: some take the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) as the body of the vehicle and the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as the white ox, but do not say that the present [wisdom] is the body of the vehicle.
If one were to take [the subsequently attained wisdom] as the principle (*tattva*), it would be no different from the "Jewel Place" mentioned below; therefore, it is not taken [as the vehicle].
If one takes fundamental non-conceptual wisdom as the guide and subsequently attained wisdom as that which is guided,

this interpretation is no different from the Guangzhai school’s view that the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*) and "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*) constitute the body of the vehicle; therefore, it was refuted by Zhanran (Zhang’an).
[Commentary]: For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are profound and far-reaching:

because the true reality (*dharmatā*) is neither-knowing-nor-seeing, yet he knows and sees the *dharmadhātu* as extending horizontally throughout the ten realms, it is "vast" and "far-reaching"; because it penetrates vertically to the source of the three truths, being one within the three, it is "profound" and "lofty."

[Commentary]: From "adorned with various jewels" to "the four analytical knowledges," this is a metaphor for the cultivation and adornment of the myriad practices (*sādhana*). *Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are likened to the immeasurable factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*), which are called "various jewels";
these are merely different names for the myriad practices.

[Commentary: Regarding the fourth point, the analysis of the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) for the sake of downward transformation: as explained in the record, the meaning clarified here is that from the time one first cultivates these four analytical knowledges with the mind of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), one is able to transform sentient beings through downward manifestation upon reaching the stage of the first dwelling (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).
[Commentary: "True myriad virtues" refers to designating them as "true" from the perspective of the stage of fruition;

when they were at the stage of the cause, the practice of unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*) permeated the *dharmatā* until, upon reaching the initial stage of the fruit—the first *bhūmi*—one was immediately able to perform acts of giving and transformation. The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-śāstra* states:

"The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are not shared with others, and thus are called 'rare and marvelous.'"

Adorned. [Commentary]: Regarding "the four great vows are firm and great compassion": the four great vows are the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*). Great compassion (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) is the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings;
this is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Great pity (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*) is the vow to sever afflictions; this is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Immeasurable joy is itself the Dharma-gate; learning these innumerable vows is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

Immeasurable equanimity is itself impartial relinquishment; the mind of compassion is itself the Buddha-way; and vowing to accomplish this is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), as explained in the "Wondrous Adornment" chapter (etc.).
[Commentary] The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) refer to giving (*dāna*), kind speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and cooperation (*samānārthatā*) (and so forth).

[Commentary] Referring to *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it says: "The path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) being well-adjusted" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) within the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) that is without action (*anabhisamskāra*).

"Excluding the factor of enlightenment" means excluding the coarseness of body and speech; this refers to coarse words and gentle speech. "Abandoning the factor of enlightenment" means completely relinquishing the ten [unwholesome paths of action].

Regarding the "elements" (*dhātu*), one realizes that both the environment and its inhabitants (*bhājanopabhogya*) throughout the nine realms are all the Buddha-realm. What is called the "limb of awakening of equanimity" (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is the state of being tranquil while illuminating;

the "limb of awakening of diligence" (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is the three karmas of body, speech, and mind tending toward the three virtues in every thought-moment; the "limb of awakening of discrimination" (*vicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is that "discrimination" is the nature of wisdom, which distinguishes the provisional to enter the real;

and the "limb of awakening of joy" (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is the joy found in one's own practice and in transforming others, as both attain entry into the real. As for the "limb of awakening of mindfulness" (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): *Note: The provided text appears to be a fragmentary excerpt from a commentary on the *Bodhipakṣadharmas*. The final term "念覺" (mindfulness awakening) is left hanging, suggesting the source text may have been truncated.*
"Discrimination" (vīmaṃsā) has the nature of clear mindfulness and is not defiled by delusion.
[Commentary] The seven factors of enlightenment take concentration and wisdom as the ornaments for the body of the vehicle.

[Commentary] "Contemplation, refinement, and cultivation" refers to the combined practice of the primary and auxiliary methods; this is because one cultivates the three types of contemplative mind during the causal stage.
If one's correct practice is unable to correspond [with the goal], one uses the aids of dhyāna, such as contemplation and training, to assist it so that one may quickly enter the principle.

When the mind of the three contemplations of the principle merges with those meditative states of phenomena, both are perfected as the true mark (*dharmatā*); this is called the "unified practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā.

It is said that when the various dhyānas and samādhis give rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they are called "repeatedly spread" (*punar-vyūha*). However, the present commentary omits the supernormal powers because they are all functions of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and thus do not require separate mention.

[Commentary]: The passage from "The red pillow" to "is three yet one" uses the analogy that movement and stillness are mutually identical; the same applies to the substantial essence (*tattva*) and its function (*vṛtti*).
The essence is stillness and the function is movement, as it is said: "From cause to fruit is movement; the *dharmatā* is the essence."
Non-movement is stillness within movement; thus, it is said that "arriving" refers to the virtue of the Dharmakāya. The myriad practices are movement, while non-action is stillness;
because one penetrates the principle at the time of correct practice, it is called "non-action," which is the virtue of liberation.

The various wisdoms are movement, while "not observing" is stillness; reaching the essence through its function is termed "not observing," which is the virtue of Prajñā. This concludes the section on cessation.
The commentary states: "Observing that the four gates return to the fundamental essence and bring all conditioned activities to rest is called the 'Crimson Pillow' (*danzhen*).
[The *Shu* (Commentary) says: 'White is the root of form' refers to the 'enlightening cause of cultivated virtue' (*xiude liaoyin*), which is the name for the prajñā of cultivated virtue;

because it unites with the originally pure enlightening cause, it is called 'correspondence. Stopping and contemplating (*zhiguan*) are likened to the four foundations of mindfulness; they destroy the 'black' of the eight inversions, hence they are called the 'white ox.'"

[Commentary]: "The essence endowed with ten thousand virtues" refers to the essence of the *liǎoyīn* (cause of realization) as inherent virtue; it is not the same as the essence of the preceding [vehicle]. [Commentary]:

Furthermore, from the section on the *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness) below, this is explained in terms of the four *asaṃskṛta-dharmas* (unconditioned truths). The objects of the foundations of mindfulness are the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); suffering itself possesses causes, which is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).

From the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*) up to the five powers (*bala*) constitutes the truth of the unconditioned path (*mārga-satya*); the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*) are... [the truth of cessation].
Regarding the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) truth of cessation, if one follows other texts, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment collectively constitute the truth of the path;
however, since the four truths of the unconditioned each contain all four [truths] within them, we shall here correlate them accordingly (and so forth).
[Commentary]: "Attendants and so forth" refers to servants following behind, ushers leading in front, and those guarding at the left and right;
this refers to the Dharma-gates that assist the Path. Those of the Two Vehicles of the two teachings serve as the attendants, while Bodhisattvas of the three teachings serve as the ushers.

Māras who delight in birth-and-death constitute the left, and non-Buddhists who delight in various views constitute the right; these are all Dharma-gates that support the vehicle, consisting of both the primary and the auxiliary.
"The non-duality of the provisional is itself the real. The rest is as explained in the *Commentary* (*Ji*) [and so forth].

[The *Commentary* states: To briefly point out the ten contemplations: the height and breadth of the vehicle is the inconceivable object; the spreading of the canopy and awning is the arousal of the mind;
the inner pillow is the settling of the mind; the wind is the universal penetration; the outer pillow is the obstacles and passages; and the white ox is the factors of the path.

The attendants immediately assist in opening [the gates] to travel in the four directions; this refers to the fact that within each successive stage, one possesses patience (*kṣānti*) and is free from attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "all dharmas tend toward [emptiness]," the *Jì* (Record/Commentary) points to the second fascicle of the *Zhǐguān* (Calming and Contemplation), which quotes the *Dàpǐn* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra):

"From form and mind at the beginning, up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) at the end, it clarifies that they all tend toward [emptiness]. The *Dàlùn* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) explains: "How does a bodhisattva act for the sake of the world..."

Because they proceed toward the intermediate [realms], Bodhisattvas who have resolved upon Bodhicitta explain to sentient beings that form proceeds toward emptiness, and so on up to the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

For the sake of sentient beings, they explain that form neither proceeds nor does not proceed, and so on up to the Knowledge of All Modes. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: that which is able to proceed toward form is the provisional (*saṃvṛti*);

that which is proceeded toward, emptiness, is the ultimate (*paramārtha*); and "neither proceeding nor not proceeding" is the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*). This applies to all other passages as well.

The "dharma-trend" (dharmagati) of form consists of both subject and object, which are all provisional; since form itself cannot be apprehended, both subject and object are empty. How, then, could there be a "trend" or a "non-trend"?

This correctly reveals the Middle Way. The preceding [analysis] of subject and object serves as the opening, while the subsequent [synthesis] of subject and object in their totality serves as the conclusion.
[Commentary]: Regarding the differentiation of the One Buddha Vehicle into three, there are two meanings: first, the partial; second, the complete.
If one clings to the three as being ultimate, this is the partial meaning; if one refers to the Tathāgata’s original intent—that it is the Dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha—this is the complete meaning.
[Commentary: If one is wealthy but not a son, or a son but poor, there should be four permutations:

first, the father is wealthy but the son is not—this refers to the "wealthy father" being the Perfect Buddha within the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, while the capacities of the three previous vehicles are called "not sons.

Second, the father is poor but the son is not—this refers to the "poor father" being the Buddhas of the three previous vehicles, who are contrasted with the capacities of the Perfect Teaching and thus called "not sons. Third...
1. "The father is poor, yet he is the son": This refers to the Buddha responding to those with the capacities for the three teachings; thus, he is called "the father is poor, yet he is the son.

2. "The father is wealthy, yet he is the son": In this present sutra, the Perfect Buddha is called the "wealthy father," while those with the capacities for the three teachings are opened to the Perfect [teaching];
because these people are called "sons," they are equal [to the former].

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Thus, as for the explanation of the two kinds of equality," the *Jì* (Record/Note) states: "I fear this is an error; it merely uses wealth to illustrate [the case of] children.

However, according to the text of Zuǒxī’s *Wénjù*, it says: "The mind being equal and the children being equal means that because of the wealth, the mind becomes equal. It does not say there is an error.

As for the term "one country," this refers to the *Sāmbhogakāya* Land of Quiescent Light (*Jíguāng*) in relation to the *Sahā* World of Co-residence (*Tóngjū*). The Land of Quiescent Light universally benefits the ten realms.

If even the children of those with the three causes have not yet reached the end, how much less so for the two-vehicle sentient beings who shared karmic conditions in the past and possess the "cause of completion" (*niṣyanda-hetu*) while dwelling together [in this realm]?
[Sūtra] Śāriputra asked whether it is not false; the assembly all harbored doubts, saying that at first he permitted the three [vehicles], but in the end...
To not grant [the Great Vehicle] when it seems as if one were speaking empty words—first refusing even a small portion and later bestowing the great—is this not indeed a falsehood?

Question: Why is it that you first refused and then granted, yet now refuse while having previously granted? Answer: It was a provisional statement used to guide and lead others; thus, I first granted it. Yet, in principle, there are fundamentally no three vehicles; therefore, I do not grant it.

Initially, if I had granted the Great Vehicle, those whose faculties and conditions were not yet mature would have been unable to leave their homes; therefore, I did not grant it at first. Thus, it is great.
Since the capacity [of the recipient] has already been activated, it accords with the Buddha’s fundamental intention;
therefore, he grants it. [Commentary: Regarding the third section on praise and narration, the Scripture says, "Excellent, excellent! This is the praise; "It is as you have said" is the narration.
[Commentary]: One who has attained the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is called "sovereign" (*vaśin*).

When one thinks, "I have already seen suffering and shall not see it again," up to "I have already cultivated the path and shall not cultivate it again," this untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) perceives what is not yet fully awakened to.

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) is called "unfettered" (*asaṃyukta*); it is defined as: "Suffering has been known by me; its origin has been abandoned by me," up to "the path has been cultivated by me. This is termed [the state of being unfettered].

The Knowledge of Exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). [Sūtra]: Regarding those who seek "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth, some say that the wisdom contemplating emptiness is common to all three vehicles;

however, we maintain this is not so, for it is the all-knowledge of the stage of fruition belonging to the Tathāgata. Regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, others say it is the wisdom contemplating phenomena with characteristics (*sabhāva-dharma*), which belongs exclusively to the Buddha.

Because these two types of wisdom arise from self-awakening and are accomplished in solitude, they are called "self-arisen wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*); because they are not heard from another, they are called "teacherless wisdom" (*anācārya-jñāna*).

Now, it is said that when spoken of in terms of the fruit of Buddhahood, it is called "Buddha-wisdom" (*buddha-jñāna*); when spoken of in terms of principle, it is called "self-arisen fruit" (*svayambhū-phala*); and at its ultimate limit, it is called "teacherless" (*anācārya*).

Regarding the verse’s phrase "the house is long-worn," some explain it as a vertical discourse on the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), asserting that its moment-to-moment arising and ceasing from beginningless time constitutes being "long-worn.

The present explanation of the "three realms" (*tridhātu*) is stated from the perspective of what is transformed: both the three realms and sentient beings are the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.
Since the aspect is not separate from the mind and there is no object external to the mind, and because the mind is beginningless, the three realms are likewise beginningless.

"Beginningless" means long-lasting; it does not refer to something recently transformed or a name newly created, because it is not something produced in the present. "Impermanent" refers to that which is base and lowly;
"suddenly obscured" refers to the eighth consciousness, whose capacity for transformation and its transformed objects are impermanent from moment to moment.

It is not a permanent, abiding dharma, hence it is called "base and lowly. Because it is not extinguished gradually, it is called "suddenly obscured. Regarding the phrase "the hall and house are high and perilous," some say:
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is impermanent; that which is high is bound to easily fall, and that which is precarious is bound to lack stability.

Herein are two explanations: first, regarding the primary retribution (*vipāka*); second, regarding the secondary environment (*bhājana-loka*). These correspond to the two meanings of contemplating the mind through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Now, regarding the primary retribution:

because the aggregate of form is a continuous succession of moments, its height is impermanent and thus precarious. Second, regarding the secondary environment: even the Buddha-lands cannot avoid falling.

To cite the basis for this: although sentient beings who have attained a correct rebirth in the higher realms may have their lifespans exhausted and fall back into the three miserable destinies, they are "high" because they were born above, yet "perilous" because they fall back down.

Regarding the phrase "the pillar's root is crushed and decays," some say it refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); here, however, it refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which is subsumed within the aggregate of formations.
It is called "crushed and decayed" because it perishes and passes away from moment to moment; "crushed" means broken, and "decayed" means ruined. As for the term "supporting," it is due to...
When past karma has not yet exhausted, life is maintained continuously without interruption; because karma has exhausted, life is immediately severed.
It is like a pillar: because it rests upon its foundation and base, if the foundation and base are destroyed, the pillar collapses and the beams and rafters tilt.

Regarding this, some say that since the aggregates of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) are impermanent, once right concentration (*samādhi*) is lost, how could there be any stability? Now it is said that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) maintains [life].
A single body takes consciousness as its primary governing principle, just as a single house takes the ridgepole and rafters as its priority.
Without pillars, the ridgepole and rafters cannot remain; likewise, without the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), consciousness does not abide.
[Commentary: The thirty-six items of the "Seal Master" (Yin-shi) are:

hair, body hair, nails, teeth, eye discharge, tears, nasal mucus, saliva, filth, sweat, feces, urine, skin, facial flesh, bone marrow, fat, grease, brain, membranes, tendons, veins, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, stomach, bladder, abdomen, and arms.

[Commentary] Regarding the two interpretations of "contemplating the mind through causes and conditions" (*yīnyuán guānxīn*), the *Jì* states: "From 'life-force' (*mìnggēn*) onwards, all belong to contemplating the mind.

I fear this is not the case, for every passage contains both interpretations. For example, regarding "life-supporting," the first is "causes and conditions" and the second is "contemplating the mind";
regarding "beams and rafters," the first is "causes and conditions" and the second is "contemplating the mind"; regarding "walls and partitions," there are likewise two interpretations.

The same applies to the two explanations regarding the thirty-six items that surround and obstruct [the practitioner]. Now, our own school’s explanation is that this is a contemplation of the mind. [Commentary]:

The birds and beasts are metaphors for the five dull *anuśayas* (latent defilements) which come first; the ghosts and spirits are metaphors for the five sharp *anuśayas* which come later. Why is this different from the sequence of entering the Path? Answer: Sentient beings have two kinds of *anuśayas*:
first, the dull *anuśayas*, which are coarse and belong to the demon of craving (*tṛṣṇā-māra*); second, the sharp *anuśayas*, which are subtle and belong to... [the demon of the aggregates].
Because of seeing Māra, craving is abandoned first; whereas now, in the True Dharma, one abandons the fetters through the principle of the right path by means of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
Within this path of vision, there are two types of persons: those of dull faculties enter the path of vision by means of the two aspects of impermanence and suffering, and thus abandon craving first;
those of sharp faculties enter the path of vision by means of the two aspects of emptiness and non-self, and thus abandon views first. Therefore, they are not the same.

[Commentary]: The eight birds are metaphors for the eight types of conceit (*māna*). Arrogance regarding physical vigor is conceit based on comparison with oneself (*māna-māna*); arrogance regarding wealth is great conceit (*adhimāna*); arrogance regarding power is excessive conceit (*abhimāna*);
arrogance regarding status is false conceit (*mithyāmāna*); arrogance regarding longevity is overweening conceit (*ūnamāna*); and arrogance regarding intelligence is... [the text continues].

Regarding "pride of conduct" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-māna*): pride is a low form of conceit; pride in physical form (*rūpa-māna*) is likewise a form of overweening pride (*abhimāna*), as previously explained, because it is identical to pride in wealth.

Thus, the seven types of pride in the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts are the same. As for the term "hawk" (*śyena*): this bird possesses great strength and is able to seize deer and elk, just as a person of power can seize the wealth of others.
As for the term "owl" (*ulūka*): the owl is strong in power such that no other birds dare to offend it, just as a man in the prime of his vigor [is not easily overcome].

To dare use deceitful words to call [a bird] a "hawk" is to value oneself so highly that one ends up devouring one's own mother; it is like a person who, not yet being noble, instead harms a poor child.
To call [a bird] a "vulture" is because it eats corpses by day and returns to its mountain dwelling at night, coming and going as it pleases with constant ease;

it is like a person who possesses sovereign power and deceives both the foolish and the wise. To call [a bird] a "crow" is because this bird has a long lifespan, and thus it is so called in common parlance.
The "thousand-year-old wild goose" refers to one who, like a person of long life, has remained free from decline or misfortune from youth until old age;
thus, having given rise to arrogance, it is called a goose. As for the magpie, when it caws, travelers arrive; it wards off evil and shows auspiciousness.

This is because the magpie harbors [virtues] such as human intelligence and broad learning throughout the past and present, yet it gives rise to arrogance. As for the dove, although its nature is greedy, it does not...

He dares to eat as humans do and grows amidst the vegetables of the *śīla* (precepts), yet because he is born of pride, his virtuous words are likened to those of a pigeon. As for the surname "Pigeon" (*kapota*), it signifies a fondness for lustful desire;
having fallen into this pigeon body, he resembles a human being who is upright and mutually cherishes others.

The *Guǎngyì* says: "'Clutch' (*chā*) means to grasp with the hands. The *Jiǎnzǐ* says: "'Clutch' (*chā*) means to grasp with the hands.
