[Commentary]: Regarding "various jewels and so forth," the *Ji* (Record) states that this is explained within the section on the "Comprehension of Dharmas" (*zhǐguān shèfǎ*). That text says:
"One principle encompasses all principles; likewise, all delusions, all wisdoms, all stages, all practices, and all teachings mutually encompass one another. One should reflect upon this.

[Sūtra] "Five thousand railings" symbolizes the Dharma-body’s five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). These five aggregates possess the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses (*tathatā*), which together constitute the five thousand virtues.
Internally they sustain [suchness] like a shield, and externally they exclude [defilements] like a railing; thus they are metaphorically termed *dhāraṇī*.
There are also those for whom the six sense faculties have not yet become stable (and so forth).

[Commentary: The Many-Treasures Buddha represents the Buddha of Dharma. That he, who previously entered extinction, now appears, signifies that although he is not born, he manifests birth; and although he appears, he remains in extinction, signifying that although he is not extinguished, he manifests extinction.
This manifestation of extinction immediately represents the Dharmakāya pervading all places, just as it pervades the ten directions—this is the realization of the Sūtra.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "Prabhūtaratna, though long extinguished, now appears to testify to the Sūtra," the intent is that this is similar to what follows regarding "extinguished" and "not extinguished.
One should say: although he appears to testify to the Sūtra, he is "born"; yet, having been extinguished for a long time, he is "unborn.
His extinction in the past is "extinguished," while his manifesting his entire body is "not extinguished. (Reflect on this.)

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the eleven chapters from this chapter downward concern the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth," the eleven characters [in the commentary] are erroneous;

it should instead say "seven chapters. From this chapter up to the "Chapter on the Merit of Discernment" (*Guǎngshòu gōngdé pǐn*), there are seven chapters of the sūtra that constitute the Wheel of Supernormal Powers (*abhijñā-cakra*).
From the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (*Suíxǐ pǐn*) onward, these are the teachings of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharma-cakra*). I fear there is an error [in the original]. (And so forth.)

[Sūtra]: Regarding the passage "possessing great vows until reaching the stage of realization," the *Śāstra* (Commentary), fascicle seven, states: "The Buddhas do not enter *nirvāṇa* unless requested by someone;

just as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Prabhūtaratna enters *nirvāṇa* because no one requests it, yet he leaves behind a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that enters the seven-jeweled stūpa to bear witness to the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, appearing all at once. This is also like the case of the younger brother of the Buddha Suśānta."
If one were to enter *nirvāṇa* before their capacity [to benefit others] has matured, there would be no contradiction in this sutra’s statement that Bodhisattvas possess vows;

for it is precisely through the conditions of their causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) that they make vows to correctly transform sentient beings. Seeing that there was no great potential among them to hear this sutra, they further made vows to act as witnesses for its propagation.
Question: For what reason did Śākyamuni designate the Buddhas of the Pure Lands as his own emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*)?

Answer: If the pure Buddha-body of the Pure Land is pure, subtle, and wondrous yet still a response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) rather than the true body, this reveals that Śākyamuni’s body in the defiled land is even more a trace (*śeṣa*) rather than the fundamental source. Therefore, [the text] collects only the Buddhas who are emanations within the Pure Land.
How is it known that both Buddhas are not the true reality, thereby revealing that the *dharmakāya* is neither pure nor defiled, like empty space?
If one asks whether this body is the true Buddha, Master Rui’s transmission from Kumārajīva states: "The manifestation of divided bodies clarifies that they are not real;

thus we know that two Buddhas are not the truth, while non-duality is the reality. Therefore, we know that the preaching of the Vow of Prabhūtaratna was intended to reveal the essence of non-duality and the traces of multiplicity;
it is for this reason that the divided bodies are assembled."
[Sūtra] By means of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, those who desire to see the Buddha’s body attain great bliss.

Some say that one who previously desired to see Prabhūtaratna intended to perceive Prabhūtaratna’s *dharmakāya*, which is without arising or ceasing, whereas the *nirmāṇakāya* does have arising and ceasing.

[Sūtra] When Mahāpratibhāna Buddha arrived, he wished to see the manifested bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). This clarifies that the desire to see the manifested bodies is precisely the desire to recognize that while Śākyamuni’s fundamental essence is one, his traces are manifold.
From the beginning to the end of this chapter, nothing is expressed other than these two meanings.
Now, it is said that although Mahāpratibhāna wished to see many [bodies], the appearance of a single stūpa among the many manifests that the Trace Gate (*śeṣamukha*) of Śākyamuni unites the manifold.
Returning to the One, the Secret manifests the Original Gate as the opening of the Traces to reveal the Source; Mahāpratibhāna wishes to see the manifested bodies,
which signifies that Śākyamuni’s Trace Gate proceeds from the One to bestow the Three Secrets, while the Original Gate proceeds from the One Source to manifest manifold traces.
[Commentary]: It is said that the present Buddha’s single body gathers many bodies as a secret manifestation of non-uniform traces.

In the Gate of Traces (*jimon*), transformation was applied at every joint and the body was divided at every joint; now, the gathering into one [body] is revealed, while the remaining divisions of the many joints are entirely not mentioned, and for this reason it is called "secret.
If this is so, the Gate of Traces would be an incomplete teaching; when will it be further opened?
Consider this "mystery" (mi). [Commentary] It says:
Although many stupas of ancient Buddhas exist, the fact that only one stupa is shown serves to manifest the non-duality of the ultimate principle.

That is to say, if it manifests the Trace Gate (jap-mon), it may be called "manifest"; however, if it manifests the Origin Gate (hon-mon), it should be called "mysterious. This must be reflected upon deeply. (Thus it is said.)

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage "At that time, the Buddha emitted light from his white tuft of hair," some explain it as follows: previously, the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Vehicle were revealed in the first part of the sutra;

now, the provisional and ultimate aspects of the [Buddha's] body are manifested in the latter part of the sutra. Formerly, the two provisional [teachings] covered the two realities, which was likened to being shrouded in defilement and darkness; now, both are abolished.
Since the meanings of both the two provisional [teachings] and the two real [teachings] have been clearly manifested, both are symbolized by the white tuft between the brows;
therefore, it is said that he "emits light from the white tuft. Question: What is designated as "the past"? Answer: That which precedes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the past.

If this is so, then when the *Prajñāpāramitā* emits light from all parts of the body and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* emits light from the mouth, how could there be any obscurity? Furthermore, in analyzing the text of this section, one must break down [these distinctions]. (It is said...)
[The Sūtra] says:
"A single ray of light. Some explain that while the Dharma mounted [by the Buddha] is non-dual, what is now being discussed is the unique nature of the body that mounts it;
therefore, a single ray of light is emitted by both. Since both the Dharma and the person are the Middle Way, a single ray is emitted by both.
The light from between the eyebrows is neither non-existent in the past nor non-existent in the future;
furthermore, as previously refuted (etc.), it is improper to regard the four chapters on the dissemination of the Trace Gate as the "Latter Part Sutra" before the Fundamental Gate has been reached.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions descend to clarify the intent behind their desire to come: they wish to see Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna.
This assembly of the Buddhas of the ten directions achieves two meanings: first, it reveals the reality-body (*dharmakāya*) of Śākyamuni’s manifested trace;
second, it reveals that while the true body (*svabhāvakāya*) of Prabhūtaratna is eternally abiding, his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) undergoes birth and cessation.
[Sūtra]: Regarding the passage "The Sahā world is itself pure," the tenth volume of the *Śāstra* explains: "It is like when a person invites a noble guest, they adorn the place;
the head of a household adorns the entire family; a lord of a kingdom adorns the entire kingdom; a Wheel-Turning King adorns the four continents;
a Brahmā King adorns the three realms; and a Dharma King adorns the ten directions."
[Sūtra]: At that time, each of the Buddhas brought a great Bodhisattva. There are generally two meanings for this:
first, the fruit of the Dharmakāya is non-dual, and the land of the Dharmakāya is likewise one;

second, as for the "one attendant," it is intended to serve as a messenger to open the stūpa, signifying that the Buddhas have gathered like clouds because they wish to open a single Dharmakāya. Thus, they bring one person with them.
[Sūtra] Reaching beneath the jewel trees signifies the meaning of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) as the king of trees.
[Sūtra] Sitting upon the lion throne intends to manifest that the Dharma-body does not fear sentient beings giving rise to doubt or terror;
as before, it now expresses: "I am joyful and fearless."

[Sūtra] "The right finger" refers to the hand's facility, which is to say the application of the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-bala*) for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings.

[Sūtra] "All you sons of good family, each contemplate this carefully" and below; this raises the difficulty of upholding [the precepts]. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, one verse of admonition and exhortation.
The Sūtra says, "O sons of good family, each of you should contemplate this with earnest attention"; this is an admonition. "Therefore, you should resolve to make a vow"; this is an exhortation.
Next, the twelve lines beginning with "Furthermore, in various sūtras" formally present the difficulty of upholding [this teaching] as an incentive for its circulation:

first, the five lines clarify the difficulty of extensive exposition; second, the two lines beginning with "Even if" clarify the difficulty of transcription; third, "If one were to take the great earth... [and so forth].

The final two lines clarify the difficulty of recitation (pāṭha-dūṣaṇa). Although some claim that the following two lines concern the difficulty of chanting (japa-dūṣaṇa), upon examining this text, it is also a statement regarding the difficulty of exposition (deśanā-dūṣaṇa).

The previous [point] was stated in terms of many people, whereas the present [point] is stated in terms of a single person; thus, it is also a difficulty. Fifth, "If one maintains... (the following three lines) concerns the difficulty of questioning the meaning (arthapraśna-dūṣaṇa).
Sixth, "If a person preaches the Dharma... (the following three lines); although some claim these clarify the difficulty of questioning (praśna-dūṣaṇa), I maintain that...

Because upholding [this sutra] is difficult, it says, "if one is able to receive and uphold it. Question: Since there are many people in the present world who uphold this sutra, how can these six kinds of difficulties exist?

Answer: It is because there are six types of people who do not believe in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*: first, those who are greedily attached to the five desires; second, non-Buddhists who cling to various views;
third, followers of the Hīnayāna who cling to provisional teachings and are deluded regarding the ultimate truth; fourth, those who... [text fragment ends].
This sutra refers to those who hear that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is eternal but do not believe it; these people possess five attachments and are deluded regarding their own fundamental nature.

Furthermore, there are those who hold to a mind that perceives existence and cling to this sutra as being definitively heard. Because there are those who give rise to faith through hearing the non-dual and non-triadic [teaching], there are nine points that have not yet been challenged and six points that have been challenged.

Regarding the name Devadatta, "deva" refers to a heavenly being (tian), and "datta" means bestowed (shou). He was the son of King Droṇodana; because he requested [the name] from heaven and heaven bestowed it upon him, he is called Devadatta.

[Commentary]: Regarding the schism of the Saṃgha and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "He instructed the king to kill his father to become the new king, and he intended to kill the Buddha to become the new Buddha.
He even went so far as to demand the followers from the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Foolish man, you are ignorant!
I would not entrust the Saṃgha even to Śāriputra or Maudgalyāyana; how much less to you, a fool who eats the spittle and snot of others? Because of this, [Devadatta] harbored resentment.
The Buddha separately formulated five dharmas to entice the followers of the Buddha. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: first, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*);
second, always begging for food; third, eating in a single sitting; fourth, always sitting in the open air; and fifth, not accepting salt or the five flavors.

This differs from the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, which says [as follows]... While the Buddha was at Rājagṛha on account of certain causes and conditions, he assembled the Saṃgha, and Devadatta rose from his seat and proposed these five dharmas.
Śāriputra said, "Those who tolerate these five matters are [acting according to] the Vinaya. At that time, there were five hundred newly ordained monks who were ignorant;
they cast their voting sticks (*śalākā*). Ānanda rose from his seat and asked, "Who tolerates these five matters that are contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya?

Devadatta addressed those five hundred, saying, "There is no need for the Buddha or the Saṃgha," and he immediately led them away to Gayā, where they performed the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) among themselves. At that time, the various bhikṣus...
He reported these five matters to the Buddha, who said, "This foolish man has extinguished his wholesome mind and will remain in hell for one kalpa without rescue;

I do not see even a hair’s breadth of wholesome merit in him. Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to observe him, and after preaching the Dharma and manifesting supernatural powers, they brought back five hundred followers (and so forth).

[Commentary]: Regarding the causal conditions: in the past he was the teacher of Śākyamuni, while now he is the disciple of Śākyamuni; this difference between teacher and disciple constitutes one world.
In the past, his teaching led immeasurable sentient beings to cultivate goodness, destroy evil, and enter the Truth;

now, by committing an act of rebellion, he causes immeasurable people not to dare commit such rebellion, so that they shall obtain good fruits—this constitutes another world where immeasurable people give rise to wholesome minds.
This refers to the person who possesses the rebellious mind that seeks to destroy [the head]; this is the remedial cultivation of goodness and the realization of principle.

Regarding the "fruit of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-sūtra-phala*): that which has a seed is called *phala* (fruit), while that which lacks a seed is called *lao* (gourd). Furthermore, the fruit of trees is called *phala*, and the fruit of herbs is called *lao*.
[Commentary]: Regarding the grouping of the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) into six: Question:

Since the abandonment of the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) constitutes *dāna* (generosity), why are they not collectively termed *dāna*, and why are only the four [actions] such as killing specifically mentioned? Answer: This is merely a provisional correspondence.

However, speaking from a comprehensive perspective, one should understand that what was asked regarding "not engaging in double-tongued speech" refers to not transmitting the words of others; "not engaging in frivolous speech" refers to subtle or refined speech; and so forth.
"Greed is merely dispersion," and so forth. [Commentary:
Regarding "the first pair of antidotes" and so on: as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, generosity counteracts stinginess and greed; ethical discipline counteracts the violation of precepts;
patience counteracts anger; diligence counteracts laziness; meditative concentration counteracts a distracted mind; and wisdom counteracts ignorance.

[Commentary: Regarding "harmonizing the faculties to know the dharma-realm": it is through the mental consciousness that one knows the dharma-realm; this is called the "Dharma-seat. That which knows the dharma-realm is the capacity for knowing, which is precisely *prajñā*. [Commentary:

Regarding "the retribution of meditative concentration reaching the destruction of afflictions": this refers to the two fulfillments (*paripūri*) of the untainted (*anāsrava*) state beneath the Bodhi tree; therefore, it is so stated.
Cutting off delusions.
[Commentary: From "body and mind unmoving" up to "the practitioner does not see," this means that one does not perceive the body that practices diligence nor the mind that practices it;
when both are non-dispersed, it is called "non-action. One who contemplates in this way is called diligent. It is neither distracted nor savoring.

In distraction there is no confusion, and in concentration there is no dullness; all is empty and like an illusion. That fools and the wise are illusory transformations is likewise identical to emptiness.
[Commentary: One who attains a mind free from entanglements takes precepts as liberation; thus there are no entanglements, or rather, the mind is not that which is entangled.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the sphere of practicing loving-kindness": meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the sphere of loving-kindness; since loving-kindness relies upon meditative concentration, practicing this concentration now is precisely practicing the sphere of loving-kindness. [Commentary]:

Regarding "absence of remorse and feverish distress": because one has attained meditative concentration, the mind is free from remorse regarding the concentration and free from the affliction of feverish distress, thereby guarding all...

The "roots" refer to the six sense faculties being unstained by the six objects of sensory dust. "Obtaining the joy of non-nourishment" means that one takes the delight of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prīti*) as food and does not rely on solid food;

thus, it is called "joy. It is the departure from craving and the greed of the desire realm. "Practicing meditation without emptiness" means arising of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) based upon meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"Liberation from Māra" means being free from the bonds of the sixth celestial Māra of the desire realm. "Abiding securely in the Buddha-realm" refers to dwelling in the sphere of the Buddhas.
Cultivating dhyāna with the aspiration for its fruits means that when liberation is matured, one successively abandons the three delusions.
[Commentary] Regarding the ten benefits of prajñā: because it sweeps away attachments to the previous five perfections, it is said to be "non-appropriating" (*anupādāna*), and so forth.

"Not being separated from diligence of body and mind" means not giving rise to partiality toward either body or mind; thus it is called "not being separated. It must necessarily involve simultaneous diligence, which gives rise to increase.
The "superior compassion" is precisely the "conditionless" (anālambana) [compassion].

[The Commentary] states: "Subsequently receiving the bliss of humans, devas, and nirvana"—the sequence of the proximate fruit (human and deva realms) and the ultimate fruit (nirvana) is analogous throughout.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "if one cultivates the body" up to "wisdom": the first four of the six perfections (pāramitās) cultivate the body; the fifth cultivates the mind; and the sixth cultivates wisdom. The *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-śāstra* states:
"The dāna of material goods and fearlessness, as well as śīla, kṣānti, and vīrya, constitute 'provisioning' (sambhāra); dhyāna and prajñā constitute the 'Dharma'.
As for "walking and sitting," this refers to contemplating the ultimate truth (paramārtha) through the four modes of deportment, abandoning the two extremes.

Abandoning objective referents and not giving rise to a mind of the two extremes is called "not transgressing. Regarding the middle way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), the metaphor of "not giving rise to a mind of existence or non-existence" means being free from "sores" (*vraṇa*).
A "sore" is a metaphor for injury and affliction; being "without sores" (*nirvraṇa*) is a metaphor for the absence of such injury.

Not abandoning the middle way is called "not abandoning," which means departing from the two extreme views and abiding in the middle way. One is not negligent regarding these matters. [In the ninth...]

The realm (*dhātu*) refers to the Buddha-realm. Regarding the non-arising nature of all phenomena, by analogy with the five aggregates (*skandha*) and eighteen realms (*dhātu*), one realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) in all cases [as indicated by "etc."].

[Commentary]: As for "the abandonment of the aggregates is *dāna*": in a single thought-moment, the ten realms are called "aggregates"; thus, not giving rise to thoughts of resentment toward the aggregates is *dāna*.
Not giving rise to the contemplations of the three preceding teachings is called the "notion of enmity.

"Not being ablaze" means not creating the causes for the aggregates of the nine realms within the aggregates of the Buddha-realm, thereby not receiving future aggregates; this is what is meant by "not being ablaze."

[Commentary]: Regarding "generosity" (dāna) as the relinquishing of the realms, it refers to relinquishing the eighteen elements within the nine dharma-realms. Not being disturbed or turbid by these nine realms is called "ethical discipline" (śīla).

[Commentary]: Regarding the relinquishing of causes and conditions within the realms, each of the nine dharma-realms contains the three categories of eighteen elements: sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses.
When causes and conditions combine, there is the grasping of objects and so forth; now, by contemplating the principle alone to dissolve those causes and conditions, it is called "relinquishing.
[Commentary] It is like a phantom person; among the twenty-five samādhis, that which is contemplated through the "phantom-like samādhi" is named "phantom."
[This is] the perception.

[Commentary: In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the fundamental characteristic of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), where the path of teaching relies on conditions to cultivate the knowledge of all modes as the cause.

In the Tripitaka Teaching (*zangjiao*), it is based on merit; furthermore, the first three teachings generally rely on cultivation to attain it. One who is a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*) brings it forth, while one who is a person of the Separate Teaching ascends to it.

The earth also manifests [these marks]; according to the *Śāstra* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), it is said that they are attained through the path of teaching (*śrutamārga*), yet it is stated that they are cultivated and attained (*bhāvanāprāpta*).

The eighth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: "The feet are firmly established and immovable; this is called the mark of the firm establishment of the feet. In the present text, "the soles of the feet are as level as the bottom of a casket" means the bottom of a mirror-casket (*darpaṇa-peṭaka*).
The *Sāncāng* (Three Cais) states: "The base of a mirror vessel is square. Regarding the "thousand-spoked wheels," there are a thousand spokes upon the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet.
The wheels are complete and clearly manifest like the impressions on a seal.
[Commentary] Regarding the "round and straight body": the height of the body is seven cubits; because it is not crooked, it is called the major mark of being "round and straight."
[Commentary: The webbed membrane and the softness are like those of a king of geese; the lines are clearly defined as if made of pure gold.
Because one observes the fibers, it is called the mark of the webbed hands and feet (*pāṇipādajāla-lakṣaṇa*) and the mark of softness (*mṛdu-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the mark of softness, it is like *tūla* tree cotton, which is called "soft" because the cotton emerges from it like willow fluff; this refers to the name of the *tūla* tree.
[Commentary]: "Deer-calf calves" means that the calves are uniform and straight, gradually becoming thicker like those of the *eṇeya* deer; therefore, it is called the mark of the deer-calf calves.

Regarding the "Ten Powers" (*daśabala*) in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, chapter ten, it says: "These so-called Ten Powers are termed 'powers' because they assist and sustain one's vital energy, being inexhaustible and incapable of being obstructed or destroyed.
Although there are ten names, they are in reality a single wisdom that takes [all things] as its object."
It is called the "Ten Powers" because of ten matters. The Buddha’s wisdom takes all matters as its object and should be immeasurable;
however, it is only ten, for these ten powers are sufficient to deliver sentient beings.

[Sūtra]: It says, "At that time, from the Heavenly Kings down to those who have attained non-retrogression. This scriptural passage is narrow; yet, that transformation fully possesses the teachings of the five periods.
When it mentions Arhats up to those with the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), this refers to the first and last of the two flavors.
However, within the examples of the first and last flavors, there should likewise be the remaining three flavors.

[The Sūtra] states: "Hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* leads one before the Buddhas of the ten directions. This sūtra also includes rebirth in the Western Land as well as in the palace of Maitreya;
these are all in accordance with the vows of sentient beings.
[Sūtra] Regarding the five obstacles of the female body, the *Chāorì sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Sun’s Transcendence) states that the Elder Bhikṣu addressed Huìshī, saying:
"One cannot attain the Buddha-way in a female body because of three matters that obstruct and five matters that hinder it. What are the three? They are:

when at home one is constrained by one's parents; upon marriage one is constrained by one's husband; and upon the husband's death one is constrained by one's son—these are likewise as prescribed in secular books."
Regarding the meaning of following [the path], the five obstacles are stated as follows: first, one cannot become a Brahmā;
for one must uphold pure conduct, practice stainless deeds, cultivate the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), and properly follow the four dhyānas to ascend to the Brahma-heaven.

If one is licentious and unrestrained, one becomes a woman. Second, one cannot become Śakra; for one who is courageous and has few desires becomes Śakra, whereas one who is full of various evils [cannot].

Furthermore, there are three conditions by which a woman cannot become a Māra-king: she must be fully endowed with the ten wholesome paths of action, revere the Triple Gem, and serve her parents with humility, obedience, and devoted attendance;
only then may she become a Māra-king. If she is arrogant, disrespectful, and disobedient, and she destroys and loses the True Teaching, she remains a woman.

Fourth, there are four conditions by which a woman cannot become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin): she must practice the Bodhisattva path, have compassion for all living beings, and make offerings [to the Buddhas].
The Three Honored Ones, the former sages, and the teachers were once wheel-turning kings who ruled over the four continents and practiced the ten wholesome deeds, honoring morality and virtue.
As wheel-turning kings, they lacked pure conduct; thus, there are five reasons why women cannot become Buddhas.

Even if one practices the bodhisattva mind, takes pity on all beings, and even realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one may then attain Buddhahood; yet for a woman, [these conditions are not met].
Regarding this matter,
the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta* [Commentary] cites the case of Piṇḍola knowing that [the king] had lost his kingdom seven years prior; the *Caturvarga-vinaya* states that King Udayana of Kauśāmbī...
King Dāyana was a close friend and acquaintance of Piṇḍola. Every morning and evening, he would go to visit him.

One day, having heard the words of wicked people, the king saw Piṇḍola but did not rise when the king approached. The king then replied, "Come again tomorrow; if you still do not rise, I shall take your life.
He went as he had been told, and Piṇḍola thought to himself: "The king comes with an evil mind. If I do not..."
"If I rise, they will surely take my life; if I do not, I shall fall into hell for having deceived the king. If I rise now, I shall lose my seven-year reign.

Thinking thus and weighing the light against the heavy, he resolved, "I would rather lose my kingdom than commit a grave offense," and so he rose to welcome and escort the king. The king then asked him, "For what reason did you rise?
He replied, "Whether I rise or do not rise, it is all for the sake of Your Majesty. The king asked, "Why are you doing this for me? He then related everything as it had happened before.

The King of Meaning asked, "In how many days shall he perish? He replied, "Seven days from now. The king then returned to his kingdom, repaired the city walls and moats, and prepared his military regalia.
On the seventh day, saying that the śramaṇa’s words were false, he entered the Ganges with his court ladies and traveled by boat for recreation.
At that time, the kingdom of the Yakṣa Eyi had not seen rain for seven years; King Brahmadatta of Po-lo-shu-ti went to Magadha.
The king went to King Bimbisāra and requested a water-extracting jewel, but failing to obtain it, he returned.
Hearing that King Udayana was sporting with his court ladies in the water, he secretly released a white elephant into the water to draw him out.

King Udayana, thinking it was a wild elephant, praised its training methods, recited incantations, and played the lute as he advanced to capture it. Having gained the advantage, [the king] bound its feet.

After returning to his country, he spent seven years [in seclusion] (and so forth). Master Chou of Shaolin Monastery during the Northern Qi dynasty was held in high esteem by the Prince of Qi, who personally visited the master’s dwelling to protect his longevity and did not rise to greet him or see him off. The Prince harbored secret resentment and thought, "I shall test him again tomorrow;
if he still does not rise, I shall take his life. Foreknowing the Prince's thought, the master immediately rose to greet and see him off. The Prince, too...
He questioned him, and the answer was that whether he arose or did not arise, it was all for the sake of the King; once the King had learned this, he passed away at the appointed time.
Such a precedent has never been heard of, and it is improper for one not to arise [to greet the King] (and so forth).

[Commentary] The verse consists of twenty lines. Regarding the phrase "not divided into minute parts": the first seventeen lines concern the robe of patience (*kṣānti-vastra*). This is divided into two sections.
First, one line provides a general heading for the vow to propagate the sutra. Second, sixteen lines specifically address wearing the robe of patience to propagate the sutra in an evil age.

Within this section, there are further two parts: first, five lines beginning with "There are those... explicitly clarify the endurance of evil; second, two lines beginning with "And then... [continue the explanation].

Regarding the first of the five initial verses on the arising of evil: the first verse concerns the endurance of the three types of evil karma; this refers to external evil and the person of external evil.
Following the phrase "in a degenerate age," the next verse concerns those who are arrogant among renunciants.

The third section, beginning with "There may be some forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*)," consists of the following three verses, which encompass all types of evil persons among renunciants. Subsequently, the section beginning with "And then, acting in such a way" constitutes the second [part].

The explicit explanation of the arising of evil has two parts: first, the explanation of the arising of slander; second, from "In the turbid kalpa" onwards, the explanation of the reasons for such slander.

The first part also has two sections: first, slander through malicious speech; second, slander through feigned virtuous speech. The first section further has three parts. The first two lines concern the private disparagement of the Dharma and the person.
Disparaging the Dharma refers to the polemical arguments of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); disparaging the person refers to those who are heterodox.
Next, the two lines following "Always among the great assembly" refer to those who destroy the Dharma and slander others in the presence of the public.

The third line, "We respectfully [rely on] the Buddha," clarifies that Bodhisattvas are able to endure. Regarding the initial question: since it was previously stated that they engage in debate with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), how can it later be said that they compose this sūtra themselves?
The answer is that the initial statement refers to expounding upon the eighteen scriptures of the non-Buddhists as being the works of non-Buddhists; furthermore, there is no contradiction.
Because this is taught, it is said that this scripture was composed by oneself; it is not the internal teaching (Buddhist doctrine), as its principles are identical to those of the non-Buddhists.
Next, for the sake of these [beings], the second section provides "wholesome words" to refute [the slander]. This is further divided into two parts:

the first half-verse clarifies the arising of the slander, and the subsequent half-verse clarifies the capacity for endurance. Regarding the phrase "you are all Buddhas," those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) consider this to be mere study.
Those of the Mahāyāna, who clearly understand that all dharmas are fundamentally quiescent and devoid of dual characteristics, speak thus:
"If sentient beings and the Buddha are without dual characteristics, then you are yourself the Buddha. This is called the offense of disparagement.
Next, regarding the second explanation of the reasons for slandering and reviling during the evil world of the *kaṣāya* age, there are generally two causes for why wicked people slander [the Dharma].
Regarding the first meaning: external māras enter the body and cause one to slander [the Mahāyāna]; this consists of three lines of text. Regarding the second:
because of internal ignorance, one does not know that the Hīnayāna is a provisional means (upāya), and thus clings to it while slandering the Mahāyāna; this consists of two and a half lines of text.
The above concludes the section on the robe of patience (*kṣānti-vastra*); the remaining two [sections] are as explained in the commentary (*śāstra*). (Et cetera.)

[Commentary on] the Chapter on Peaceful and Joyful Practice: There are two interpretations of "peaceful and joyful practice": first, that peace and joy are themselves the practice; second, that it is the practice for the sake of peace and joy.
Peace and joy constitute the fruit, while the practice constitutes the cause of that fruit.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "cultivating and attaining that which accords with conditions and responds to things": this refers to cultivating the three virtues (san-de) in contrast to their inherent nature (xing).

To clarify cultivation through nature, it is understood as being common to both delusion and awakening, common to both sages and ordinary beings, common to both cause and fruit, and common to both the revealed and unrevealed [teachings], as explained previously.

This is as stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter: that the three truths do not descend for the sake of ordinary beings, nor are they superior for the sake of sages, and so forth. If we consider this in terms of...
Regarding the cultivation and attainment of the "following names to reach objects," there are ten sets of three dharmas;

as explained in the *Xuan* commentary on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, although their names vary, their essence is no different. Therefore, the three metaphors of the "name," "room," and so forth, refute the thirteen [objections] (and so on).

As for the statement "Śākyamuni is in the empty seat," this expresses the seat by way of its location, the emptiness. Regarding "the robe entering the stūpa," this is spoken from the perspective of that which enters.
The stūpa where the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa in his physical body is the robe of patience (*kṣānti*).

The chamber for propagating the sūtras is called a "chamber" because one preaches the Dharma everywhere therein, thereby uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness. Furthermore, the robe of Many Treasures is described from the perspective of that which it covers;

what is covered is the *dharmakāya*, and what covers it is the robe of patience. Thus, by naming the means of manifestation after that which is manifested, it is called a "robe. As for the seat of Śākyamuni:
That which gives rise to the manifest [form] (vijñapti) and the wisdom that gives rise to the manifest form belongs to the Saṃbhogakāya.

As for the chamber of the emanation bodies (nirmāṇakāya), because it is called "liberation" (vimukti) in the sense of taming sentient beings, it belongs to the Nirmāṇakāya. All other cases should be understood accordingly (*etc.*).

[Commentary] Regarding the statement "within this, there are five [sections]," one should first explain the names according to the general pattern of the various chapters, and then explain the meanings based on the text.
Of these five, the first is the explanation of the name, and the latter four are the explanation of the meaning.

[Commentary: "Clothed in the Tathāgata and reaching peace" differs from what preceded. Previously, it was the Dharma-body attained through cultivation, adorned by meditative concentration and wisdom, which served as the robe;
now, it refers to the Dharma-body of innate virtue being clothed in the robe of patience attained through cultivation, hence it is called "peace.
"Entering the Tathāgata’s chamber and delighting in the mind" means to be free from the two types of death.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the sick child's room": in the *Xuánwén*, it is explained that "sick child" refers to the patient, while "room" refers to the object of patience (*kṣānti*), which is taken as the garment corresponding to the capacity for patience.
[Sūtra]: "Abiding on the ground of patience. Patience is the practice to be performed; the "ground" is the realm of the true reality (*dharmatā*) upon which one relies.
Because the abiding on the ground of the practice of patience encompasses both the subject (the capacity) and the object (the realm), it is so described.

[Commentary: As for "not ending," according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the principle of the samādhis as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is called "peaceful bliss" (*anābhirati*).

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the "Dharma-gate" (*dharmamukha*), the text contains three parts: the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. First is the introduction; second, from "Peaceful Bliss" downward is the explanation;

third, "This is the Dharma-gate" is the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are again two parts: first, from "Peaceful Bliss" downward is the listing of names; second, from "Immovable" downward is the explanation.
As the text says (and so forth). [Commentary:

That which contemplates all things up to their ultimate marks is the wisdom that guides; because it guides the myriad practices toward the true reality mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is called "Vīrya" (Diligence).
[Commentary] Regarding the passage "He reaches the tree," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, fascicle ten, states: Furthermore, good son, as I said in a verse in the past:
"All rivers must have bends; all thickets must be called trees."
"All women are necessarily full of guile; all those who possess sovereign power necessarily experience peace and happiness.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke these verses:
Not all rivers necessarily have bends; not all forests are entirely composed of trees;
not all women necessarily harbor deceit; and not all who possess sovereignty necessarily experience pleasure.

These are the verses spoken by the Buddha, whose meaning is intentional (*sāvaśeṣārtha*). Even in that continent where there are rivers, some are straight and not crooked, as is illustrated by this analogy.
The cord and ink-line extend straight into the Western Sea; furthermore, the precious trees of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli are also called "forests";
moreover, there are women who delight in upholding the prohibitions and precepts, whose merit is perfected, and who possess great compassion;
and even the various devas such as Brahmā and Śakra, though they have attained sovereignty, are all impermanent and possess only a remainder [of suffering], and so forth.

【Commentary】 Regarding "the practice of long-form [recitation] and so forth": among the aforementioned headings, it was termed "methods" (*fangfa*); in this current explanation, it is termed "practice" (*xiuxing*).
Because one initiates action in accordance with the Dharma, the former is called "methods" and the latter is called "practice"; though the names differ, the meaning is the same.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the first stage of the inner ordinary person (ābhyantarapṛthagjana) is called the "place of practice" (*caryā-bhūmi*), this is explained according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyākaraṇa*).

The thirty minds are termed "inner ordinary persons," while the final mind of the stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is termed the "near place" (*upaniṣad-bhūmi*) because it is proximate to the first ground (*bhūmi*). As for the reference to the preceding chapter, it points to the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*), which cites being near *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as proof.

[Commentary: Regarding the clarification of the two emptinesses through the categories of the real and the conventional, and the provisional and the real: "real and conventional" refers to the objects (*viṣaya*), while "provisional and real" refers to the wisdom (*jñāna*).

Alternatively, in relation to the Two Patiences (*kṣānti*) of the Hīnayāna, both are the patience regarding arising (*utpatti-kṣānti*); whereas in the Mahāyāna, the ultimate meaning of the Middle Way is the patience regarding dharmas (*dharma-kṣānti*).
Although the name "patience regarding arising" is established based on the real and the conventional, because arising is itself dharma, it is said that "all see the Middle Way."
[Commentary]: "Both the beginning and the end are cessation" means that at the initial stage of the five ranks, one ceases through the practice of the ten practices;

from the entry into the six faculties up to Equal Enlightenment, one ceases through the practice of entering Wondrous Enlightenment. In all these cases, because the practice accords with principle, it is called "cessation," yet it does not mean that one does not practice at all.

[Commentary]: Regarding the question, "Why is it called 'near-abode' (*upaniṣad*)?", all [the texts] state that these assist meditation (*vipaśyanā*). The Record says: "The 'place of practice' (*caryā-sthāna*) is the primary practice, while the 'near-abodes' are the auxiliary practices;
thus, the primary and auxiliary are practiced in combination. Now, I fear this may not be the case, for all [texts] state they assist meditation.

Meditation is the primary practice. Within the preceding "place of practice," there are three types of practice: *śamatha*, compassion (*karuṇā*), and loving-kindness (*maitrī*). That is to say, the practice of *śamatha* is itself the practice.

The practice of the contemplation of the true nature of reality (*tattva-śamatha-vipaśyanā*) is neither practice nor non-practice; this is the cessation of the two extremes. The practice of compassion is non-practice as practice;
this is the cessation that accords with conditions (*anupratyaya-śamatha*). These are collectively termed "cessation" (*śamatha*).

Now, within the proximate stage (*upasthāna*), there are likewise three types by analogy, which are collectively termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). Therefore, what was stated above directly corresponds to these three meanings. As for the statement that these words are attached to the precepts (*śīla*):
First, regarding the distant sphere, the two practices of śamatha and vipaśyanā within bodily karma constitute the two proximate practices.

Next, regarding the near sphere, the two practices of loving-kindness and compassion constitute the two proximate practices. Finally, regarding the sphere that is neither distant nor near, the practice of vipaśyanā constitutes the two proximate practices.

Although there are differences in their extensive and concise formulations, they are essentially comprised of the three types of śamatha, the three types of vipaśyanā, and the three types of loving-kindness and compassion as guides.
The physical actions are, in brief, entirely right conduct; they rely upon the three [categories] beginning with morality as their support (reflect on this).

[Commentary]: Regarding "first, power and influence," etc.: generally, one avoids ten conditions. First, avoiding the king means avoiding the condition of pride. Second, avoiding wicked people means avoiding the condition of false views.
For a person who has only recently begun their practice, they are unable to maintain an equal contemplation of the false and the true; therefore, they should not [associate with them].
The nearby commentary states that because one has not yet been able to regard heaven and earth as a single finger and all things as one, it is said that one "should not" [follow] the *Lokāyata*.
Some say it is translated as "worldly conduct," while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* calls it "praising and chanting in sequence.
As for "contrary *Lokāyata*," this is translated as "contrary worldly conduct," while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* calls it "associating with and practicing worldly customs."
Third, those who have abandoned the conditions for fierce and dangerous games, because these lead to distraction;
"Nara" is translated here as "Power," and the commentary notes that it refers to physical form in relation to arts and so forth, whereby the body is painted with various colors to make it variegated.
Fourth, the Caṇḍālas, who have abandoned the conditions for evil karma; "Caṇḍāla" means "Terrifying" or "Evil Sinner," referring to those of the lowest caste. Fifth, those of the Two Vehicles.
Those who have turned away from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and are practitioners beginning their journey must ensure that the Bodhisattva’s great illumination is not yet perfected;

for fear they might become defiled by the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, one should maintain a separation between voice and form and avoid sharing in their daily conduct. If they should come at times, preach the Dharma to them as appropriate, provided they harbor no expectations.

If there is a karmic affinity or resonance, then preach the Dharma for them, but do not do so for the sake of fame or profit. Those who are free from the six desires and thoughts are separated [from such defilements].

Regarding "afflicted by desire": those aged five years and younger are called "little girls" (*kumārikā*); they are not permitted to marry and are termed "virgins" (*kanyā*) because they have not yet gone out [of the house].
Furthermore, those who resolve not to marry are also termed "virgins. Regarding the "seven types of non-males" (*ṣaṇḍha*): this refers to those who lack the capacity for sexual intercourse.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the first of the seven dharmas consists of: first, those born as non-males (*jāti-ṣaṇḍha*); second, those who are non-males for half a month (*pakṣa-ṣaṇḍha*).

1. The impotent through birth (*jāti-paṇḍaka*); 2. the impotent through envy (*īrṣyā-paṇḍaka*); 3. the impotent through castration (*cheda-paṇḍaka*); 4. the impotent through loss of semen (*śukra-paṇḍaka*); and 5. the impotent through disease (*roga-paṇḍaka*).

Furthermore, regarding "heavenly punishment" (*deva-daṇḍa*), it refers to those whose nature is transformed by half. "Nature" (*svabhāva*) means one who is naturally incapable from birth; the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains this as "born.

Second, "punishment" (*daṇḍa*) refers to being subjected to physical mutilation; the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains this as "severing. Third, "transformation" (*parivarta*) refers to envy; the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains that "envy" means [envying] oneself or others. Fourth, "transformation" (*parivarta*) refers to... [text ends].
1. Being unable to transform from female to male; 2. The "five-and-a-half" [types of impotent men], namely those who are male for half the month and impotent for the other half;
3. The eighth: distant causes for harm, as the Sūtra says: "One should not enter the homes of others alone"; 4. The ninth: distant causes for reproach, as the Sūtra says:
"If one preaches the Dharma to women, it may give rise to desire in them"; 5. The tenth: distancing oneself from keeping livestock.
Regarding the "condition" (*pratyaya*), the Sūtra states: "One should not take pleasure in keeping young disciples. [Commentary] As for "the nameless":
if one tentatively speaks of the Middle Way, it further possesses emptiness and the provisional; if one tentatively speaks of emptiness and the provisional, their essence is again the Middle;

if one tentatively speaks of possessing these three essences, they are in fact only one; if one tentatively speaks of this single essence, it necessarily possesses the three; and if one speaks of the three simultaneously, [they are likewise so].
The single essence is eternally neither three nor one; yet, when we speak of it as neither three nor one, it constantly illuminates the three and the one.
When we speak of it as the essence, it constantly gives rise to function, and that function is itself eternally quiescent. Therefore, it cannot be named; to name it otherwise is a misunderstanding.
To claim that names cannot name it is merely to grasp at emptiness—how does this differ from the Lesser Vehicle? (and so forth).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "birth and death arise from the causes and conditions of delusion": taking contaminated karma as the cause and afflictions as the condition, one brings about the fruit of maturation (vipāka) consisting of suffering within the five destinies;
this is called birth and death, which refers to the phenomena produced. Regarding the statement that "Nirvana arises from the understanding of causes and conditions":
taking the capacity for the untainted (anāsrava) as the cause and the Tathāgata’s teaching as the condition, one attains the fruit of the untainted; this is called Nirvana.
Nirvāṇa is a produced phenomenon. [Commentary:
The phrase "is said to arise from inversion" means that, as stated below, it arises from inversion; thus, "is said" refers to arising.
Because there are two extremes due to inversion, one thereby attains liberation from those two extremes.
[Commentary]: It is not strictly necessary to say "perversion" (viparyāsa), because the teachings on the two extremes mentioned above all constitute the inconceivable teaching of the three truths;
thus, they are called "wondrous teachings. However, the subsequent text differs from what precedes it for this reason.

[Commentary] Regarding "the faculty and the speech are pervasive": the faculty is pervasive across the nine realms and both extremes; the speech is restricted, being limited to the principles of emptiness and the provisional.
However, the reality of emptiness and the provisional is also pervasive across the nine realms.

[Commentary] Regarding "there is nothing to be separated or combined": this is not like the conditions where one separates from two objects and subsequently explains their combination into a single delusion.
The first is the realm of the two extremes; the third is the realm of the three truths. Now, regarding the phrase "Eternal and Blissful," there is nothing to be separated or combined.

[Commentary] "Non-turning" refers to: 1) the emptiness of emptiness (kong-kong), 2) the specific emptiness of emptiness (kong-kong bie), 3) the general emptiness of emptiness (kong-kong tong), 4) the treasury of emptiness of emptiness (kong-kong zang), and 5) the external emptiness of emptiness (kong-kong wai).
"The Path cuts off views and perceives emptiness.
[Commentary] Regarding the fact that the sequence is omitted in this verse: the tenth stage, "Supporting Life," is missing; the first stage, "Initial Entry," is abbreviated;

and the subsequent fourteen stages are condensed into three. The first half-verse provides a dual heading for the practice and its proximity, while the following twelve and a half lines provide the explanation.

Regarding "practicing near the three," this refers to the first line of the verse which concludes the section on proximity. Within the second explanation, the phrase "always remaining far from" constitutes the first [avoidance];
"the powerful, the fierce, and the dangerous" constitutes the third avoidance; "those who play with the *caṇḍālas*" constitutes the fourth avoidance;
and "the killers, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and the *brahmins*" constitutes the second avoidance of wicked persons.
The phrase "nor do they associate with the Dharma" and the following two lines constitute the fifth [point]: being free from deep attachment to the Two Vehicles and the five desires.
The following three lines and one phrase constitute the sixth: being free from the notion of desire and various forms of impotence.

The following three phrases constitute the seventh: being free from impotence. Furthermore, the following five phrases are a reiteration of being free from killing; the final two phrases are a further reiteration.
The single phrase "Clearly abandon thoughts of desire; do not associate with them" is the conclusion regarding the second [point], selling one's physical beauty.

The two phrases beginning with "fierce and dangerous" are a reiteration of the previous "fierce and dangerous" point. The two phrases beginning with "all those courtesans" are a reiteration of the previous "abandon thoughts of desire.
The line beginning with "Do not go alone" is the ninth [point], and the line beginning with "entering a village" is the tenth.
Eighth, because they are free from harm and danger, it is called "not sequential. [Commentary]:

This is also the sphere of activity for the realization of the emptiness of persons. Regarding the previous passage on the sphere of activity, it says: "Abiding in the ground of patience, gentle, compliant, and not impetuous, their minds are not startled.
This refers to the patience arising from the emptiness of persons; now, as one draws near, one is free from the ten kinds of afflictive disturbances.
It is also said "also" because one gives rise to the patience regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-kṣānti*).

[Commentary: Taking the essential meaning, it encompasses the three aspects of the "near-dwelling" (*upaniṣad*): constantly delighting in seated meditation, dwelling in a secluded place, and cultivating the gathering and restraining of the mind—these are called the three aspects.
By means of these three aspects of the near-dwelling, one is externally able to remain free from the ten disturbances.
[Sūtra] *Tian* (pronounced tú jiàn or jué jiàn) means to hunt wild birds and beasts; it refers to holding them by hand. It is not what is used today.
*Yu* (pronounced yǔ jū) also means to capture.
[Sūtra] "Què" (pronounced *kǔ huí*) means executioner; "huì" (pronounced *gǔ wài*) means to butcher.
[Sūtra] A "lǐ" (village) consists of five households making a "líng" (neighborhood), and five "líng" making a "lǐ. Furthermore, those who engage in hunting and fishing:
killing on land is called hunting (*tiánliè*); killing in water is called fishing (*yúchǔ*); and killing in the air is called trapping (*bǔ*).

[Commentary]: Vaiśeṣika (Vaiśeṣika) is here translated as "Unconquerable" (Mu-sheng). It takes the six categories (*ṣat-tattva*) as its fundamental tenets: 1. **Dravya-tattva** (translated as *zhuti* or "Principal Category"):

This refers to earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, the universal self (*ātman*), and the internal organ (*manas*). These nine are called the "Principal Categories" because they serve as the substrata for all things; the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* calls them the "real category" (*dravya-pada*). 2. **Guṇa-tattva** (translated as *yi-ti* or "Dependent Category"):

This refers to color, sound, fragrance, [taste, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort]. These sixteen are called the "Dependent Category" because they depend upon the Principal Categories. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* calls this the "quality category" (*guṇa-pada*). ... [The text continues with further categories] ... taste, smell, [and so forth].

1. The Truth of Taste, Touch, Number, Measure, Unity, Diversity, Separation, Conjunction, Beauty, Ugliness, Suffering, Pleasure, Aversion, and Affection—because these depend upon the aforementioned nine categories, they are called the "Truth of Dependence" (*āśraya-satya*);
in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this is termed the "category of qualities" (*guṇa-pada*). 2. The Truth of Karma (*karma-satya*), here translated as the "Truth of Action":

this refers to such things as looking up and down, bending and stretching, coming and going, and moving slowly or quickly; in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this is termed the "category of action" (*karman-pada*). 3. The Truth of Samaya (*samaya-satya*), here translated as "Totality."

1. *Samyaktva-satya* (the truth of common characteristics): This refers to the generalization of all phenomena (*dharmas*) as "existence" (*asti*). It signifies that within the three categories of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karma*), there is no sense in which they are non-existent;

this is the "phrase of existence. 2. *Vaiśeṣika-satya* (the truth of specific characteristics): This refers to the myriad phenomena of the universe, each of which is distinct from the others. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states, this is the "phrase of identity and difference.

3. *Apratisaṃkhyā-satya* (the truth of non-conjunction): This refers to the formation of a jar from constituent particles (*dust*). It signifies that the parts do not combine with one another to form a single, unified whole.
[The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*] states: "They do not obstruct one another;
this is the phrase 'conjunction' (*saṃyoga*), etc. [The *Śāstra*] says: "From Kapila to the twenty-five principles (*tattva*). The old transcription "Kapila" is an error.

*Sāṃkhya* is translated here as "Number-Theory" (*Shùlùn*). It is so named because wisdom (*prajñā*) can enumerate and measure all phenomena; thus it is called "Number" (*sāṃkhya*). From this enumeration, the treatise (*śāstra*) arises.
Therefore it is called Sāṃkhya. Furthermore, because calculation (*saṃkhyā*) can produce a treatise (*śāstra*), it is also termed Sāṃkhya.
In ancient times there was a seer named Kapila—translated here as "Yellow-Red"—referring to one whose head was yellow and whose hair was red. This seer received his name from his physical appearance;
while absorbed in meditative concentration, he realized the meaning of the twenty-five *tattvas*. Eventually, he transformed into a blue stone, as detailed in the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*.
The "Exposition" (Yùnmíng) states that the twenty-fifth [principle] is the *svabhāva* (self-nature), which is also called the three qualities (*guṇas*:

*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*), and is also termed *prakṛti* (the primordial source). This is because when the twenty-five principles have not yet undergone transformation, [the self-nature] lies latent within them.
It is called "self-nature" because it serves as the self-nature for the twenty-five principles. Master Yuǎn says: "It attains the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*)."

He perceives eighty thousand kalpas, but beyond eighty thousand kalpas he does not see; he then asserts that there must not be a lack of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and that there must be a latent nature (*mṛtyu-bhava* or *avyakta-svabhāva*) from which real cognition subsequently arises.
Following this, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises, and from this, the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) arises.

From this "I," two kinds of phenomena arise: first, material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), which consist of twenty-one types, namely: the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*), and the five faculties of perception (*pañca-indriya*).

The faculties of action (*karmendriya*) refer to the hands, feet, mouth, the male and female organs, the organ of excretion, and the mind-faculty (*manas*), making eleven; together with the five sense-faculties and the life-faculty, they constitute twenty-two.

Regarding the mental factors (*caitasika*), there are three types: defiled, coarse, and dark—also called "bold," "coarse," and "dark"—which are precisely the three poisons of greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*).
When the three cravings arise in the mind, one feels love for the mother and hatred for the father; being obscured by this hatred, one fails to understand, which constitutes delusion. First.
